#1 10. Reserving 2. Gross premium valuation What are the features of the gross premium method? 0.7765

2. Gross premium valuation — What are the features of the gross premium method?:

  • Liabilities: All liabilities to policyholders arising from the contract should be allowed for:
  • Future expenses
  • Future benefits and expected future bonuses
  • Guarantees and options
  • Guaranteed surrender values (the reserve > surrender value)
  • Future office premiums
  • Term: Projection to end of policy duration
  • Assumptions:
  • Mortality rates and lapse rates, based on the policyholder profile
  • Discount rate based on the yields of assets matching the liabilities or the risk-free rate (market-consistent valuation)
  • Negative reserves: realistic basis could produce negative reserves, however negative reserves are zeroised for solvency purposes
  • Sensitivity: Sensitive to changes in the valuation basis, because the office premium used is based on initial pricing basis
  • Surplus emergence: Profit emerges gradually over the duration, the valuation discount rate must be consistent with future bonus rates
#2 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7720

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#3 10. Reserving 2. Gross premium valuation What is the GPV formula method? 0.7593

2. Gross premium valuation — What is the GPV formula method?:

For a standard regular premium without-profits endowment assurance, the reserve at duration _t_ is expressed as:


$$V_t = SA \cdot A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}} + RE \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}} - P' \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$$


  • SA (Sum Assured): The contractual benefit to be paid.
  • RE (Renewal Expenses): The expected future costs to maintain the policy.
  • P' (Office Premium): The actual gross premium the policyholder is expected to pay

An alternative to the formula approach is to use a cashflow approach where the net cashflows are calculated for each future period and then discounted back.

#4 16. Reinsurance 3.2 Retention limits Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve 0.7592

3.2 Retention limits — Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve:

In this approach, insurers aim to minimize the total cost of two components:

  • the cost of obtaining reinsurance and
  • the cost of financing a mortality fluctuations reserve.

The process follows these steps:

1. Set a risk criterion: such as a maximum 1% probability that net losses will exceed a specific amount e.g. 25m

2. Model total costs: for different retention limits, the insurer stochastically models the expected net loss by varying the mortality rates. As the retention limit increases, the cost of reinsurance decreases, but the size of the required fluctuations reserve (and its associated financing cost) increases.

3. Calculate the financing cost: The cost of the reserve ($M$) is calculated as $M \times (j - i)$, where $j$ is the required rate of return on the company's capital and $i$ is the actual investment return earned on the reserve's assets.

4. Optimize: The insurer identifies the specific retention limit where the combined cost of the reserve and reinsurance is lowest while still satisfying the ruin probability target.

#5 12. Surrender values 2. Methods of calculation Explain the prospective method 0.7591

2. Methods of calculation — Explain the prospective method:

The discounted value of future benefits and expenses, net of future premiums using best estimate assumptions.

  • ensures the surrender value progresses smoothly into the maturity value
  • allows the company to capitalize future profits
  • used primarily after the initial early stage of the policy.
  • It is very sensitive to future assumptions, particularly the interest rate assumption

Example: $$SV = SA \cdot A_{x+t} + e \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t} + f \cdot A_{x+t} - G \cdot \ddot{a}^{(m)}_{x+t} - C$$

F102_NOVEMBER_2015_Papergeneral_Q6

2015 · NOVEMBER Assumptions; Monitoring Experience
Question

QUESTION 6


i.

(a) Embedded value profit can be calculated as the sum of:

 The shareholder-owned share of net assets, where net assets are defined as the excess

of assets held over those required to meet liabilities.

 The present value of future shareholder profits arising on existing business.

(b) Assumptions:

 Mortality rates and mortality improvements

 Disability rates

 Withdrawal rates

 Expenses and expense inflation

 Benefit inflation and claim sizes

 Premium collection rate

 Commission claw back rate (i.e. the rate at which commission claw backs is

successful)

 Investment returns, valuation discount rate or valuation interest rate

 Volatility of investment returns

 Future asset mix

 Future new business volumes (may affect the future per policy expense assumption)

 Future changes in tax rates

ii.

Discussion of the proposal to allow for analysis of Embedded Value (EV) profits:

 Using the analysis of EV profit means the remuneration scheme allows for changes in

the expected future profits from existing business across all future years, and not only


for the profits made during the most recent year. This aligns the remuneration scheme

more closely with the interest of shareholders.

 EV also allows for cost capital (which could in some cases be an allowance for

riskiness), so basing executive remuneration on EV profit means that cost of capital

(and potentially riskiness) is also allowed for.

 It more accurately reflects the impact of new business. Usually new business makes a

negative contribution to profits (due to new business strain), but should make a

positive contribution to EV.

 Executive remuneration can be determined more fairly, as aspects of the company’s

performance that are outside the management’s control can be excluded from the

executive remuneration assessment. For example, to the extent that investment

performance is outside the management’s control this can be excluded from their

remuneration assessment.

 Executive remuneration can be tailored to be specific to each executive’s role by only

using those elements of the EV profit that is relevant to them. For example, a sales

manager’s remuneration would be affected more heavily by the contribution to EV

from new business, while an investment manager’s remuneration will be affected

more heavily by the reduction in EV due to mismatch losses.

 It might bring the company’s remuneration scheme more in line with those of

competitors.

 It might not be appropriate to only base executive remuneration on EV profits, as the

company’s short term profits are also important and hence also need to be allowed for

(at least to some extent) within the executive remuneration scheme.

 Benchmarks for management should be set at a reasonable and appropriate.

 The actions of some executives might take a while to influence the EV, in which case

manual adjustments to their remuneration might be required.

iii.

Other reasons for performing an analysis of EV profits:

 Validate the calculations, assumptions and data used in the EV calculation.

 Reconcile the EV values for successive years.

 Show the financial effect of deviations between the best estimate assumptions and

actual experience.

 Show the financial effect of writing new business.

 Provide management information.

 Provide detailed information for publication in the company’s accounts or those of

any parent company.

 To be consistent with the reporting being performed by competitors.

Examiner comments

Part (i)(a) was mainly bookwork and was well answered.

For part (i)(b) many students erroneously mentioned that cashflows and reserve rates are

assumptions. This is not correct, as cashflows and reserves are calculated (i.e. not assumed).

A number of students discussed the risk discount rate (this is not an assumption about future

experience, but rather the return required by shareholders) and commission (commission is

usually calculated using pre-specified rules). These points did not score any marks.


Part (ii) was well answered by students who understood the question. However, a number of

students did not understand the term “EV profit” and hence commented on “after tax profits”

or simply on “EV”, which was not asked by the question. Some students made generic points

regarding performance remuneration, but did not link this to EV profits and hence did not

score marks. Some students mentioned that EV profits can be manipulated (e.g. if

management changed the assumptions and or by other methods). But, this issue is not unique

to EV calculations as it is also a concern for profits made during the year (as these profits

also depend on reserves, which are based on models and assumptions).

For part (iii) many students gave reasons for calculating EV instead of reasons for

performing an analysis of EV (AOEV). It should be noted that the AOEV cannot be used to

determine a value for a takeover or merger. Some aspects of the AOEV, e.g. VNB, can be used

for this, but this had to be mentioned explicitly to score marks. Many students mentioned that

an AOEV might be required by the regulator: this is unlikely, as regulators are concerned

with solvency and market conduct, not with profitability.

#1 9. Assumptions 15.14 Embedded value What is the difference between a Best estimate vs Embedded value valuation? 0.7783

15.14 Embedded value — What is the difference between a Best estimate vs Embedded value valuation?:

  • Best estimate valuation: calculates the present value liability using realistic assumptions and compares the total to the current assets to provide a measure of realistic solvency: $\text{(Value of assets) - (Realistic Liability/Reserve)}$
  • Embedded value: focuses on shareholder profit, by adding the shareholder's share of net assets to the present value of future profits that emerge in excess of reserves.
  • $\text{(Net Assets) + (Present value of future shareholder profits)}$
  • Where: $\text{(Net Assets) = (Value of assets) - (Supervisory reserve)}$

The EV calculation will give a slightly different result than a realistic profit calculation because it allows for the shareholders cost of capital. The difference stems from the deferral of profits.

  • Life companies are required to hold supervisory reserves, which are prudent/larger than realistic reserves.
  • Profits cannot be distributed to shareholders until they arise in excess of these prudent supervisory reserves. This locks in capital within the company.
  • EV discounts these future profits using the risk discount rate (RDR) which is typically higher than the realistic investment return earned on the reserves.
  • Under market consistent valuations the EV calculation deducts an explicit risk margin to account for the opportunity cost to shareholders of having capital locked in by the company.
  • $\text{EV = (Assets - BEL) - Risk Margin}$

This means that EV produces a lower valuation because it accounts for the opportunity cost to shareholders of having their profits deferred while being held as required supervisory reserves.

#2 9. Assumptions 15.14 Embedded value How is embedded value calculated? 0.7660

15.14 Embedded value — How is embedded value calculated?:

Embedded value is calculated as the sum of:

  • Shareholders share of excess assets over reserves
  • Recorded at market value or discounted at a lower discount rate to reflect "lock-in" because they are invested cautiously
  • The present value of future shareholder profits arising on existing business (PVFP).
  • Discount of the Profit signature for existing business, the calculation may differ by type of business:
  • Conventional without-profit = $\text{PV (Net cashflow + Interest on reserves - Change in reserves)}$
  • Unit-linked: $\text{PV (Non-unit cashflow + Interest on non-unit reserves - Change in non-unit reserves)}$
  • With-profit: $\text{PV (Future shareholder transfers)}$
#3 9. Assumptions 15.14 Embedded value How to determine assumptions (EV Basis)? 0.7580

15.14 Embedded value — How to determine assumptions (EV Basis)?:

To calculate EV we need two bases:

  • Reserving basis: use to calculate net assets and future changes in reserves to get the profit to shareholders
  • Projection basis: projects actual best estimate experience to estimate future shareholder profits

The nature of the projection assumptions depends on why the EV is being calculated:

  • Internal management or published accounts: use best estimate assumptions
  • Sale of a company: The seller uses best estimate assumptions to show the highest justifiable appraisal value.
  • Purchase of a company: A buyer might use cautious assumptions that include margins for risk to avoid overpaying.
#4 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Profitability of existing business 0.7362

13.5 Model uses — Profitability of existing business:

12. Data: The assessment can be performed using:

  • Full policy data: on a policy-by-policy basis, requires computing resources and time.
  • Model points: group policies into homogeneous groups. Verification may be done by calculating the reserves on them and comparing them with the published value.

13. Cashflow projection: the model projects all real and notional cashflows for each policy or model point.

14. Discounting: the net cashflows are discounted back to the valuation date to determine the PVFP (Present Value of Future Profits which feeds into Embedded Value).

15. Risk discount rate (RDR): the RDR used for existing business is typically lower than the rate used for pricing new business because the risks associated with new business (e.g. uncertainty over sales volumes and mix of business) are no longer applicable to in-force policies.

16. Use of results: Management uses these models to gain insights such as:

  • Breakdowns: analysing by product line, product class, distribution channel or subsidiary to compare relative contributions to the firm
  • Financial health check: simply checking that the PVFP for a specific product is positive serves as an indicator that its nothing is badly going wrong with the financial management of that product.
  • Appraisal value: when the company is valued for sale, the embedded value serves as the starting point, which is then added to goodwill (the value of future new business) to determine the appraisal value.
#5 20. Monitoring experience 6. Using the results Capital & Investment (The "Money") 0.7171

6. Using the results — Capital & Investment (The "Money"):

Actions dealing with the balance sheet, the assets, and the distribution of value:


  • (m) Changing investment strategy: Fixing ALM mismatches if investment surplus is volatile.
  • (n) With-profits distribution: Adjusting the split between reversionary and terminal bonuses.
  • (p) Raising capital: Seeking new funds if surplus is negative or solvency is threatened.
  • (q) Capital allocation: Redirecting capital to lines of business with higher risk-adjusted returns.

F102_NOVEMBER_2015_Papergeneral_Q7

2015 · NOVEMBER With-profits surplus distribution; Investments
Question

QUESTION 7


i.

The investments selected should be appropriate to the nature, term and currency of the

liabilities. The extent to which the appropriate investments referred to above may be departed

from in order to maximise the overall return will depend, inter alia, on the extent of the

company's free assets/risk appetite.

The part of the benefit in the form of the basic sum assured and existing declared bonuses is

guaranteed in nature. These benefits are best matched by bonds/fixed interest securities

(government or corporate bonds).

Part of the benefit (future bonuses) will be discretionary. The insurer will aim to maximise

the discretionary benefits (i.e. maximise returns), but this would be subject to the expectations

of policyholders and their attitude to risk. Policyholders will usually expect the proceeds of

their contracts to maintain their value in “real” terms. Hence the assets should be those that

are expected to provide a “real” return (equities and property).

Part of the expected future outflows relating to this business will be expenses, which are

likely to be linked to an inflation index (index-linked bonds).

But assets selected will depend on:

 The bonus philosophy of the insurer (split between reversionary and terminal

bonuses).

 Policyholder expectations of smoothing of bonuses/company’s smoothing philosophy

 The level of free assets.

The assets should have the same discounted mean term as the liabilities.

Assets should be denominated in the same currency as the liabilities, to reduce currency risk.

Some holdings in cash are likely to be necessary for the company to operate on a daily basis

without needing to realise any non-cash assets.

The company should consider the different tax treatment of different asset classes.

The assets held should be sufficiently diversified (across type, sector and counterparty) so as

to minimise the risk of over-exposure to any one asset class, sector to counterparty.

Regulatory rules may limit the types of amounts of assets of certain types that can be held.

Consider the effect of selected assets on solvency requirements.


ii.

The effect of the change in investment strategy:

 The proposed investment strategy is moving away from risky assets into lower risk

assets.

 The insurer will earn higher running yields on underlying investments (more certain

sources of profits). In addition returns on portfolio slightly smoother, but lower in

long run.

 The insurer could increase the reversionary bonus component and decrease terminal

bonus. But should consider current levels of bonus compared to running yields and

determine if there is scope for increase.

 The change in the investment strategy might improve the matched position of the

insurer. The change might have been necessary due to high proportion of guaranteed

liabilities on book.

 The insurer may decide not to change bonus distribution strategy at all. The new

proposal may be a better match for the existing strategy and change is just bringing

the investment and bonus distribution strategy in line with each other.

 In either case the insurer will need to consider whether the bonus distribution strategy

be sustained with the new asset mix and expected returns on these assets.

Factors to consider around the bonus distribution strategy:

 The decision will be affected by policyholders’ reasonable expectations and extent of

the change.

 Communications to policyholders around the bonus distribution philosophy whether

the new investment strategy is in line with this.

 The effect on the competitive position/marketability of the insurer.

 Implications for the solvency position of the insurer. The insurer may want to keep

reversionary bonuses low to keep guarantees low to improve the solvency position of

the insurer.

 The insurer will need to decide whether to implement the change the bonus

philosophy for new business only or also for existing business

 The insurer should consider equity between different generations of policyholders e.g.

if current funding level is high, then unfair to be for undistributed funds to be

distributed to policyholders who did not help to contribute to funds.

 Consider whether a special reversionary bonus should be declared before the change,

based on funding level or current level of retained profit.

Other factors to consider

 Reasons for lower risk investment strategy.

 Consistency with overall business strategy e.g. efficient use of capital or shareholders

required rate of return.

 Capital requirements may change due to the lower risk investment strategy; it is likely

that less solvency capital will be required.

 Potential impact on profit.

 Costs of implementing the change e.g. disinvesting and re-investing.

 The economic outlook and if change is related to expected returns on bonds vs

equities for the foreseeable future.


iii.

Advantages for the policyholder:

 The cash bonus is received earlier than on the insured event.

 May meet the need for income e.g. repayment of loan.

 Less subjective decisions (less discretion on bonus to be declared), which protects

policyholders against ungenerous companies.

 The bonus may appear fairer/more equitable if contribution method is used (where the

bonus distribution is related to the contribution to the total profit of each of expense,

mortality and investment profit for the group of policies).

 May be tax advantages/disadvantages depending on how cash dividends are taxed vs

bonuses on final payout.

Disadvantages for the policyholder:

 This method may not be preferred if policyholder’s intention is to save and ensure

savings keep up with inflation.

 The returns may be reduced due to non-deferral of surplus as with the terminal bonus

structure.

 Reinvestment risk for the policyholder if they want to save the bonuses till maturity

date.

Advantage for the company:

 Marketing – the policyholder may more easily understand the basis, hence more sales.

 Marketing – policyholders may like the certainty of receiving benefit earlier rather

than later, hence more sales.

 Possibly lower withdrawals because policyholders get cash in hand regularly.

Disadvantages for the company:

 Constraints on investment policy due to no deferral of bonus payment.

 No ability to use deferred profits as margins against adverse experience.

 Reduces the contribution to free assets to enable writing of new business as in case of

deferred method.

 Reduces funds under management.

 Increased administration compared to other methods because of annual payment.

 Requires complex calculations.

 May be competitive disadvantage if customers do not understand the product because

they are more familiar with the other method.

Part (i) was answered reasonably well except where students went into too much detail about

the types of assets to invest in and not the factors to consider for with-profits products

specifically. A few students didn’t know what UK style with-profits business was, even though

in the third part of the question it was explained!

Part (ii) was poorly answered. Not enough points were made, and only one or two students

mentioned that the new assets could be matching the current bonus strategy better or at least

the importance of considering current levels of matching to decide if bonus philosophy

needed to change.

Part (iii) was reasonably well answered. Be careful not to mention advantage for one as

disadvantage for another, because the point will only be scored once.

Top Matching Notes 5 matches
#1 9. Assumptions 15.5 Investment return assumptions Using the 5-step framework for setting the investment assumption 0.7605

15.5 Investment return assumptions — Using the 5-step framework for setting the investment assumption:

  • Identify importance: because the contracts build up large reserves and involve a fixed monetary guarantee at maturity, the investment return assumption is very important.
  • Asset choice: typically government or corporate fixed interest securities will be selected to match the liabilities.
  • Best estimate: The actuary uses the concept of discounted mean term (duration) to select assets whose proceeds will align with the expected timing of liability outgo. The starting point is the current weighted average redemption yield available on matching securities in the market.
  • Future changes: For a regular premium contract and/or coupon paying bonds, there is a need to account for the fact that future premiums and coupon payments will be received at various points and must be invested at unknown future interest rates.
  • Taxation: if the company is taxed on investment income, it must net the investment return for taxation to reflect the actual investment return it will receive.
  • Balancing credibility and judgement: The actuary will have to balance the amount of weight that they place on historical experience and expected changes. The final estimate is a weighted adjustment of the best estimate parameter and expected changes.
  • Margins for prudence: to protect the company against the risk that future yields are lower than anticipated, a margin is deducted from the established expected investment return.
#2 18. Investments 3. Free assets How do free assets affect the investment strategy of an insurance company? 0.7578

3. Free assets — How do free assets affect the investment strategy of an insurance company?:

Free assets act as a financial cushion that allows insurers to move away from a strictly "matched" investment position to seek higher returns.

  • Maximizing returns: Companies can invest in riskier assets to improve overall returns, which can lead to higher bonuses for with-profits policyholders or higher dividends for shareholders.
  • Solvency buffer: Free assets reduce the probability of insolvency by absorbing potential falls in the market value of assets backing guaranteed benefits
  • Investment freedom: the greater the level of free assets the more freedom to mismatch the nature, term, and currency of liabilities, provided the risks remain within the company's total financial resources.
#3 18. Investments 2. Principles of investment How does the nature, term and currency of liabilities affect asset selection? 0.7571

2. Principles of investment — How does the nature, term and currency of liabilities affect asset selection?:

  • The liability outgo consists of:
  • Benefit payments
  • Expense outgo
  • minus: premium income
  • In any given year the liability outgo depends on the monetary amount of its constituents and the probability of it being received or paid out.

  • The liabilities may be:
  • Guaranteed in money terms: Match with fixed-interest bonds or cash
  • Guaranteed in terms of an index: use index-linked bonds or potentially property investment (rental income) or equities that move in line with CPI.
  • Short-term index linked liabilities could be matched by fixed interest stocks

  • Discretionary: backed by real assets like equity or property for higher bonuses
  • Investment-linked: hold the exact assets the benefits are linked to.

Term:

  • The focus is on the discounted mean term (duration) of the liability. By matching the duration of assets to liabilities, the company ensures that if interest rates change, the values of both assets and liabilities move in line with each other.
  • However insurance liabilities tend to be longer term that available assets in the market.
#4 9. Assumptions 15.5 Investment return assumptions Key factors influencing the investment assumption 0.7469

15.5 Investment return assumptions — Key factors influencing the investment assumption:

  • Significance of the assumption: The first step is to establish how important the assumption is for the results, which will depend on the level of reserves and investment guarantees given.
  • Onerous guarantees: Onerous guarantees require the insurer to be more cautious in asset selection, which should be reflected in a lower (more prudent) investment return assumption.
  • Reinvestment risk: If the insurer expects positive cashflows in the future (e.g. from regular premiums or bond coupons), which must be invested at unknown future rates, it faces the risk that future yields will be lower than expected.
  • Taxation: If the insurer is subject to tax on its investment income, the actuary must net down the interest rate to reflect the actual investment return.
  • Asset mix: the assumption should reflect the intended mix of assets (equities, bonds, property, etc.) and the current and likely future returns on those specific assets.
  • Free assets: The asset mix is also influenced by the company's free assets as higher assets will allow for a riskier, higher yielding investment strategy.
  • With-profit business: Insurers may use conservative investment assumptions to implicitly allow for future bonus declarations, or use realistic assumptions with an explicit "bonus" loading.
#5 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.5 Summary comparison of Surplus Distribution Systems Provision of Capital 0.7462

9.1.5 Summary comparison of Surplus Distribution Systems — Provision of Capital:

The timing of profit distribution affects the insurer's free assets. If profit distribution is deferred (delayed), the retained funds augment the company's free assets in the meantime.


• Investment Freedom: Greater deferral—achieved through terminal bonuses or super-compound reversionary bonuses—gives the company greater investment freedom to seek higher returns in riskier assets like equities or property.


• Financing New Business: These "extra" free assets can be used to support the new business strain of selling new policies.


• Distribution Mismatch: Over time, there must be a balance; sustained over-distribution of bonuses (distributing more than is generated) will lead to an excessive drain on free assets and the company's capital.

F102_NOVEMBER_2016_Papergeneral_Q1

2016 · NOVEMBER Risk; Reinsurance
Question

QUESTION 1


(i)

Possible reasons include:

 ABC may consider the price offered to be very good value for money.

 ABC might not have sufficient experience of selling this product.

 ABC may need solvency relief, which could be achieved by passing on all of the risk

to the reinsurer.

 ABC may not see this as a core part of their business, and thus be happy for the

reinsurer to take on all of this risk and manage the portfolio.

 ABC may have no particular risk appetite for that particular market segment.

 ABC may want to reduce the volatility of its claims experience.

(ii)

Reasons why the reinsurer might agree:

 If the reinsurer has priced correctly the quoted price should result in the required level

of profit to the reinsurer.

 Expenses will probably be spread over a larger premium than initially expected, so it

should generate even better profit than originally priced.

 The reinsurer may agree to reinsure 100% of the risk to maintain a good relationship

with ABC if the remainder of ABC’s reinsurance programme is profitable to the

reinsurer.

Reasons why ABC might not agree:

 ABC has no interest in the experience and management of the portfolio if 100% of

the risk is reinsured.

 This could lead ABC to be less vigilant on underwriting and claims decisions.

 The reinsurer may specify strict underwriting and claims assessment requirements as

part of this agreement.

 This is especially true if the reinsurer cannot re-price the business at a later point in

time.

 The request to reinsure 100% of the business may lead the reinsurer to re-evaluate its

pricing (the reinsurer may have been too aggressive in the pricing initially).

(iii)

Risks taken on:

Counterparty risk / Credit risk – The reinsurer may be unable to pay the claims as they arise.

Legal risk – A reinsurance contract will need to be entered into, and no contract is completely

clear and unambiguous.

Systems risk – ABC will need to pay over the reinsurance premium (which have to be

calculated) and ensure that the reinsurer is informed of every life covered. This will need to

be done electronically and thus systems risks arise.

Operational risk – ABC will remain responsible for the underwriting and claims. Failure to

perform these processes as per the reinsurance contract would introduce operational risks.

Students lost out on a few easy marks due to not reading the question properly.


Part i was answered satisfactorily, but part ii was answered poorly with a large number of

students missing the point that 100% reinsurance reduces incentive to manage the

underwriting and claims properly. Most students also missed the point that the reinsurer had

already tendered, so the reinsurer clearly has terms on which at least a part of the risk can be

accepted. So to say that the reinsurer is concerned about the distribution channel or product

design does not make sense. The question targeted why it may or may not be feasible to take a

100% share.

In part iii most students mentioned the credit risk, but many students lost easy marks by not

mentioning the legal and operational risks being introduced.

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 1


(i)

Possible reasons include:


  • ABC may consider the price offered to be very good value for money.

  • ABC might not have sufficient experience of selling this product.

  • ABC may need solvency relief, which could be achieved by passing on all of the risk to the reinsurer.

  • ABC may not see this as a core part of their business, and thus be happy for the reinsurer to take on all of this risk and manage the portfolio.

  • ABC may have no particular risk appetite for that particular market segment.

  • ABC may want to reduce the volatility of its claims experience.

(ii)

Reasons why the reinsurer might agree:


  • If the reinsurer has priced correctly the quoted price should result in the required level of profit to the reinsurer.

  • Expenses will probably be spread over a larger premium than initially expected, so it should generate even better profit than originally priced.

  • The reinsurer may agree to reinsure 100% of the risk to maintain a good relationship with ABC if the remainder of ABC's reinsurance programme is profitable to the reinsurer. Reasons why ABC might not agree:

  • ABC has no interest in the experience and management of the portfolio if 100% of the risk is reinsured.

  • This could lead ABC to be less vigilant on underwriting and claims decisions.

  • The reinsurer may specify strict underwriting and claims assessment requirements as part of this agreement.

  • This is especially true if the reinsurer cannot re-price the business at a later point in time.

  • The request to reinsure 100% of the business may lead the reinsurer to re-evaluate its pricing (the reinsurer may have been too aggressive in the pricing initially).

(iii)

Risks taken on: Counterparty risk / Credit risk - The reinsurer may be unable to pay the claims as they arise.


Legal risk - A reinsurance contract will need to be entered into, and no contract is completely clear and unambiguous.


Systems risk - ABC will need to pay over the reinsurance premium (which have to be calculated) and ensure that the reinsurer is informed of every life covered. This will need to be done electronically and thus systems risks arise.


Operational risk - ABC will remain responsible for the underwriting and claims. Failure to perform these processes as per the reinsurance contract would introduce operational risks.


Students lost out on a few easy marks due to not reading the question properly.


Part i was answered satisfactorily, but part ii was answered poorly with a large number of students missing the point that 100% reinsurance reduces incentive to manage the underwriting and claims properly. Most students also missed the point that the reinsurer had already tendered, so the reinsurer clearly has terms on which at least a part of the risk can be accepted. So to say that the reinsurer is concerned about the distribution channel or product design does not make sense. The question targeted why it may or may not be feasible to take a 100% share.

In part iii most students mentioned the credit risk, but many students lost easy marks by not mentioning the legal and operational risks being introduced.

Top Matching Notes 5 matches
#1 16. Reinsurance 3.1 Cost of reinsurance How does the cost of the reinsurance affect decisions about reinsurance arrangements? 0.7533

3.1 Cost of reinsurance — How does the cost of the reinsurance affect decisions about reinsurance arrangements?:

  • Reinsurance comes at a cost, these costs reduce the expected profit for the cedant
  • The reinsurance adds profit margins to its risk premiums.
  • The reinsurer may insist on more stringent risk management than the insurer would like e.g. stricter underwriting or claims processes
  • The reinsurance processes may result in a slower service offering to the policyholder (facultative, claims, delays)
  • The insurer will have increased counterparty risk, as it is exposed to the risk of the reinsurer failing to meet its obligations.
  • The direct writer must balance the cost of reinsurance against the risk of loss from adverse experience if less reinsurance were to be used.

However, the risk reduction caused by reinsurance could leverage up the return or risk-adjusted return on capital

#2 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7457

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#3 16. Reinsurance 3. Considerations before reinsuring What are the considerations before reinsuring? 0.7405

3. Considerations before reinsuring — What are the considerations before reinsuring?:

Before deciding whether and how to reinsure, an insurer evaluates several strategic and financial factors:

  • Type of reinsurance: The type of reinsurance (whether it is OTR, Risk premiums or excess of loss or Fin Re), will depend will depend on:
  • The reason the insurance company is using reinsurance
  • The reinsurance cost
  • The type of insurance business for which the reinsurance is to be arranged
  • Cost of Reinsurance: Because reinsurers include their own profit margins and expenses, which reduce the insurer's absolute profit level. the insurer must balance security versus return. It must determine if the reduction in volatility justifies the reduced expected return.
  • Retention Limits must be set by considering the company's risk appetite, its level of free assets, and the distribution of sum assured across its portfolio. A company with higher free assets can generally afford a higher retention limit.
  • Counterparty (Credit) Risk: The insurer retains liability according to the contract, to pay benefits even if the reinsurer cannot meet claim payments (becomes insolvent)
  • Alternatives, such as holding a mortality fluctuation reserve may be more cost-effective than purchasing reinsurance.
  • Legal Risks: Finally the company should consider legal risk by ensuring treaties are legally watertight.
#4 16. Reinsurance 1.1 Coinsurance - original terms In what ways might a reinsurer be more attractive to the insurer? 0.7316

1.1 Coinsurance - original terms — In what ways might a reinsurer be more attractive to the insurer?:

  • Offer higher commissions
  • Great financial strength to reduce the insurer's credit risk of the insurer defaulting
  • Broader coverage, willingness to accept higher benefit limits or automatic acceptance limits
  • Technical assistance offering expertise in underwriting, product design and systems
  • Profit-sharing: experience-refund arrangements where the insurer receives a share of any profits the reinsurer makes from the ceded portfolio
  • Financial reinsurance support (e.g. nil premium payment)
  • Offer lower risk premium rates by leveraging tax advantages or lower capital requirements
#5 4. External environment 10. The external environment 11. Reinsurance availability 0.7134

10. The external environment — 11. Reinsurance availability:

The insurer should consider whether reinsurance is available and whether it is needed.


Reinsurance may help with: reducing volatility, managing large claims, reducing capital requirements, accessing specialist underwriting or claims expertise, supporting new product development.


However, reinsurance introduces counterparty risk and may reduce retained profits. The cost and terms of reinsurance may also affect the viability of the product.

(i)

Should take into account ‘boundary conditions’ i.e. should consider which alterations are

yet received

changes in premium (ignoring expenses of the alteration).

change and when it occurs in policy’s lifetime).

The costs associated with carrying out the alteration should be recovered.

Method should be easy to calculate and to explain to policyholders.

The method should consider potential for selection against the insurer, and allow for this in

the basis, or disallow such alterations.

Policyholders’ circumstances could change eg redundancy, making future premiums

unaffordable

The total profit expected from the paid-up contract will depend on the relationship between

PUP sum assured should be consistent with surrender values so that surrender values before

Therefore use the surrender value at time of PUP as the policy value before alteration, thereby

The policy value after PUP would then be: (PUPSA)t Ax+t:n-t + eax+t:n-t (annual expenses

And to ensure that policy still contributes to profit after becoming PUP, this should be

policy value after PUP to ensure contribution to profit after making PUP.)

Mainly bookwork.

Many candidates failed to generate enough points by failing to consider how offering a paid-

up policy could be beneficial to the company (or more beneficial than losing the policy.).

3. Retention of profit on surrender — How does the choice of surrender basis influence how much future profit is extracted/capitalized?:

The profit on surrender is equal to the Asset share per policy less the surrender benefit paid.

The capitalized value of future profit arises from the differences between the premium rate assumptions and the surrender values assumptions.

F102_NOVEMBER_2016_Papergeneral_Q3

2016 · NOVEMBER Risk; Life Insurance Products
Question

QUESTION 3


(i)

Longevity risk and policyholder behaviour

Conventional annuity

The life insurer carries the longevity risk of the annuity book i.e. it will have to fund the

annuity payments should policyholders live longer than expected.

As this is a developing country there may not be adequate data to understand longevity trends

increasing the risk exposure to the life insurer.

Special unit-linked annuity

Longevity risk is transferred to the policyholder.

There will be minor mortality risk at early stages of the policy.

Investment risk

Conventional annuity

The investment risk is carried by the life insurer.

The life insurer needs to ensure that the assets chosen to back the liabilities are adequate to

cover the annuity payments into the future.

As the market is developing, there are unlikely to be assets of adequate duration to back the

annuities increasing the investment risk (reinvestment risk).

Special unit-linked annuity

The investment risk is transferred to the policyholder to some extent.

The life insurer will, however, still be exposed to investment risk due to the following:

 Investment guarantee

 Its income from the product is dependent on the asset management fee which is

charged on the underlying assets under management.

Investment guarantee for unit-linked business

Offering the guarantees exposes the insurer to significant investment losses if market returns

are negative.

This risk can be even more significant in this case, due to the markets in this developing

country potentially being volatile.

Offering the guarantees will increase the reserving and capital requirements of the company.

This may increase the capital strain for this product.

The markets are unlikely to have available instruments to hedge the exposure, so it will be

difficult to reduce reserving and capital requirements by hedging the guarantees.

The company is unlikely to have the necessary skills and it may not be cost effective to obtain

the skills to manage the risk and valuation of the guarantees.

The cost of the guarantees may be prohibitive and result in lower value for the clients over the

long term. This will impact on the insurer’s reputation.


Expense risk

For both products there is a risk that expenses are higher than expected due to inflation being

higher than expected or poor management of costs.

Expense risk is exacerbated by the flexibility that policyholders have on the unit linked

product: if the rate at which policyholders draw down on their unit funds is greater than the

rate expected, the fees earned on the assets under management will be lower.

Competition

Conventional annuity

This product is currently offered by other competitors in the market. There is therefore a risk

that new business sales reduce and margins come under pressure as competition increases.

Special unit-linked annuity

The product is not offered by other providers at the moment so it may be possible to include

higher margins.

If the product is successful, however, there is a risk that competitors will enter the market

compressing margins.

Furthermore, unit linked annuities may be transferred between providers so there is a risk of

losing business to competitors in the future. This is not a risk for the conventional annuity.

Volume of new business

Conventional annuity

High levels of new business volumes will increase the initial capital strain on the insurer,

possibly putting pressure on the solvency of the insurer.

Special unit-linked annuity

There is a lower risk of high volumes causing strain/insolvency as the product offers no

longevity protection, and therefore has relatively smaller reserving requirements.

There will however still be new business strain as the upfront costs (3% commission +

administration) exceed the income (98% allocation) and the investment guarantee will most

likely result in additional reserves and/or capital requirements being held at policy inception.

Volumes will therefore still need to be actively managed if the insurer is unable to recognise

any of the future profits from the product upfront (via actuarial funding or negative non-unit

reserves).

Distribution – risk of poor advice

Conventional annuity

Brokers understand the product well as it is a common and simple product in the market.

There is low risk of poor advice.

Special unit-linked annuity

Brokers may not understand the product well as it is new to the market. There is risk of mis-

selling if adequate training is not provided to brokers.

This risk is increased by the fact that this is an annuity that does not cover longevity risk,

which is something that policyholders might not be used to.

Systems and controls

Conventional annuity

As this product has been on offer for a long time, systems and controls are likely to be

adequate.

Special unit-linked annuity


The new product will require significant system development in order to conduct unit pricing

and allow for the restrictions on drawdowns.

There is high operational risk due to the need to create new processes.

Data risk

Conventional annuity

Product has been sold for a long time so adequate data to price. However developing country

so there may still be volatility.

Special unit-linked annuity

No data on which to base fee structure and pricing. Will be difficult to know what average

rate of drawdown will be to set the fee.

Regulations

As the unit-linked product is new to the market there is a risk that the regulator may introduce

regulations related to the product that may result in further development and system costs if

the product needs to be changed.

There may be a risk of tax changes that impacts the profitability of the product.

There is a risk of fraud on both annuities but greater on conventional annuity as need to track

death of individuals.

Reputational risk

Conventional annuity

Low as the product is simple, clients understand what they will receive upfront. The only risk

is if the insurer cannot meet annuity payments.

Special unit-linked annuity

There is a reputational risk as there is a risk that policyholders do not understand the product.

If investment markets collapse, policyholders could be materially impacted.

There is a risk that the unit-linked fund is depleted before the death of the policyholder

leading to reputational risk.

The reputational risks related to investments are exacerbated by the fact that there single

investment fund determined by the insurer.

(iii)

Reduce the premium allocation rate to 97% (or less).

The company could employ actuarial funding or use negative non-unit reserves.

The maximum commission upfront could be reduced from 3%.

The company could introduce a bid offer spread charge.

The investment portfolio guarantees could be removed.

Overall the question was reasonably answered. Quite a few candidates did not

understand how a living/linked annuity worked compared to a conventional annuity

and thus did not identify the risks correctly. Some candidates did not lay out the

structure of their answers well resulting in overlap and/or missed points. A good

approach would have been to run through each risk type and then consider the impact

on each product.

#1 1. Life insurance contracts 3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer Investment risk 0.7860

3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer — Investment risk:

  • The insurer must invest the single premium to cover regular outgo over an unknown timeframe.
  • This risk can be mitigated by matching liabilities with fixed-interest securities with redemption dates matching the amounts being paid each year.
  • In a perfectly matched strategy, assuming that annuitants die exactly as expected, the insurance company should not need to buy or sell any of its assets during the term of the contract because the cash needed is provided by the coupons and redemption amounts.
  • This removes interest rate volatility risk and yield uncertainty because the cashflows and yields are locked in at the time when the contract was priced.
  • This scenario is impractical because:
  • Timing: The term of the annuity payments uncertain
  • Availability: Assets with perfectly matching terms may not be available (reinvestment risk)
#2 1. Life insurance contracts 3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer Longevity risk 0.7722

3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer — Longevity risk:

  • Mortality improvements: The main risk is that annuitants live longer than the insurer allowed for in pricing, often due to understating the rate of improvement in life expectancy.
  • Anti-selection: When purchase is voluntary, those in good health or with a family history of longevity are most likely to buy an annuity (self-selection).
#3 5. Risks 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk Directions of mortality risk 0.7644

11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Directions of mortality risk:

The impact of mortality depends on the nature of the insurance contract:

  • Mortality: For life insurance products like term assurance, the risk is that deaths are higher than expected, leading to a reduction in profit or capital shortfall. The risk is most significant at the start of a contract when the sum at risk is at its highest.
  • Longevity: For survival-contingent products like immediate annuities, the risk is that policyholders live longer than expected. In this scenario, the insurer risks paying out more income than they had initially priced for through the initial single premium and reserved for.

See mortality question example: Question 13.3

#4 1. Life insurance contracts 3.2.1 Deferred annuity - Customer needs Protection against longevity risk 0.7421

3.2.1 Deferred annuity - Customer needs — Protection against longevity risk:

  • Deferred annuities address the significant risk of running out of money if a policyholder becomes very old, this protects the individual's standard of living
#5 1. Life insurance contracts 4.1.3 Unit-linked contracts - Risks to the insurer External risks 0.7412

4.1.3 Unit-linked contracts - Risks to the insurer — External risks:

  • Marketing and reputational risk: Because these contracts have lower guarantees, they produce greater uncertainty of return for the policyholder. If investment performance is poor, it can lead to policyholder dissatisfaction, bad publicity, and reduced future sales, especially if the risks were not clearly understood at the time of purchase.
  • Marketing pressures, competition, or legislative restrictions may prevent an insurer from increasing reviewable charges enough to cover deteriorating expense performance
  • Changes in Legislation: There is a risk that regulatory changes could restrict an insurer's ability to hold negative non-unit reserves or use actuarial funding to reduce capital strain (taking advance credit for future contributions toward initial expenses that were already incurred)

QUESTION 4


(i)

Need assumptions for both the best estimates and margins to be included.

Mortality: pre claim and during claim (see below)

Claim termination rates, which are dependent on recovery rates and mortality rates

Discount rate/ investment return (to set up reserves): before claim and once claim is in

payment

Expense assumptions

 Renewal expenses and any on-going commission

 Claims assessment at claim inception and at any subsequent re-assessments

 Expense inflation rate

(ii)

The actuary will need to:

 Choose a suitable investigation period.

 Long enough so that the results are credible (enough data).

 Recent enough so that the results are relevant.

 Create homogenous groups.

 E.g. males and females; occupational classes

 Balanced against having sufficient data in each group so that results are

credible.

 Data issues may have to be dealt with (e.g. anomalies in the data etc.).

 Calculate exposed to risk and the number of claims received per group, used to

calculate crude rates for each group.

The actuary will then compare the results to the existing assumptions and either:

 Adjust the existing assumptions if the internal experience cannot be considered to be

fully credible, or

 Graduate the crude rates to replace the existing assumptions.

Further adjustments would be required to ensure that the assumption can be applicable to

future expected experience, in particular there is a need to allow for:

 The policy conditions (e.g. deferred period and replacement ratio) will influence the

claim inception and claim termination rates.

 Trends over time (e.g. due to medical advances).

 Correlation with economic environment (e.g. there is often higher claim inception

during economic down turn).

 The potential impact of government provision of welfare and tax.

Finalising the assumption would also involve considering other sources, to assess

reasonability (e.g. standard table, reinsurer or global data).

Include a margin for prudence.

(iii)

Potential impact on risk rates:

The company will now receive claims from relatively less severe disability conditions. As a

result, one can expect an increase in the claim inception rates.

However, claim termination rates are also likely to increase, at least at early claim durations.


 That is because it is more likely that claimants for the less severe conditions will

recover.

 However, once benefits are in payment, some claimants for the less severe conditions

may try to “prolong” payment, so the termination rates may not increase by as much

as one would initially expect.

Potential impact on mortality:

The average mortality for claimants is likely to decrease, given that now more relatively

healthy lives will be included.

Potential impact on expenses:

Claim assessment costs will increase, both at:

 initial claim stage (due to more claims having to be assessed), and

 the management stage of claims in payment (more frequent follow ups will be

necessary to manage claims from relatively less severe conditions).

Unlikely to have a significant impact on the investment return/ discount rate.

(i)

Most candidates failed to identify a sufficient number of assumptions and some identified

pricing rather than reserving assumptions.

(ii)

Few candidates gave a sufficiently detailed description of the full process to score well. Some

candidates failed to answer the question and considered mutli-state models rather than the

inception disability approach.

(ii)

Most candidates identified the impact on claims inception and expense experience. Better

candidates considered the impact of larger number of less severe claims on the claim

termination and mortality rates.

#1 9. Assumptions 15.3 Mortality assumptions Base mortality 0.7994

15.3 Mortality assumptions — Base mortality:

  • The initial mortality rates should reflect the expected future experience of the target market, distribution channel and the underwriting applied at the point of sale.
  • Data sources: Actuaries typically adjust standard mortality tables rather than creating new ones. If a company has sufficient data, it uses its own historical experience or the experience of a similar class of business. If internal data is insufficient, industry sources (such as CMI reports in the UK), population statistics, or data from reinsurers are used.
  • Homogenous grouping: data must be divided into homogeneous groups, typically by age, sex and smoker status subject to adequate levels of data being retained within each cell to remain credible.
  • Historical investigation period: investigations usually cover a 3 to 4 year period to ensure adequate data volume without introducing excessive heterogeneity from different generations and trends.
#2 9. Assumptions 15.4 Morbidity assumptions Income protection (IP) 0.7872

15.4 Morbidity assumptions — Income protection (IP):

IP benefits are modelled using a multi-state model, tracking policyholders through states like healthy, sick (within deferred period), claiming, recovered or dead.


Actuaries must estimate transition intensities (inception, recovery, and death rates), which should be subdivided by homogeneous groups such as age, duration of claim and type of disability:

  • Duration of claims: recovery rates reduce significantly as the duration of the claim increases. A policyholder who has been sick for a week is much more likely to recover soon than one who has been incapacitated for a year.
  • Type of disability: recovery rates differ significantly according to the underlying cause of the sickness or disability. For example, the path to recovery for a broken limb is very different from that of a chronic mental illness.
  • Claims history: A sophisticated model may subdivide the healthy state based on whether a policyholder has claimed previously because individuals who have had periods off work due to sickness in the past are statistically more likely to claim again in the future

These intensities are heavily influenced by Economic morale, the provision of government welfare, rehabilitation benefits, tax and the replacement ratio.

Once transition intensities have been estimated, the are converted into transition probabilities, which are used to calculate expected numbers or proportions of lives in each each state at future ages.

#3 14. Guarantees and options 4. Valuing Mortality options What are the extra assumptions the insurer would need to make? 0.7720

4. Valuing Mortality options — What are the extra assumptions the insurer would need to make?:

  • Option take-up rates: the probability that the policyholder will exercise the option at each available date
  • Conventional approach: assumes 100% of eligible policyholder will take the maximum benefit
  • Realistic approach: uses percentages based on past experience
  • Mortality of exercisers: Due to anti-selection, those who exercise the option are assumed to have heavier mortality than standard lives. (e.g. 150% of the base table)
  • Mortality of non-exercisers: assume lower than standard mortality so that the weighted average amounts to the original best estimate level.
  • Benefit choice: if the policyholder has a choice of benefit levels, an assumption is made about which level will be chosen (often assume the most expensive option for the insurer)
  • Additional expenses: Allow for the costs of notifying policyholders of their option and the administrative work to process the change.
#4 9. Assumptions 15.8 Withdrawal (Persistency) Assumptions Methodology for setting withdrawal assumptions 0.7714

15.8 Withdrawal (Persistency) Assumptions — Methodology for setting withdrawal assumptions:

  • Best estimate: assumptions should ideally be based on an analysis of the company's own recent historical experience for the specific contract or a similar class of business. If internal data is inadequate, industry-wide experience may be used as a starting point.
  • Adjustments: Professional judgement is used to adjust historical data to reflect the expected future experience of new policyholders, particularly if there have been changes in:
  • Target markets or the level of client sophistication
  • Distribution channels or sales tactics e.g. aggressive sales pressure
  • Policy benefits, such as changes in bonus rates or surrender value scales
  • Balance credibility and judgement: The extend of reliance on data versus judgement depends on the relevance, volume and predictability of the available information.
  • Incorporating margins for unpredictable economic and commercial factors, to protect the insurer against underestimating withdrawals. using judgement to assess the uncertainty.

Question

QUESTION 5


(i)

Profitability

The premiums need to be sufficient to cover claims, expenses and make a contribution to

profit.

The contribution to profit should be sufficient to meet the shareholders’ required return for

this product.

Critical illness incidence assumptions should cover the risk involved and allow for future

changes in the risk.

Expense loadings need to cover the marginal costs relating to the policy as well as make a

contribution to overhead expenses.

Revenue from the product will need to cover the costs of developing and launching the

product (e.g. marketing).

There are likely to be high initial expenses high lapses early in the duration of the policy (i.e.

the asset share is negative) will impact on the profitability of the insurer.


Sensitivity of the profit to changes in expected experience (e.g. claims or business volumes)

should be investigated.

The design of the product should aim to reduce the sensitivity of the profit of the insurer to

adverse changes in experience e.g. reduce initial expenses to reduce losses on lapses at early

durations.

The extent of cross-subsidies (e.g. relating to expense loading for small and large policies will

exacerbate the sensitivity of profit to mix and volume of business).

The cost of reinsurance will impact on the profitability.

Lower profitability might be acceptable if the company can cross sell other (more profitable)

products to the same policyholders.

Marketability and competitiveness

The marketability and competitiveness of the product of the will depend on the product

offering of the insurer’s competitors.

The competitiveness of the product will depend on the competitiveness of the premium for

this product.

Level premiums may have the advantage of certainty, but may be high initially for young

policyholders will low disposable income.

Focus on core conditions and fixed sum assured makes the product relatively simple and more

marketable and should make the product cheaper than other critical illness offerings that

cover a wider variety of conditions.

Due to the technical nature of claims definitions, these may be difficult for policyholders to

understand.

This product may need to be sold through brokers and sales agents so that features of the

product can be explained accurately to policyholders.

Risk characteristics

The uncertainty relating to future claims experience (e.g. critical illness diagnosis rates) for

critical illness is likely to increase the risk of the product, particularly since level guaranteed

premiums will apply for the duration of the contract.

Risks may be exacerbated by a lack of data on critical illness claims experience or changes in

future diagnoses of conditions due to medical advances.

Margins may be included in the premium for the higher levels of uncertainty but this will

contradict the need for competitive premiums.

The insurer should consider whether there are any features in the product design or target

market that would increase the risk of the business (e.g. targeting workplaces where there is a

higher risk of employees suffering from lung cancer).

The insurer will need to consider whether underwriting processes will be sufficient to manage

the anti-selection risk reinsurance may be used as a risk mitigation strategy.

(ii)

Pricing using a deterministic model:

 Determine a set of model points which represent the expected new business based

on the profile of the existing business allowing for any expected changes in the

profile.

 Set assumptions for the expected critical illness diagnosis rates, mortality,

morbidity, lapses, expenses, investment returns and tax.

 These assumptions should reflect that expected future experience of the lives

covered and the economic environment.


 For each model point project the cashflows allowing for projected solvency and

reserving requirements.

 The following cash flows are required in the projections: premiums, claims,

expenses and investment returns on reserves.

 The future profits are then calculated as the net cash flow, less the increase in

reserves.

 The company should discount the projected profit at a risk discount rate that

reflects the return required by the company and the level of risk attached to the

profits.

 The premiums will be set so that the company achieves its required profit target.

 The premiums need to be considered for marketability.

 This may lead to reconsideration of the design of the product, changes to the

distribution channel, reconsideration of the profit requirement etc.

 The profit from these model points, scaled up for the expected new business can

be incorporated into a model of the whole company.

 It may be possible that the required level of profit can be reached in aggregate

without each individual model point being profitable in its own right.

 However if this is the case the company may be exposed to the risk of a change in

the mix of business.

 Once acceptable premiums have been determined for the model points, premiums

for all product variations can be determined.

This question was relatively poorly answered.

(i)

The majority of candidates failed to write sufficient points to score well. Candidates failed to

discuss a wide enough range of points in sufficient detail, A number of candidates made

vague points e.g. uncertainty in claims and failed to relate points to the product in the

question with a sufficient level of explanation.

(ii)

Better candidate gave a logical step-by-step explanation of the full modelling process.

Weaker candidates only considered parts of the modelling process.

  • Set assumptions for the expected critical illness diagnosis rates, mortality, morbidity, lapses, expenses, investment returns and tax.

  • For each model point project the cashflows allowing for projected solvency and reserving requirements.

  • The following cash flows are required in the projections: premiums, claims, expenses and investment returns on reserves.

  • The future profits are then calculated as the net cash flow, less the increase in reserves.

  • The company should discount the projected profit at a risk discount rate that reflects the return required by the company and the level of risk attached to the profits.

  • The premiums will be set so that the company achieves its required profit target.

  • The premiums need to be considered for marketability.

  • This may lead to reconsideration of the design of the product, changes to the distribution channel, reconsideration of the profit requirement etc.

  • The profit from these model points, scaled up for the expected new business can be incorporated into a model of the whole company.

  • It may be possible that the required level of profit can be reached in aggregate without each individual model point being profitable in its own right.

  • However if this is the case the company may be exposed to the risk of a change in the mix of business.

  • Once acceptable premiums have been determined for the model points, premiums for all product variations can be determined. This question was relatively poorly answered.

(i)

The majority of candidates failed to write sufficient points to score well. Candidates failed to discuss a wide enough range of points in sufficient detail, A number of candidates made vague points e.g. uncertainty in claims and failed to relate points to the product in the question with a sufficient level of explanation.

(ii)

Better candidate gave a logical step-by-step explanation of the full modelling process.

Weaker candidates only considered parts of the modelling process.

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#4 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7682

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.
