#2 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7498

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#3 2. Health and care products 5.1 Income Protection (IP) contracts Definition 0.7462

5.1 Income Protection (IP) contracts — Definition:

Income Protection is a health and care insurance product designed to replace a portion of the income an insured individual would have earned if they become incapacitated (unable to work).

  • Claims due to accident and/or illness
  • Benefits will be paid on temporary disability (not only on permanent as is the case with lump sum disability cover)
  • The benefits (a regular annuity) are paid until the insured recovers, dies or the policy term ends (usually normal retirement age).
  • A number of separate benefit periods can occur without the policy ceasing
  • In some instances the regular income may be commutable to a lump sum
  • Benefits can escalate before claim payment commences
  • Benefits can also escalate once the claim is in payment
  • Premiums are usually level, but may also increase if the benefit is increasing
  • The benefit may include a waiver of premium benefit
  • The sum insured (annuity benefit) is set so as to avoid over-insurance (replacement ration <=100%)
  • Several definitions of disability are possible, for example:
  • Unable to do own occupation, any or reasonable occuation
  • Inability to perform certain activities of daily living
  • Functional assessment tests
  • A partial benefit is possible if the policyholder is able to return to work on a parttime basis
  • There is usually no surrender of maturity benefit
#4 2. Health and care products 5.1.4 Income Protection (IP) contracts - Product Variations Guaranteed and reviewable premium rates 0.7421

5.1.4 Income Protection (IP) contracts - Product Variations — Guaranteed and reviewable premium rates:

  • IP premium designs exist at two extremes: A full guarantee of future premiums or no guarantee whatsoever
  • A frequent "middle ground" is to guarantee the premium amount for an initial period, such as the first 5 years, with the insurer gaining the freedom to review and change rates thereafter
  • Reviewable premium structure:
  • Changes are made based on the experience of the entire portfolio of policies, rather than the claims history of the individual policyholder.
  • Reviewable approaches are used because IP risks are influenced by unforeseen economic and social factors, such as unemployment trends and long-term changes in the workplace or medical science
  • Insurers with reviewable policies face the risk of selective withdrawal, where healthy individuals leave the portfolio following a premium increase, leaving the pool with sub-standard lives who are more likely to claim.

  • Guaranteed premiums
  • Generally more expenses because they require a substantial contingency loading to protect the insurer against the high uncertainty of future claims experience.

Question

QUESTION 8


i.

Embedded value is calculated as the sum of:

• The shareholder-owned share of net assets, where net assets are defined as the excess

of assets held over those required to meet liabilities.

• The discounted value of future shareholder profits arising on existing business; often

referred to as ‘present value of future profits’.

ii.

Net asset value:

• The assets may be valued at market value or may be discounted to reflect ‘lock-in’ to

the extent that assets backing solvency capital requirements are invested more

cautiously and as a result are expected to earn a lower return.

• The insurance liabilities are valued on the supervisory basis.

The future cashflows on the existing business are projected on the embedded value basis and

are used to estimate the future shareholder profit.

These cashflows include future premiums, investment income, claims and expenses, plus the

release of supervisory reserves.

The cashflows are discounted at an appropriate risk discount rate to determine the present value

of future profits (PVFP).

The risk discount rate incorporates a risk margin for unpredictability in the emergence of profit.

The PVFP is effectively the release of any margins within the supervisory reserves relative to

the embedded value basis used.

The embedded value basis is usually a realistic basis.

The insurance liabilities used in the calculation of the present value of future profits are

consistent with the insurance liabilities in the calculation of the net asset value i.e. the projected

future liabilities are on the supervisory basis.

Tax on profits and investment returns is allowed for, as appropriate.

iii.

Moving from a prudent to a best-estimate basis for determining supervisory reserves will result

in a release of reserves at the point in time that the basis changes which will increase the net

asset value.

As reserves have reduced the release of reserves over the policy lifetime will be reduced

reducing the level of the present value of expected future profits.

The impact of any possible increase in the solvency capital requirement due to the move to a

risk-based approach may have the effect of reducing the embedded value if assets are

discounted to reflect ‘lock in’ of assets to support the solvency requirements that are expected

to be invested more conservatively.

Examiners’ comments:

Part (i) was pure book work. Many students correctly identified the two components, but lost

marks by failing to indicate “shareholder’s portion of” in one or both of the components.

Part (ii) was again bookwork or the application thereof, but the question was answered less

comprehensively than expected. Many students missed marks by not describing the basis for

valuing assets, or by getting confused with a market consistent valuation method. Most students


were able to list the basic steps of projecting the cashflows, listing the cashflow components

and discounting the cashflows at an appropriate rate, but missed the points on the valuation

bases applicable to the cashflow components and the reserves.

For Part (iii), most students identified the impact on the NAV, but missed the reduction in the

release of reserves component.

#1 9. Assumptions 15.14 Embedded value How is embedded value calculated? 0.8307

15.14 Embedded value — How is embedded value calculated?:

Embedded value is calculated as the sum of:

  • Shareholders share of excess assets over reserves
  • Recorded at market value or discounted at a lower discount rate to reflect "lock-in" because they are invested cautiously
  • The present value of future shareholder profits arising on existing business (PVFP).
  • Discount of the Profit signature for existing business, the calculation may differ by type of business:
  • Conventional without-profit = $\text{PV (Net cashflow + Interest on reserves - Change in reserves)}$
  • Unit-linked: $\text{PV (Non-unit cashflow + Interest on non-unit reserves - Change in non-unit reserves)}$
  • With-profit: $\text{PV (Future shareholder transfers)}$
#2 9. Assumptions 15.14 Embedded value What is the difference between a Best estimate vs Embedded value valuation? 0.8265

15.14 Embedded value — What is the difference between a Best estimate vs Embedded value valuation?:

  • Best estimate valuation: calculates the present value liability using realistic assumptions and compares the total to the current assets to provide a measure of realistic solvency: $\text{(Value of assets) - (Realistic Liability/Reserve)}$
  • Embedded value: focuses on shareholder profit, by adding the shareholder's share of net assets to the present value of future profits that emerge in excess of reserves.
  • $\text{(Net Assets) + (Present value of future shareholder profits)}$
  • Where: $\text{(Net Assets) = (Value of assets) - (Supervisory reserve)}$

The EV calculation will give a slightly different result than a realistic profit calculation because it allows for the shareholders cost of capital. The difference stems from the deferral of profits.

  • Life companies are required to hold supervisory reserves, which are prudent/larger than realistic reserves.
  • Profits cannot be distributed to shareholders until they arise in excess of these prudent supervisory reserves. This locks in capital within the company.
  • EV discounts these future profits using the risk discount rate (RDR) which is typically higher than the realistic investment return earned on the reserves.
  • Under market consistent valuations the EV calculation deducts an explicit risk margin to account for the opportunity cost to shareholders of having capital locked in by the company.
  • $\text{EV = (Assets - BEL) - Risk Margin}$

This means that EV produces a lower valuation because it accounts for the opportunity cost to shareholders of having their profits deferred while being held as required supervisory reserves.

#3 9. Assumptions 15.14 Embedded value What is embedded value? 0.7849

15.14 Embedded value — What is embedded value?:

Embedded value is the present value of future shareholder profit in respect of the existing business of a company, including the shareholder owned net assets.

The purpose of an embedded value is to give a realistic assessment of the value of the insurance company to its shareholders.

It is also used as a starting point in calculating the Appraisal Value of a life insurance company.

#4 9. Assumptions 15.15 Consistency of assumptions Consitency between bases 0.7667

15.15 Consistency of assumptions — Consitency between bases:

  • Asset-liability valuations must be consistent, for example if assets are valued at market value, the investment return assumption for liabilities must reflect current market yields.>
  • Pricing vs Reserving: The reserves assumed during the pricing process must align with the actual supervisory reserving basis. If actual reserves are more prudent than those priced for, the cost of capital will be higher than allowed for in premiums, reducing profitability.
  • Embedded value (EV): The reserves used to calculate "net assets" must be consistent with the reserves used to determine the present value of future profits. Furthermore, the EV basis should be compared side-by-side with the pricing basis to understand the value of new business.
  • Previous basis: Any new basis should use the previous basis as a starting point. Any changes must be justifiable and the financial impact of each change should be reported separately.
#5 9. Assumptions 15.14 Embedded value How to determine assumptions (EV Basis)? 0.7518

15.14 Embedded value — How to determine assumptions (EV Basis)?:

To calculate EV we need two bases:

  • Reserving basis: use to calculate net assets and future changes in reserves to get the profit to shareholders
  • Projection basis: projects actual best estimate experience to estimate future shareholder profits

The nature of the projection assumptions depends on why the EV is being calculated:

  • Internal management or published accounts: use best estimate assumptions
  • Sale of a company: The seller uses best estimate assumptions to show the highest justifiable appraisal value.
  • Purchase of a company: A buyer might use cautious assumptions that include margins for risk to avoid overpaying.

  • Linked-claim periods: See Income Protection (IP) contracts - Features

  • Fair alteration terms: to prevent lapse and re-entry

#3 20. Monitoring experience 3. Analysis of experience What is the process for conducting a withdrawal (persistency) investigation? 0.7780

3. Analysis of experience — What is the process for conducting a withdrawal (persistency) investigation?:

1. Data collection

2. Group data into homogenous risk groups,

1. Type of contract

2. Duration in force

3. Sales method / distribution channel

4. Frequency and size of premium

5. Premium collection method (cash/debit order)

6. Original term of contract

7. Sex and age

3. Calculate persistency rates:

  • First year rates: number of contracts that survive until their first policy anniversary divided by the number of contracts issued by the company in the the last financial year
  • Subsequent years: a similar procedure is used, but there are two approaches:
  • divide by the number in force at the beginning of that year
  • divide by the number in force at the outset of the contract.

4. Regrouping the data into broader categories if the rates are similar at close durations or if differences are due to random fluctuations.

5. Analyse other forms of discontinuance:

1. paid-up policies

2. partial withdrawals

6. Consolidate and interpret the results: using

  • the general economic environment and
  • the competitive landscape or
  • the perceived value of the product to the customer.
#4 9. Assumptions 15.8 Withdrawal (Persistency) Assumptions Methodology for setting withdrawal assumptions 0.7694

15.8 Withdrawal (Persistency) Assumptions — Methodology for setting withdrawal assumptions:

  • Best estimate: assumptions should ideally be based on an analysis of the company's own recent historical experience for the specific contract or a similar class of business. If internal data is inadequate, industry-wide experience may be used as a starting point.
  • Adjustments: Professional judgement is used to adjust historical data to reflect the expected future experience of new policyholders, particularly if there have been changes in:
  • Target markets or the level of client sophistication
  • Distribution channels or sales tactics e.g. aggressive sales pressure
  • Policy benefits, such as changes in bonus rates or surrender value scales
  • Balance credibility and judgement: The extend of reliance on data versus judgement depends on the relevance, volume and predictability of the available information.
  • Incorporating margins for unpredictable economic and commercial factors, to protect the insurer against underestimating withdrawals. using judgement to assess the uncertainty.
#5 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7644

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

the defined contribution context).

• Contributions to pension schemes may be lower than expected.

• More pension scheme members take the maximum amount in cash permitted by

regulations than expected.

• Low take up of the default option because pension scheme members elect to

purchase open-market annuities:

(cid:1) Particularly members who have their own brokers and members who want a

different design feature of the annuity (for example increasing vs level

benefit payments).

(cid:1) Default annuities are a new feature so more marketing may be required.

(cid:1) Members may get better rates elsewhere.

iii. Effect of premium volumes being different than expected:

• If premium volumes are lower than expected:

(cid:1) Profits may be lower than anticipated.

(cid:1) Fixed expenses and development costs may not be covered.

(cid:1) Percentage of premium charges may be inadequate.

(cid:1) Investment freedom may be reduced.

• If premium volumes are higher than expected:

(cid:1) The company may experience capital strain depending on how onerous

solvency requirements for this type of business are.

(cid:1) There may be pressure on administration systems and servicing of customers

may be compromised.


iv. Other risks relating to the product:

Mortality and longevity:

• Mortality may be lighter than anticipated.

• This may arise due to over-estimation of base mortality or under-estimation of

mortality improvements.

• The company may have little previous experience of mortality for this target

market.

• Longevity risk is exacerbated by the risk of anti-selection, if members in poor

health elect income draw down products.

• Guaranteed death benefits expose the insurer to the risk of higher mortality early

in the policy term.

Source of business:

• There is going to be a concentration by source as one would anticipate a large

number of policies arising from each pension scheme.

• There may be some correlations between policyholders in terms of annuity

amount and mortality early in the term. Although this is only really a downside

risk if there are guarantees.

Investment returns:

• Assets that match the liability may not be available, particularly if the discounted

mean term is long.

• Matching assets may not be available for the benefit increase structure of the

insurer.

• If following an unmatched strategy, the insurer is exposed to:

(cid:1) Reinvestment risk;

(cid:1) Risk that investment returns are lower than anticipated; and

(cid:1) Movements in assets that may create solvency difficulties.

Expenses:

• Base expenses may be higher than anticipated.

• Expense inflation may be higher than anticipated.

Business volumes for other business:

• Business volumes on other annuity and income draw down products may be

reduced.

• Particularly if brokers are angered by the introduction of a no commission

product and recommend products from other insurers to customers.

Competitive pressures:

• Competitive pressures to acquire the business from pension funds may encourage

the insurer to reduce premium rates; or

• Offer additional guarantees on the product increasing the risks relating to the

product.


Reinsurance/risk transfer:

• Reinsurance may not be appropriate to manage the risks.

• Longevity swap may be the preferred risk transfer measure, but may not be

available.

• Reinsurer may default on its obligations.

Reputational risk if product does not meet the expectations of policyholders:

• No advice is given at the sales stage of this product, so members may

misunderstand the terms and conditions of the policy.

• Policyholders may select high cash lump sums resulting in low annuity payments

and hence the product failing to meet their expectations.

• Inflation may erode purchasing power, resulting in reputational risk (even for an

inflation-linked which typically increases annually).

Fraud:

• Families may claim the pension benefit after the pensioner has died.

Regulation:

• Regulation may permit entities other than life insurers to compete for example

pension schemes and may result in regulatory arbitrage.

This question required candidates to read the question carefully and plan the answers for all

four parts. The reference to “other” risks in part (iv) would have indicated this. It was clear

that many candidates did not plan their answers and needlessly lost marks for answering one

part of the question in the wrong sub-section. Many candidates did not seem to understand

what a product feature is and others lost marks through only answering half of part (iii).

Candidates are reminded that question wording is very deliberate and they must answer the

question that is asked, not the one they think should follow logically. A disturbing number of

candidates showed a complete lack of understanding of single premium products generally,

annuities in particular and how a compulsory purchase annuity would work specifically.

#1 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7635

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#2 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7615

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#3 8. Product design 14.6 Risk characteristics Accepting risk 0.7237

14.6 Risk characteristics — Accepting risk:

The acceptability of a products design and risk profile depends on the company's willingness and ability to absorb risk internally or its capacity to transfer that risk.


If a company faces a large parameter risk (such as uncertain mortality rates in a new market), it may adjust the product design in several ways:

  • Offering reviewable terms instead of long term guarantees, which allows the insurer to adjust charges if experience deteriorates
  • Offering a unit-linked version of the product, which passes on the investment risk to the policyholder
  • Reinsure a large part of the risk to limit its exposure
  • Risk margins: incorporate ample risk margins in the premium rates to protect against adverse experience.
  • Rider benefits: offer the contract as an additional rider benefit rather than a standalone.
#4 1. Life insurance contracts 3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer Investment risk 0.7226

3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer — Investment risk:

  • The insurer must invest the single premium to cover regular outgo over an unknown timeframe.
  • This risk can be mitigated by matching liabilities with fixed-interest securities with redemption dates matching the amounts being paid each year.
  • In a perfectly matched strategy, assuming that annuitants die exactly as expected, the insurance company should not need to buy or sell any of its assets during the term of the contract because the cash needed is provided by the coupons and redemption amounts.
  • This removes interest rate volatility risk and yield uncertainty because the cashflows and yields are locked in at the time when the contract was priced.
  • This scenario is impractical because:
  • Timing: The term of the annuity payments uncertain
  • Availability: Assets with perfectly matching terms may not be available (reinvestment risk)
#5 8. Product design 14.3 Marketability Marketability 0.7189

14.3 Marketability — Marketability:

Speaks the attractiveness of the product in the market:

  • Customer needs: a product must be designed to meet specific financial needs.
  • Affordability: premiums must be perceived as reasonable relative to benefits provided.
  • Expectations: design choices must respect traditional practices e.g. level premiums
  • Utility: maximizing the Utility of a product to the consumer.
  • Distribution channels: the distribution channel will have a major influence on product design
  • Volume of new business: Higher volumes could reduce per-policy fixed expense loadings

Insurers face market risk if they fail to manage policyholders expectations in the design phase due to reputation risk which could lead to loss of future sales.

2019 · NOVEMBER Supervisory Reserves and Capital Requirements; Cost of guarantees and options
Question

QUESTION 3


i. The reserve will be made up of two elements, a unit reserve and a non-unit reserve.

Unit reserve:

• The unit reserve would be equal to the value of the units held on the valuation

date, calculated by multiplying the number of units held by the bid price of a unit

on that date.

• This would ensure that, for a contract maturing on the valuation date, a unit

reserve is being held sufficient to cover the maturity benefit.

Non-unit reserve:

• A non-unit reserve is necessary if expenses are likely to exceed charges at any

future time.

• A non-unit reserve is also necessary because there is a minimum guaranteed

death benefit, of a fixed amount, that may exceed the bid value of the units.

(cid:1) This is particularly so at early durations when the guaranteed death benefit is

likely to be significantly higher than the bid value of the units.

• The non-unit reserve would be calculated by determining all the non-unit cash

flows arising under each contract, allowing for decrements. These cashflows

include:

(cid:1) Unallocated premiums, mortality charges and any other charges received (for

example annual management charge, bid/offer spreads etc.)

(cid:1) Expected renewal and claims expenses

(cid:1) Expected death benefits

(cid:1) Any profits/losses on surrender or part-surrender

• Projected cashflows will most likely be discounted at the risk-free rate.

• If the discounted value of the projected net cashflows is negative the regulator

may require the insurer to zeroise (set the present value equal to zero) on a per

policy basis or on a portfolio basis.

ii. Suggested approach for reserving for the investment guarantee:

• A stochastic model would be the preferred approach to determine the reserve for

any shortfalls in the value of the unit fund relative to the guaranteed minimum

maturity value.

Reasons why a deterministic model would be inappropriate:

• Under a deterministic model the future value of the fund may be projected using

the expected level of investment returns less charges based on the expected asset

allocation for the investment fund.

• The fund value projected on this basis is likely to exceed the minimum

guaranteed value at maturity, resulting in a zero reserve for the investment

guarantee.

• Although a few investment outcome scenarios can be tested using a deterministic

model, the scenarios selected are subjective and it is difficult to assign a

probability to them, in addition this type of model is unlikely to give a sufficient


range of investment outcomes to determine the reserve for an investment

guarantee.

Use of a stochastic model will produce a range of outcomes of fund values based on the

simulated investment returns, a number of these outcomes will reflect a shortfall in the

unit fund compared to the guaranteed minimum maturity value.

Use of a stochastic model in this regard could follow the approach outlined below:

• A stochastic model would project the unit fund using many different simulated

investment scenarios, where the future investment returns are governed by a

probability distribution function.

• The assumptions underlying the model should reflect the investment strategy of

the unit fund.

• The shortfall relating to the investment guarantee (i.e. where the fund value lower

than the guaranteed minimum payment at maturity) will be determined for each

investment scenario.

• The projected future shortfall may be reduced by the projected value of future

charges on the unit fund relating to the investment guarantee.

• The present value of the shortfall can be determined by discounting the projected

shortfalls at a suitable discount rate.

• The probability of the policy maturing should be taken into account through

relevant decrements (for example mortality and withdrawals).

• Repeated simulation (1000s of simulations) will generate the probability

distribution of outcomes for the reserves for the investment guarantee.

• The reserve for the investment guarantee could be set as the expected (i.e.

average) present value of the simulated outcomes.

• If more prudence is required at point on the distribution of outcomes representing

the regulator’s risk tolerance for example 75% level could be chosen.

• Care should be taken in the level of confidence placed on the results as they are

sensitive to distribution and the calibration of the parameters for the investment

returns.

(cid:1) Since this is a developing country there may not be sufficient data available

to calibrate the model with confidence.

This question was relatively poorly answered. In general candidates structured their answers

poorly and failed to focus their answers on the key aspects of the question. This resulted in

wasted time on unnecessary points and missing important points.

For part (i) stronger candidates explained the method for reserving for both the unit fund and

non-unit fund in a methodical manner, while weaker candidates discussed reserving in

general. A number of candidates wasted time by giving too much detail on general issues for

reserving.

In part (ii) the majority of candidates failed to give sufficient detail in explaining the method

stochastic modelling.

#1 10. Reserving 3. Non-unit reserves How is the non-unit reserve calculated in a Prudential valuation? 0.7940

3. Non-unit reserves — How is the non-unit reserve calculated in a Prudential valuation?:

The non-unit reserve is defined as the amount required to ensure that the company is able to pay claims and expenses without needing further financing.


The company projects forwards its year-by-year non-unit cashflows on the reserving basis and works backwards from the end of the policy term.

1. Project cashflows

2. Identify the last negative cashflow

3. Zeroise the shortfall by holding the required money at the start of that period and allowing for investment returns during the year.

4. Deduct from the cashflow at end of the previous period.

5. Repeat backward.


At the end of the zeroization process (valuation date), if the discounted adjusted cashflow is negative then a non-unit reserve is set up equal to the absolute value of that negative amount. In a prudential valuation if the discounted adjusted cashflow is non-negative the non-unit reserve is typically set to zero.

#2 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor 0.7887

12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:

Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.

  • Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be

$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$

  • Where:
  • $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
  • $x$ is the entry age
  • $n$ is the policy term
  • Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.
#3 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding example 0.7883

12.2 Actuarial funding — example:

The setup:

  • Single premium: R10 000 (purchasing 10 000 units at R1 each)
  • Annual FMC: 5 (levied only on units physically held)
  • Discount rate for funding $(i)$: 4%
  • Policy term: 5 years
  • Age ($x$): 40 year old
  • Investment return $(g)$: 7%
  • Actuarial funding factor ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$): A multiplier that determines the required reserve based on the 4% and the probability of the contingent events (death or maturity)

----

Year 0: Inception

At the start, the insurer calculates the actuarially funded unit reserve instead of holding the full R10 000.

  • Funding factor ($A_{40:\overline{5|}}$): $0.8219$ (based on 4% discount over 5 years)
  • Reserve physically held: $$V_0 = R 10,000 * 0.8219 = R 8,219$$
  • Cashflow to non-unit fund: $R10,000 - R8,219$
  • This positive cashflow is used to pay for initial expenses like commission and underwriting.
  • The insurer is now missing $1,781$ units that it must buy back later.

---

#4 16. Reinsurance 3.2 Retention limits Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve 0.7879

3.2 Retention limits — Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve:

In this approach, insurers aim to minimize the total cost of two components:

  • the cost of obtaining reinsurance and
  • the cost of financing a mortality fluctuations reserve.

The process follows these steps:

1. Set a risk criterion: such as a maximum 1% probability that net losses will exceed a specific amount e.g. 25m

2. Model total costs: for different retention limits, the insurer stochastically models the expected net loss by varying the mortality rates. As the retention limit increases, the cost of reinsurance decreases, but the size of the required fluctuations reserve (and its associated financing cost) increases.

3. Calculate the financing cost: The cost of the reserve ($M$) is calculated as $M \times (j - i)$, where $j$ is the required rate of return on the company's capital and $i$ is the actual investment return earned on the reserve's assets.

4. Optimize: The insurer identifies the specific retention limit where the combined cost of the reserve and reinsurance is lowest while still satisfying the ruin probability target.

#5 10. Reserving 3. Non-unit reserves What is a non-unit reserve? 0.7807

3. Non-unit reserves — What is a non-unit reserve?:

Due to the complexity of unit linked-contracts a cashflow approach is necessary. We refer to the gross premium cashflow reserve of a unit-linked contract as the non-unit reserve.

$$\text{Non-unit reserve} = \text{EPV[Non-unit Outgo]} - \text{EPV[Non-unit Income]}$$

Where:

  • Non-unit outgo: includes future costs, such as administration expenses, benefit outgo in excess of the unit fund.
  • Non-unit income: includes unallocated premiums, fund management charges, risk charges and bid-offer spreads

QUESTION 4


i. The approach for determining surrender values should take the following principles into

account:

• For both methods, whether the principle that the surrender value should take

policyholder reasonable expectations into account is met depends on whether the

calculated surrender values are consistent with the information provided to

customers at the sales stage.

• Both methods are likely to meet this principle that the surrender value should not

appear too low compared to premiums paid at early durations by definition of the

surrender value.

• Traditional products are unlikely to meet the principle that the surrender value

should be consistent with projected maturity values at later durations.

(cid:1) The guaranteed maturity value is should be higher than premiums paid as it

takes investment earnings over the term of the policy into account.

• New-generation products are likely to meet the principle above as the prospective

surrender value is likely to progress smoothly towards the maturity value over

time.

• Traditional products are unlikely to meet the principle that the surrender value

should not exceed the earned asset share in aggregate, over a reasonable period.

(cid:1) As, the surrender value is likely to be higher than the asset share at early

durations and lower at later durations in the policy term.

• New-generation products are likely to meet the principle above as the prospective

method is likely to be lower than the earned asset share.

• The traditional products do not meet the principle that the surrender value should

produce a reasonable contribution to profit of the insurer and maintain equity

with continuing policyholders and shareholders.

(cid:1) There will be losses at early durations and excessive profits at later durations.

• Whether above principle is met for new-generation products depends on whether

the basis used for the prospective method allows the insurer to recover the losses

at early durations and produce a profit that is not excessive after the second

policy anniversary.

• Traditional products are unlikely to meet the principle that the surrender value

should avoid selection against the insurer.

(cid:1) As early surrenders are encouraged and later surrenders are discouraged.

• For new-generation products surrenders prior to the second policy anniversary

may be encouraged, but the effect may be less severe than for the traditional

products.

• Surrender values for traditional products are not consistent with those for new-

generation products, thus do not take the approach taken by all competitors into

account.

• Consistency of surrender values across new-generation products depends on the

basis used for the prospective method.

• Traditional products are likely to meet the principle that the surrender value

should avoid discontinuities by duration.


• New-generation products are unlikely to meet this principle as there is likely to be

a discontinuity at the second policy anniversary where the method changes.

• Both methods are likely to meet the objective that the surrender value should not

be subject to frequent change, unless the basis for the prospective method is

changed frequently.

• Both methods are likely to meet the objective that the surrender value should not

be excessively complicated to calculate, unless the basis is complicated for the

prospective calculation for the new-generation products.

• Both methods are likely to meet this principle that the surrender value should be

capable of being clearly documented.

ii. Profit arising for each of the bases under consideration for the prospective method of

determining surrender values:

• The total profit retained by the insurer is the excess of the earned asset share over

the surrender value paid (EAS – SV)

• This can be separated into two parts: the profit earned to date (EAS – SV(p)), and

the capitalised value of the profit that will arise in the future due to differences

between the original premium rate assumptions and the surrender value

assumptions (SV(p) – SV), where SV(p) is the prospective surrender value on the

original premium basis.

• At early durations there will be a loss on surrender where the asset share is lower

than the premiums paid to date or the prospective surrender value.

• After early durations the profit earned to date is the difference between actual

experience and that assumed in the original premium basis.

• The value for capitalised future profits will be:

(cid:1) zero if the original premium basis is used for determining the surrender value;

and

(cid:1) equal to the expected future profits as if the policy had not been surrendered,

if the best estimate of future experience is used.

• Depending on how the expenses relating to the policy surrender are allowed for in

the charge for the surrender, these expenses may reduce the profit.

Part (i) was poorly answered by many candidates. The question related to a relatively

straightforward application of the bookwork on surrender value principles to two example

products. Candidates who approached the question in a systematic way and explained the

extent to which each product meets each of the surrender principles scored well, with some

even able to earn full marks for the question. A very large number of candidates however

merely stated the theory, with little reference to the question and no substantive explanation

of how each product meets each of the surrender value principles, and consequently were not

able to score very well.

Part (ii) was bookwork, but answers were largely a “hit-or-miss”, with candidates either

getting close to full marks or close to zero. Those candidates that took a structured approach

to work through each of the components of profit at the point of surrender scored well.

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 4


i. The approach for determining surrender values should take the following principles into

account:


  • For both methods, whether the principle that the surrender value should take policyholder reasonable expectations into account is met depends on whether the calculated surrender values are consistent with the information provided to customers at the sales stage.

  • Both methods are likely to meet this principle that the surrender value should not appear too low compared to premiums paid at early durations by definition of the surrender value.

  • Traditional products are unlikely to meet the principle that the surrender value should be consistent with projected maturity values at later durations. The guaranteed maturity value is should be higher than premiums paid as it takes investment earnings over the term of the policy into account.

  • New-generation products are likely to meet the principle above as the prospective surrender value is likely to progress smoothly towards the maturity value over time.

  • Traditional products are unlikely to meet the principle that the surrender value should not exceed the earned asset share in aggregate, over a reasonable period. As, the surrender value is likely to be higher than the asset share at early durations and lower at later durations in the policy term.

  • New-generation products are likely to meet the principle above as the prospective method is likely to be lower than the earned asset share.

  • The traditional products do not meet the principle that the surrender value should produce a reasonable contribution to profit of the insurer and maintain equity with continuing policyholders and shareholders. There will be losses at early durations and excessive profits at later durations.

  • Whether above principle is met for new-generation products depends on whether the basis used for the prospective method allows the insurer to recover the losses at early durations and produce a profit that is not excessive after the second policy anniversary.

  • Traditional products are unlikely to meet the principle that the surrender value should avoid selection against the insurer. As early surrenders are encouraged and later surrenders are discouraged.

  • For new-generation products surrenders prior to the second policy anniversary may be encouraged, but the effect may be less severe than for the traditional products.

  • Surrender values for traditional products are not consistent with those for newgeneration products, thus do not take the approach taken by all competitors into account.

  • Consistency of surrender values across new-generation products depends on the basis used for the prospective method.

  • New-generation products are unlikely to meet this principle as there is likely to be a discontinuity at the second policy anniversary where the method changes.

  • Both methods are likely to meet the objective that the surrender value should not be subject to frequent change, unless the basis for the prospective method is changed frequently.

  • Both methods are likely to meet the objective that the surrender value should not be excessively complicated to calculate, unless the basis is complicated for the prospective calculation for the new-generation products.

  • Both methods are likely to meet this principle that the surrender value should be capable of being clearly documented.

ii. Profit arising for each of the bases under consideration for the prospective method of

determining surrender values:


  • The total profit retained by the insurer is the excess of the earned asset share over the surrender value paid (EAS - SV)

  • This can be separated into two parts: the profit earned to date (EAS - SV(p)), and the capitalised value of the profit that will arise in the future due to differences between the original premium rate assumptions and the surrender value assumptions (SV(p) - SV), where SV(p) is the prospective surrender value on the original premium basis.

  • At early durations there will be a loss on surrender where the asset share is lower than the premiums paid to date or the prospective surrender value.

  • After early durations the profit earned to date is the difference between actual experience and that assumed in the original premium basis.

  • The value for capitalised future profits will be: zero if the original premium basis is used for determining the surrender value; and equal to the expected future profits as if the policy had not been surrendered, if the best estimate of future experience is used.

#2 12. Surrender values 4. Surrender basis How to determine the basis for a prospective surrender value? 0.7938

4. Surrender basis — How to determine the basis for a prospective surrender value?:

Determining a prospective surrender basis involves selecting assumptions for future experience that balance profit retention with policyholder equity.

  • Interest rate: The most critical parameter. It is typically set based on the current weighted average redemption yield of matching fixed-interest securities
  • Expenses: Derived from the company's latest expense investigation.
  • Includes the costs of processing the surrender
  • renewal expenses and commissions
  • excludes prudential margins.
  • Mortality: reflects the expected lighter mortality of those who choose to leave.
  • select mortality could be used (although the selective process is not the same as that of the standard table used)
  • use unadjusted mortality and rely on other margins in the basis for diferrences in the mortality of leavers.
  • Inflation: set consistently with investment returns i.e. The link between inflation and investment returns
  • price-inflation and earnings inflation
#3 12. Surrender values 4. Surrender basis How to determine the basis for a retrospective surrender value? 0.7826

4. Surrender basis — How to determine the basis for a retrospective surrender value?:

To determine the basis for a retrospective surrender value, and insurer examines its actual past experience for the specific policy or group of policies.

  • Investment earnings: The actual rates of return earned on the backing assets, which may be smoothed over time for regular premium contracts.
  • Expenses: The actual marginal acquisition and administration costs incurred to date
  • Mortality/morbidity: The actual claims experience
  • Taxation: any tax paid on investment income or capital gains attributable to the policy

Insurers may deviate from "true" experience for specific reasons, such as:

  • Profit retention: They might an investment return lower than actual to ensure the company retains a profit margin
  • Marketability: They might deduct lower than actual expenses if the true asset share would results in an embarrassingly low value for the policyholder
#4 12. Surrender values 2. Methods of calculation Explain the prospective method 0.7810

2. Methods of calculation — Explain the prospective method:

The discounted value of future benefits and expenses, net of future premiums using best estimate assumptions.

  • ensures the surrender value progresses smoothly into the maturity value
  • allows the company to capitalize future profits
  • used primarily after the initial early stage of the policy.
  • It is very sensitive to future assumptions, particularly the interest rate assumption

Example: $$SV = SA \cdot A_{x+t} + e \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t} + f \cdot A_{x+t} - G \cdot \ddot{a}^{(m)}_{x+t} - C$$

#5 12. Surrender values 3. Retention of profit on surrender How does the choice of surrender basis influence how much future profit is extracted/capitalized? 0.7745

3. Retention of profit on surrender — How does the choice of surrender basis influence how much future profit is extracted/capitalized?:

The profit on surrender is equal to the Asset share per policy less the surrender benefit paid.

The profit on surrender is zero when the surrender benefit is equal to the earned asset share.


The capitalized value of future profit arises from the differences between the premium rate assumptions and the surrender values assumptions.

  • Best estimate basis: If the insurer uses realistic, best estimate assumptions for calculating the surrender value, it effectively retains the same total profit it would have made if the contract stayed in force until the end
  • Premium basis: If the insurer uses the original premium basis (with margins), it only retains the profit made up to date.
  • Blended basis: Capitalising future profits may be considered unfair to surrendering policyholders so many companies use a "blended" approach, which is a basis between the realistic basis and the premium basis

F102_NOVEMBER_2019_Papergeneral_Q5

2019 · NOVEMBER With-profits surplus distribution
Question

QUESTION 5


i. Description of bonus types:

Regular reversionary bonus:

• A regular reversionary bonus is a bonus that is declared on a regular basis,

usually annually, during the lifetime of the contract.

• Once declared it attaches to the benefits and is guaranteed.

• It may be declared as a percentage of basic benefit and/or any bonuses already

declared (using a simple, compound or super compound method).

Special reversionary bonus:

• A special reversionary bonus is a once-off/irregular increase to the sum assured.

• It could result from surplus from an isolated event for example restructure of a

fund or some investment windfall.

• Should declared and communicated in a way that does not change policyholders’

reasonable expectations.

Terminal bonus:

• A terminal bonus is an addition to the benefit payable, but only determined at the

time of the claim or maturity.

• In theory this implies a potentially constantly changing bonus. In practice this

does not happen, but even so a company will not guarantee to maintain the bonus

at any particular level.

• It is particularly useful for distributing profits that come from volatile sources,

such as capital gains on equity shares.

• The bonus may vary by term and duration.

• It is often used to bring the policy value in line with the asset share at date of

maturity/claim.

ii. Allowance in pricing:

Regular reversionary bonus:

• The pricing basis may include an explicit margin to price for some minimum

bonus every year.

• This will be achieved through a reduction in the interest rate.

• This will be particularly the case if policyholders’ reasonable expectations

include a regular bonus.

• Any margins for prudence in the basis may implicitly allow for regular bonuses to

be declared if emerging experience is better than the prudent assumptions.

Special reversionary bonus:

• It is unlikely that this will be allowed for explicitly in the pricing, since:

(cid:1) any historic special bonuses would typically have been granted without

creating an expectation of this being a regular feature of the product.


Terminal bonus:

• It is unlikely that this will be priced for explicitly.

• Unless, however, it has become well known that there is a terminal bonus payable

on every claim at this life office, which one can argue changes the reasonable

expectations of the policyholder.

(cid:1) This might be the case for a company that operates with-profits business,

with no regular or special bonus declarations.

iii. Impact on choice of bonus type:

• Once a reversionary bonus is declared it becomes part of the guaranteed benefits

under a policy, and will therefore be included in the supervisory reserves.

• Terminal bonuses will not increase the supervisory reserves.

• Given the company’s high level of free reserves and investment approach, it is

likely that it invests in riskier asset classes and does not match assets and

liabilities closely.

• The company might prefer to postpone distributing bonuses and lean towards

more terminal bonuses, since:

(cid:1) investment returns on riskier asset classes may be volatile;

(cid:1) if decreases in asset values are not matched by decreases in liabilities, the

solvency position might deteriorate.

• The company may also want to add any surplus arising to free assets in order to

maintain its solvency position or to use a strong level of free assets to make

higher risk investments in the hope of generating higher returns. This will make it

lean towards postponing the surplus distribution.

• Alternatively, since the insurer has a healthy solvency margin it may tend towards

declaring regular bonuses rather than at the end of the policy term in order to

improve the marketability/sales of their product.

• However, the impact of higher supervisory reserves on the solvency margin and

new business strain must be considered.

• The company is therefore likely to use a low level of regular reversionary bonus,

in conjunction with high terminal bonuses on its endowment assurance portfolio.

Part (i) was bookwork and answered very well.

Part (ii) was also answered well, although many candidates only considered either explicit or

implicit allowance for bonuses and not both.

Part (iii) was answered satisfactorily, but many candidates struggled to articulate their

arguments clearly. Many wasted time discussing various investment strategies required by a

given bonus philosophy, instead of answering the question of how the investment strategy

might impact the choice of bonus.

QUESTION 5


i. Description of bonus types:

Regular reversionary bonus:


  • A regular reversionary bonus is a bonus that is declared on a regular basis, usually annually, during the lifetime of the contract.

  • Once declared it attaches to the benefits and is guaranteed.

  • It may be declared as a percentage of basic benefit and/or any bonuses already declared (using a simple, compound or super compound method). Special reversionary bonus:

  • A special reversionary bonus is a once-off/irregular increase to the sum assured.

  • It could result from surplus from an isolated event for example restructure of a fund or some investment windfall.

  • Should declared and communicated in a way that does not change policyholders' reasonable expectations. Terminal bonus:

  • A terminal bonus is an addition to the benefit payable, but only determined at the time of the claim or maturity.

  • In theory this implies a potentially constantly changing bonus. In practice this does not happen, but even so a company will not guarantee to maintain the bonus at any particular level.

  • It is particularly useful for distributing profits that come from volatile sources, such as capital gains on equity shares.

  • The bonus may vary by term and duration.

  • It is often used to bring the policy value in line with the asset share at date of maturity/claim.

ii. Allowance in pricing:

Regular reversionary bonus:


  • The pricing basis may include an explicit margin to price for some minimum bonus every year.

  • This will be achieved through a reduction in the interest rate.

  • This will be particularly the case if policyholders' reasonable expectations include a regular bonus.

  • Any margins for prudence in the basis may implicitly allow for regular bonuses to be declared if emerging experience is better than the prudent assumptions. Special reversionary bonus:

Terminal bonus:


  • It is unlikely that this will be priced for explicitly.

  • Unless, however, it has become well known that there is a terminal bonus payable on every claim at this life office, which one can argue changes the reasonable expectations of the policyholder. This might be the case for a company that operates with-profits business, with no regular or special bonus declarations.

iii. Impact on choice of bonus type:


  • Once a reversionary bonus is declared it becomes part of the guaranteed benefits under a policy, and will therefore be included in the supervisory reserves.

  • Terminal bonuses will not increase the supervisory reserves.

  • Given the company's high level of free reserves and investment approach, it is likely that it invests in riskier asset classes and does not match assets and liabilities closely.

  • The company might prefer to postpone distributing bonuses and lean towards more terminal bonuses, since: investment returns on riskier asset classes may be volatile; if decreases in asset values are not matched by decreases in liabilities, the solvency position might deteriorate.

  • The company may also want to add any surplus arising to free assets in order to maintain its solvency position or to use a strong level of free assets to make higher risk investments in the hope of generating higher returns. This will make it lean towards postponing the surplus distribution.

  • Alternatively, since the insurer has a healthy solvency margin it may tend towards declaring regular bonuses rather than at the end of the policy term in order to improve the marketability/sales of their product.

  • However, the impact of higher supervisory reserves on the solvency margin and new business strain must be considered.

#1 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.1 Addition to benefits - conventional with profits Regular reversionary bonuses 0.8055

9.1.1 Addition to benefits - conventional with profits — Regular reversionary bonuses:

  • Usually declared annually
  • Guaranteed: Once a reversionary bonus is declared, it becomes a Guarantee.
  • Smoothed: The insurer uses smoothing to change bonus rates gradually overtime rather than suddenly, which helps meet Policyholders’ Reasonable Expectations (PRE).
  • Calculation methods:
  • Simple: the bonus is a percentage of the basic benefit only
  • Compound: the bonus is a percentage of the basic benefit plus any previously attached bonuses.
  • Super-compound: The bonus uses two percentages - one applied to the basic benefit and a second (typically higher) percentage applied to previous bonuses. This method defers the distribution of surplus as compared to simple or compound.

!ASSA/F102 Life Insurance Principles/Diagrams/Pasted image 20260127071545.png

  • Capital Efficiency: Methods that defer the build-up of these guarantees, such as the super-compound method, are more capital efficient because they keep supervisory reserves lower in the early years.
#2 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.1 Addition to benefits - conventional with profits Special reversionary bonus 0.7964

9.1.1 Addition to benefits - conventional with profits — Special reversionary bonus:

A once-off bonus declared on an ad-hoc basis in addition to any regular reversionary bonus.

  • Managing expectations of policyholders: The primary intention of declaring a bonus as "special" is to grant an increase in benefits without creating a reasonable expectation that similar increases will be granted in the future.
  • Use cases: Used to distribute surplus from sources that are unlikely to arise again, for example:
  • The restructuring of a with-profits fund
  • Surplus from a demutualisation or a takeover
#3 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.1 Addition to benefits - conventional with profits Terminal bonuses 0.7686

9.1.1 Addition to benefits - conventional with profits — Terminal bonuses:

A terminal bonus is an additional profit distribution paid only when the contract reaches maturity, or upon death or surrender.

  • Purpose: Used to distribute other sources of surplus such as
  • volatile sources e.g. capital gains
  • withdrawal
  • expense and
  • mortality profits
  • Deferral: The primary purpose of a terminal bonus is that it defers the distribution of surplus until the very end of the contract. This slows the build-up of fixed guarantees, providing the insurer with greater investment freedom to invest in volatile higher returning assets like equities.
  • Link to asset share: Ensures that the final payout is equal to the policy's asset share. (the accumulated net cashflow of the policy)
  • Calculation method: It is often expressed as a percentage of of total reversionary bonuses or total claim amount before the terminal bonus is added.
  • Lack of guarantee: Unlike reversionary bonuses, terminal bonuses are not guaranteed until the insured event actually occurs. Insurers typically set the terminal bonus rates annually but may decrease them suddenly in response to market crashes.
#4 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.2 Addition to benefits - accumulating with profits Regular annual bonuses 0.7565

9.1.2 Addition to benefits - accumulating with profits — Regular annual bonuses:

In Accumulating With-profits contracts, bonuses are added annually based on the total of premiums paid to date plus any bonuses that have been declared. These bonuses act like interest:

$$ F_{t+1} = (F_t + P_t - c_t)(1 + b_t)$$

Where:

  • F is the Benefit/Fund value
  • P is the Premium
  • c represents charges
  • b is the regular bonus rate

There is an explicit relationship between the premiums paid and the addition to the benefit (allocation rate). These contracts are often unitised, however it is not necessary for the contract to be unitised

#5 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.2 Addition to benefits - accumulating with profits Unitised with-profits 0.7392

9.1.2 Addition to benefits - accumulating with profits — Unitised with-profits:

If the contract is structured as unitised with-profits, the regular bonuses are delivered in one of two ways:

  • Constant unit price: the price of a unit remains fixed and the insurer allocates additional units to each contract (usually annually) at the bonus declarations. There could be a minimum bonus declaration of zero or some positive percentage.
  • Variable unit price: The insurer changes the price of the units (usually on a daily basis). The increase is made up of a guaranteed part (possibly zero) and a bonus part.

• The insurer would look to match assets and liabilities as closely as possible. The

(cid:1) The risk of insolvency is likely to be too high.

QUESTION 6


i. Liability characteristics and matching assets:


  • The insurer would look to match assets and liabilities as closely as possible. The extent to which the insurer will deviate from this fully matched approach will depend on its risk appetite and free capital.

  • The nature of the benefits is without-profit, and this is best matched by fixed interest stocks.

  • Fixed interest stock issued by government should be risk free.

  • Corporate bonds might be considered if the insurer is willing to accept (and hold capital for) default and illiquidity risk in order to enhance returns.

  • If the benefits for any of the products are linked to an index (for example indexlinked immediate annuity) then these liabilities are best matched by index-linked bonds.

  • The term of suitable fixed interest stocks depends on the outstanding term of policies and annuities issued by the insurer: Term assurance policies may have terms of less than 10 years. Immediate life annuities and whole of life policies are likely to have terms greater than 10 years.

  • Future insurer expenses are likely to be inflation-linked, and these are best matched by index-linked bonds of suitable terms or a mix of real assets that includes a limited exposure to equities.

  • Currency is likely to be local, and hence assets need to be of the same currency.

  • Shorter-term liabilities (of less than one year) and working capital are best matched by money market stocks: Money market stocks are highly liquid in nature, have stable capital values and are hence a good match for short-term liabilities.

  • In practice it might not be possible to find fixed interest stocks of long enough term for the annuities: The insurer will then need to consider whether to accept (and hold capital) for the term mismatch or find alternative investments (for example, foreign bonds of long duration with a currency hedge).

iii. Director's proposal:

#1 1. Life insurance contracts 3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer Investment risk 0.7836

3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer — Investment risk:

  • The insurer must invest the single premium to cover regular outgo over an unknown timeframe.
  • This risk can be mitigated by matching liabilities with fixed-interest securities with redemption dates matching the amounts being paid each year.
  • In a perfectly matched strategy, assuming that annuitants die exactly as expected, the insurance company should not need to buy or sell any of its assets during the term of the contract because the cash needed is provided by the coupons and redemption amounts.
  • This removes interest rate volatility risk and yield uncertainty because the cashflows and yields are locked in at the time when the contract was priced.
  • This scenario is impractical because:
  • Timing: The term of the annuity payments uncertain
  • Availability: Assets with perfectly matching terms may not be available (reinvestment risk)
#2 18. Investments 2. Principles of investment How does the nature, term and currency of liabilities affect asset selection? 0.7719

2. Principles of investment — How does the nature, term and currency of liabilities affect asset selection?:

  • The liability outgo consists of:
  • Benefit payments
  • Expense outgo
  • minus: premium income
  • In any given year the liability outgo depends on the monetary amount of its constituents and the probability of it being received or paid out.

  • The liabilities may be:
  • Guaranteed in money terms: Match with fixed-interest bonds or cash
  • Guaranteed in terms of an index: use index-linked bonds or potentially property investment (rental income) or equities that move in line with CPI.
  • Short-term index linked liabilities could be matched by fixed interest stocks

  • Discretionary: backed by real assets like equity or property for higher bonuses
  • Investment-linked: hold the exact assets the benefits are linked to.

Term:

  • The focus is on the discounted mean term (duration) of the liability. By matching the duration of assets to liabilities, the company ensures that if interest rates change, the values of both assets and liabilities move in line with each other.
  • However insurance liabilities tend to be longer term that available assets in the market.
#3 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7676

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#4 18. Investments 2. Principles of investment Issues with matching equity-index linked liabilities 0.7652

2. Principles of investment — Issues with matching equity-index linked liabilities:

  • The assets should be invested to match or replicate the equity index
  • Index replication requires holdings in the correct weights
  • Tracking the index requires monitoring and rebalancing
  • purchasing every stock in the index may be impractical
  • transaction costs from frequent trading may reduce returns below the required index-linked return
  • buying and selling at the same time as other index trackers may move prices
  • inflows and outflows must be invest/disinvested in line with the index, this may be difficult for small cashflows
  • the insurer may use specialist index-tracking strategies
  • proxy portfolios or quantitative replication techniques may be used

#5 5. Risks 11.3 Investment risk Mismatching risk 0.7356

11.3 Investment risk — Mismatching risk:

This involves a discrepancy between the discounted mean term (duration) of the assets and the liabilities

  • Reinvestment risk: If assets have a shorter duration than liabilities, proceeds are available earlier than required and must be reinvested at unknown future rates. If interest rates fall, the insurer may be unable to secure the yields needed to meet long-term guarantees
  • Capital values risk: If assets have a longer duration than liabilities, the insurer may be forced to sell assets to meet claims. If interest rates rise, the market value of the assets will fall more than the value of the liabilities, potentially causing insolvency.
