Top Matching Notes 5 matches
#1 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7948

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#2 4. External environment 10. The external environment 1. Volume and mix of new business 0.7583

10. The external environment — 1. Volume and mix of new business:

The insurer should consider the expected volume of new business, since this affects profitability, expense recovery, solvency strain and operational capacity.


If volumes are too low, the insurer may not recover fixed costs such as product development, systems, marketing, distribution and regulatory approval costs.


If volumes are too high, the insurer may suffer from new business strain, especially where initial expenses, commission or reserving requirements are high.


The insurer should also consider the expected mix of business, for example by: age, gender, sum assured or benefit level, premium term, policy duration, distribution channel, socio-economic group, underwriting class. A change in business mix may alter the risk profile, capital requirements, claims experience, expense assumptions and profitability of the business.

#3 1. Life insurance contracts 4.1.3 Unit-linked contracts - Risks to the insurer External risks 0.7527

4.1.3 Unit-linked contracts - Risks to the insurer — External risks:

  • Marketing and reputational risk: Because these contracts have lower guarantees, they produce greater uncertainty of return for the policyholder. If investment performance is poor, it can lead to policyholder dissatisfaction, bad publicity, and reduced future sales, especially if the risks were not clearly understood at the time of purchase.
  • Marketing pressures, competition, or legislative restrictions may prevent an insurer from increasing reviewable charges enough to cover deteriorating expense performance
  • Changes in Legislation: There is a risk that regulatory changes could restrict an insurer's ability to hold negative non-unit reserves or use actuarial funding to reduce capital strain (taking advance credit for future contributions toward initial expenses that were already incurred)
#4 4. External environment 10. The external environment 12. Capital and solvency requirements 0.7499

10. The external environment — 12. Capital and solvency requirements:

The insurer should consider the capital required to write the business.


Capital requirements may be affected by: guarantees, long-term liabilities, uncertainty in assumptions, investment risk, lapse risk, expense risk, mortality or morbidity risk, operational risk.


If capital requirements are high, the product may need higher premiums or may not meet the insurer's target return on capital. Rapid growth may also create solvency strain.

#5 4. External environment 10.4 Economic Environment The state of the economy 0.7468

10.4 Economic Environment — The state of the economy:

The state of the economy in which an insurer operates will carry risks for the insurer by influencing the:

  • Availability of asset types: the available assets and their short and long term expected yields will influence investment strategy and interest rate assumptions. From the consumers point of view, insurance products may be seen as more or less attractive when compared with other available investment options e.g. bank accounts, unit trusts, shares or not investing at all
  • Volatility of investment markets: e.g. in developing markets, will tend to increase the cost of capital for insurers (higher capital requirements), so increasing premiums, and can also affect the demand for life insurance products.

F102_NOVEMBER_2020_Papergeneral_Q8

2020 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 8


i. Suitability of corporate bonds:

 The assets match the benefit liabilities in respect of:

 Nature: The non-profit annuity is fixed in nature, while the corporate bond returns are

fixed in nature (provided they are held to maturity).

 Currency: The assets and liabilities are both in local currency terms.

 It is unclear if the assets match the liabilities by term, however this may be unlikely since:

 Life annuities are likely to have long terms (exceeding 20 years).

 Corporate bonds are unlikely to exceed 20 years due to the investment risk associated

with such a long term.

 It is therefore likely that there exists significant reinvestment risk for the insurer in

needing to roll-over the investments.

 As this is a developing country, there may not be a well-developed corporate bond

market, which will make it difficult to achieve exact term matching.

 The insurer’s expenses in respect of annuities are real in nature, and therefore the bonds do

not provide a suitable match by nature for these liabilities.

 Corporate bonds are likely to be far less liquid than government bonds, however this may

not be a large concern for the insurer if bonds can be held to maturity.

 Corporate bonds carry a risk of default, and this is unlikely to make them suitable for

matching guaranteed benefits:

 The insurer may have a high level of capital assets to absorb some defaults, however it

is unlikely to have sufficient free assets in the event of large-scale defaults.

 Corporate bonds are likely to offer higher expected returns compared to government bonds,

to compensate for the higher default risk and lower liquidity:

 This may allow the insurer to offer better annuity rates than competitors (provided it

only takes credit for the liquidity premium, not the default risk premium).

ii. The insurer can use a model to determine the suitability of proposed investment strategies as

follows:

 The liabilities, minimum regulatory capital and the assets are projected forward on

assumptions that represent expected future experience.

 The insurer will also consider the effect of variations in the assumptions on the asset and

liability projections.

 The insurer will determine an appropriate projection period (e.g. for the current strategic

business planning or capital planning period) and an appropriate projection frequency (e.g.

quarterly but at least annually to provide sufficient information on the free assets of the

insurer).

 Liabilities and regulatory minimum required capital will be projected on the current

supervisory basis based on the:

 Current in-force policies using all the individual policies or model points and

expected future new business using model points for the expect profile of new

policyholders.

 Assumptions for this model should be consistent with the assumptions for the asset

model (e.g. the inflation rate should be consistent with investments returns).


 Assets (including free assets) will be projected using:

 A stochastic investment model to simulate future investment returns and capital gains

and losses.

 The asset mix will be based on the current asset mix and expected future changes in

asset mix.

 Considering any regulatory restrictions on asset admissibility and liquidity needs of

the insurer.

 The level of free assets will be determined at the end of each quarter for the entire projection

period.

 The insurer will assess whether the projected levels of free assets meet the requirement of free

assets being at least double of the minimum capital required by the regulator.

 The stochastic models can be run many (1000s) of times using the randomly generated

investment returns.

 This will produce a statistical distribution of the free assets relative to the regulatory

minimum required capital available each quarter.

 From this, the probability of not meeting the insurer’s targeted level of free assets can be

estimated given a particular investment strategy.

 The insurer will repeat the process for the different proposed investment strategies.

 The investment strategy that meets the targeted level of free assets in each quarter with the

highest probability may be selected.

 The insurer may also assess the effect of the investment strategy on future shareholder

earnings and choose an investment strategy that maximises future shareholder income

achieving the targeted level of free assets with a certain probability.

For part (i) candidates who scored well gave a wide range of points focusing on the current investment

strategy relative to the liabilities and the expenses. A number of candidates lost time giving points on

improved investment strategies which was not asked for in the question.

For part (ii) weaker candidates gave vague and general points on modelling instead of focusing on the

modelling of the assets and the liabilities for this product. Stronger candidates considered the steps for

modelling assets and liabilities with a stochastic model for investment returns.

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 8


i. Suitability of corporate bonds:


  • The assets match the benefit liabilities in respect of:

  • Nature: The non-profit annuity is fixed in nature, while the corporate bond returns are fixed in nature (provided they are held to maturity).

  • Currency: The assets and liabilities are both in local currency terms.

  • It is unclear if the assets match the liabilities by term, however this may be unlikely since:

  • Life annuities are likely to have long terms (exceeding 20 years).

  • Corporate bonds are unlikely to exceed 20 years due to the investment risk associated with such a long term.

  • It is therefore likely that there exists significant reinvestment risk for the insurer in needing to roll-over the investments.

  • As this is a developing country, there may not be a well-developed corporate bond market, which will make it difficult to achieve exact term matching.

  • The insurer's expenses in respect of annuities are real in nature, and therefore the bonds do not provide a suitable match by nature for these liabilities.

  • Corporate bonds are likely to be far less liquid than government bonds, however this may not be a large concern for the insurer if bonds can be held to maturity.

  • Corporate bonds carry a risk of default, and this is unlikely to make them suitable for matching guaranteed benefits:

  • The insurer may have a high level of capital assets to absorb some defaults, however it is unlikely to have sufficient free assets in the event of large-scale defaults.

  • Corporate bonds are likely to offer higher expected returns compared to government bonds, to compensate for the higher default risk and lower liquidity:

  • This may allow the insurer to offer better annuity rates than competitors (provided it only takes credit for the liquidity premium, not the default risk premium).

ii. The insurer can use a model to determine the suitability of proposed investment strategies as

follows:


  • The liabilities, minimum regulatory capital and the assets are projected forward on assumptions that represent expected future experience.

  • The insurer will also consider the effect of variations in the assumptions on the asset and liability projections.

  • The insurer will determine an appropriate projection period (e.g. for the current strategic business planning or capital planning period) and an appropriate projection frequency (e.g. quarterly but at least annually to provide sufficient information on the free assets of the insurer).

  • Liabilities and regulatory minimum required capital will be projected on the current supervisory basis based on the:

  • Current in-force policies using all the individual policies or model points and expected future new business using model points for the expect profile of new policyholders.

  • Assets (including free assets) will be projected using:

  • A stochastic investment model to simulate future investment returns and capital gains and losses.

  • The asset mix will be based on the current asset mix and expected future changes in asset mix.

  • Considering any regulatory restrictions on asset admissibility and liquidity needs of the insurer.

  • The level of free assets will be determined at the end of each quarter for the entire projection period.

  • The insurer will assess whether the projected levels of free assets meet the requirement of free assets being at least double of the minimum capital required by the regulator.

  • The stochastic models can be run many (1000s) of times using the randomly generated investment returns.

  • This will produce a statistical distribution of the free assets relative to the regulatory minimum required capital available each quarter.

  • From this, the probability of not meeting the insurer's targeted level of free assets can be estimated given a particular investment strategy.

  • The insurer will repeat the process for the different proposed investment strategies.

  • The investment strategy that meets the targeted level of free assets in each quarter with the highest probability may be selected.

#1 1. Life insurance contracts 3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer Investment risk 0.7656

3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer — Investment risk:

  • The insurer must invest the single premium to cover regular outgo over an unknown timeframe.
  • This risk can be mitigated by matching liabilities with fixed-interest securities with redemption dates matching the amounts being paid each year.
  • In a perfectly matched strategy, assuming that annuitants die exactly as expected, the insurance company should not need to buy or sell any of its assets during the term of the contract because the cash needed is provided by the coupons and redemption amounts.
  • This removes interest rate volatility risk and yield uncertainty because the cashflows and yields are locked in at the time when the contract was priced.
  • This scenario is impractical because:
  • Timing: The term of the annuity payments uncertain
  • Availability: Assets with perfectly matching terms may not be available (reinvestment risk)
#2 18. Investments 2. Principles of investment How does the nature, term and currency of liabilities affect asset selection? 0.7602

2. Principles of investment — How does the nature, term and currency of liabilities affect asset selection?:

  • The liability outgo consists of:
  • Benefit payments
  • Expense outgo
  • minus: premium income
  • In any given year the liability outgo depends on the monetary amount of its constituents and the probability of it being received or paid out.

  • The liabilities may be:
  • Guaranteed in money terms: Match with fixed-interest bonds or cash
  • Guaranteed in terms of an index: use index-linked bonds or potentially property investment (rental income) or equities that move in line with CPI.
  • Short-term index linked liabilities could be matched by fixed interest stocks

  • Discretionary: backed by real assets like equity or property for higher bonuses
  • Investment-linked: hold the exact assets the benefits are linked to.

Term:

  • The focus is on the discounted mean term (duration) of the liability. By matching the duration of assets to liabilities, the company ensures that if interest rates change, the values of both assets and liabilities move in line with each other.
  • However insurance liabilities tend to be longer term that available assets in the market.
#3 5. Risks 11.3 Investment risk Mismatching risk 0.7343

11.3 Investment risk — Mismatching risk:

This involves a discrepancy between the discounted mean term (duration) of the assets and the liabilities

  • Reinvestment risk: If assets have a shorter duration than liabilities, proceeds are available earlier than required and must be reinvested at unknown future rates. If interest rates fall, the insurer may be unable to secure the yields needed to meet long-term guarantees
  • Capital values risk: If assets have a longer duration than liabilities, the insurer may be forced to sell assets to meet claims. If interest rates rise, the market value of the assets will fall more than the value of the liabilities, potentially causing insolvency.

#5 9. Assumptions 15.5 Investment return assumptions Using the 5-step framework for setting the investment assumption 0.7251

15.5 Investment return assumptions — Using the 5-step framework for setting the investment assumption:

  • Identify importance: because the contracts build up large reserves and involve a fixed monetary guarantee at maturity, the investment return assumption is very important.
  • Asset choice: typically government or corporate fixed interest securities will be selected to match the liabilities.
  • Best estimate: The actuary uses the concept of discounted mean term (duration) to select assets whose proceeds will align with the expected timing of liability outgo. The starting point is the current weighted average redemption yield available on matching securities in the market.
  • Future changes: For a regular premium contract and/or coupon paying bonds, there is a need to account for the fact that future premiums and coupon payments will be received at various points and must be invested at unknown future interest rates.
  • Taxation: if the company is taxed on investment income, it must net the investment return for taxation to reflect the actual investment return it will receive.
  • Balancing credibility and judgement: The actuary will have to balance the amount of weight that they place on historical experience and expected changes. The final estimate is a weighted adjustment of the best estimate parameter and expected changes.
  • Margins for prudence: to protect the company against the risk that future yields are lower than anticipated, a margin is deducted from the established expected investment return.

F102_NOVEMBER_2021_Paper1_Q1

2021 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 1


i. Define the expropriation price of a unit and explain briefly how it is calculated.


A life insurance company plans to launch a unit-linked product for the first time.

ii. Outline briefly, the principal risks specific to the derivation of the price of a unit that the life insurance

company is exposed to.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 1


i.

Expropriation price:


  • The expropriation price is the price at which a company would cancel a unit, and is calculated as:

  • The market bid price value of assets held by the fund;

  • less the expenses incurred in the purchase and stamp (and other duties) payable in respect of such a purchase;

  • plus the value of any current assets, such as cash on deposit or investments sold but not yet settled;

  • less the value of any current liabilities, such as investments purchased but not yet settled or loans to the fund;

  • plus any accrued income such as interest income from fixed-interest securities and deposits, net of any outgo, such as fund charges;

  • less any allowance for accrued tax, if applicable.

  • This gives the net asset value of the fund on a bid basis, which is divided by the number of existing units at the valuation date. ii. Principal risks:

  • Unit prices are generally set at discrete points in time, whereas the underlying asset values effectively change continuously.

  • This is a particular risk if:

  • The underlying asset values are volatile or if there is a sudden once-off movement in market values.

  • Any timing delay in adjusting unit price introduces a pricing risk for the company due to the mismatch between the company's liabilities, dependent on the unit price, and the value of the underlying assets.

  • The unit price calculation would include some approximations, including:

  • An allowance for tax on unrealised capital gains.

  • An allowance for accrued assets and liabilities, e.g. accrued interest not yet received.

  • Estimates of the market value of assets, where the market value is not immediately observable.

  • For example, property, as there is a risk that the actual values are very different to the estimates.

  • There could be errors in the actual unit price calculations:

  • This could be a particular risk if:

  • Unit prices are based on the appropriation/ expropriation prices of the underlying assets, depending on whether the company is creating additional (net) units or cancelling (net) units. There is a risk that the company uses the wrong basis when calculating the unit prices.

  • The unit prices could be based on incorrect data (e.g. the asset managers provided the incorrect market values of assets).

SOLUTION 2

i.

Accumulating with-profits:


  • Bonuses are declared annually in relation to the premiums paid to date and previously declared bonuses, with an interim bonus applying for claims between bonus declarations.

  • There may be a guaranteed minimum annual bonus. This minimum could be zero.

  • A terminal bonus may be added at maturity and possibly withdrawal.

  • The insurer may be able to apply a market value reduction (MVR) on withdrawal.

  • Regulation or market practice may dictate that the MVR is zero.

  • Bonuses declared and the MVA are at the discretion of the insurer, subject to policyholder expectations. ii. General

  • The general principle will be to use historical experience to derive best estimates of each assumption, and adjust for expected future conditions for the period the assumptions will apply. Accumulating with-profits business

  • With-profits fund growth:

  • Expected return on the with-profits fund based on the asset mix of the fund.

  • This return will be reduced for expected investment expenses (these will be based on the product information for investments available in the market).

  • These returns may be compared to government bonds of suitable term.

  • A stochastic investment model is required if there is a minimum guarantee on regular bonuses or the MVR is zero.

  • Expenses:

  • Use the recent expense investigation i.e. the expenses allocated to this product.

  • Allowance needs to be made for expected business volumes and new business mix in terms of size of premiums to allocate overheads.

  • Expense inflation:

  • Needs to be a mix of salary and price inflation.

  • Assumptions for expense inflation need to be consistent with the assumptions for the growth in the with-profit fund and risk discount rate assumptions.

  • Withdrawal assumptions:

  • Needs to be based on the past experience for this business adjusted for expected future changes.

  • The insurer may consider expected future economic conditions and employment rates and how this may impact on the withdrawal experience for this business.

  • Tax:

  • Is based on current tax rates on this type of business and expected changes.

  • Profit margin:

  • Risk discount rate:

  • Will be based on risk free rate (yield on government bonds) with an allowance for return for shareholders and to reflect the risk of the business.

  • Margins for uncertainty may be included in the individual assumptions or allowed for in the risk discount rate. Group life business

  • Mortality rates:

  • Use the recent mortality investigation for this product.

  • Depending on the amount of internal data insurer has, mortality rates may be combined with standard table rates using credibility theory.

  • Mortality rates may be calculated separately for different industries.

  • Permanent disability rates:

  • Follow a similar process to that of mortality assumptions.

  • Although data will be more limited for permanent disability cover.

  • Expenses:

  • Expenses will be determined in a similar way to the accumulating withprofits product.

  • Expense inflation is not relevant as the product is renewed every year.

  • Profit margin:

  • Margins for uncertainty are likely to be included in the assumptions.

#1 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.1 Unit pricing Appropriation and expropriation prices 0.8078

12.1 Unit pricing — Appropriation and expropriation prices:

To maintain this equity, insurers distinguish between the price at which units are created and the price at which they are cancelled.

  • Appropriation price: this is the price at which the company creates a unit. It is calculated on an offer basis, i.e. using the market's "offer price" for the underlying assets plus purchases expenses, taxes and accrued income.
  • This represents the amount of money of money that must be put into the fund for the creation of a unit
  • Expropriation price: this is the price at which the company cancels a unit. It is calculated on a bid basis, i.e. using the market's "bid price" (the proceeds from selling the assets minus sale expenses)
#2 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.1 Unit pricing Unit pricing 0.7598

12.1 Unit pricing — Unit pricing:

1. The appropriation price is the price at which a unit would be created determined as:

  • the net asset value of the fund on an offer basis
  • divided by the number of existing units at the time of the calculation

2. The net asset value of the fund on an offer basis is calculated as:

1. The market value of the assets obtained from the exchange (mark-to-market)

2. If some assets do not have an observable market value, e.g. property a professional valuation may be needed

3. Alternatively, a mark-to-model approach may be used. A model may project expected cashflows using financial economic assumptions and the cashflows are discounted.

4. Any expenses involved in purchasing additional assets must be added (incl. stamp duty)

5. Current assets must be added (e.g. cash on deposit)

6. Current liabilities must be deducted (e.g. investments purchased but not yet settled)

7. Accrued income must be added (e.g. interest income on deposits) net of any outgo (e.g. charges)

8. Accrued tax must be deducted

#3 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding Absence of investment risk 0.7545

12.2 Actuarial funding — Absence of investment risk:

The expected return on the unit fund is irrelevant to the discount rate because there is no investment risk in the buy-back process.

  • The liability ($l$) (the missing units) is denoted in units: $l = (n-x)* UnitPrice$
  • The source of funding (management charge) is a fixed percentage of the units. $FMC=percentagexUnitPrice$
  • Therefore: $l \approx FMC$

If the unit fund doubles in value due to high investment returns, the monetary cost of buying the missing units also doubles. However, because the management charge is a percentage of that fund, the amount of money to buy those units also doubles. Because both the cost of the units and the funding source (the management charges) move in direct proportion to the unit price. The insurer effectively "borrows" units rather than cash, and since the "repayments" are also unit-linked, the investment risk is eliminated from the buy-back process

#4 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12 Unit pricing and actuarial funding Principal risks in unit pricing 0.7528

12 Unit pricing and actuarial funding — Principal risks in unit pricing:

  • Timing risk: Unit prices are set at discrete points in time, while asset values move continuously
  • Asset values are volatile
  • Sudden movements in asset values
  • Outdated asset valuations (property)
  • Approximations
  • tax on unrealised gains
  • accrued interest
  • Errors: Incorrect data/calculation errors
  • Wrong basis (appropriation vs expropriation price)
  • Regulatory changes (restrictions on charges included in the unit price)
  • Reputational risk: from violating basic equity principle or unclear communication
  • Anti-selection: Policyholder selection against the company if the price overstates the asset value
#5 10. Reserving 9. Cost of capital approach The Three-Step Calculation Process 0.7522

9. Cost of capital approach — The Three-Step Calculation Process:

1. Project Required Capital: The insurer projects the future capital required to be held $(C_t​)$ for each period during the "run-off" of the business. (this is the SCR)

2. Apply Cost of Capital Rate: These projected capital amounts are multiplied by a cost of capital rate (e.g., 6% per annum).

3. Discount to Present Value: The resulting annual costs are discounted back to the valuation date using risk-free (market-consistent) interest rates to produce the total risk margin. $$\text{Risk margin} = \displaystyle{\sum_t \dfrac{k_tC_t}{(1 + r_t)^t}}$$

#1 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7216

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#2 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7168

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#3 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.2 Addition to benefits - accumulating with profits Regular annual bonuses 0.7166

9.1.2 Addition to benefits - accumulating with profits — Regular annual bonuses:

In Accumulating With-profits contracts, bonuses are added annually based on the total of premiums paid to date plus any bonuses that have been declared. These bonuses act like interest:

$$ F_{t+1} = (F_t + P_t - c_t)(1 + b_t)$$

Where:

  • F is the Benefit/Fund value
  • P is the Premium
  • c represents charges
  • b is the regular bonus rate

There is an explicit relationship between the premiums paid and the addition to the benefit (allocation rate). These contracts are often unitised, however it is not necessary for the contract to be unitised

#4 1. Life insurance contracts 1.4 Endowment Assurances - Structures ASSA/F102 Life Insurance Principles/Summary/1. Life insurance contracts/1.1 Endowment assurances - Structures 0.7136

1.4 Endowment Assurances - Structures — ASSA/F102 Life Insurance Principles/Summary/1. Life insurance contracts/1.1 Endowment assurances - Structures:

Without-profits:

  • Offers a guaranteed amount of money at the end of the term or upon earlier death in exchange for single or regular premiums

With-profits (Participating):

  • The initial sum assured is enhanced by the declaration of bonuses (reversionary, special or terminal). Policyholders expect better returns than without-profits version, though premiums are typically higher.

Unit-linked:

  • Premiums are invested in pooled funds, and the maturity benefit depends on the performance of underlying assets and the level of charges levied by the insurer. Highly versatile, allowing policyholders to choose between protection-heavy or savings-heavy designs therefore can be used to meet different needs.
#5 15. Pricing health & care contracts 1. Income protection How is the model adjusted for deferred periods? 0.7056

1. Income protection — How is the model adjusted for deferred periods?:

To adjust the integral for a deferred period ($d$), we must incorporate the requirement that the policyholder remains continuously sick from the time they fall ill until benefits begin:


The adjusted integral is: $$EPV(Benefit) = S \cdot \int_0^\infty v^t \cdot {}_tp_x^{HH} \cdot \mu_{x+t} \cdot (v^d \cdot {}_dp_{x+t}^{SS} \cdot \overline{a}_{x+t+d}^{S})dt$$


${}_dp_{x+t}^{SS}$ is the probability that a life who falls sick at age $x+t$ remains continuously sick for the duration of the deferred period $d$

F102_NOVEMBER_2021_Paper1_Q3

Question

QUESTION 3


You work for a start-up insurance company which plans to start selling business in a few months' time. Your first product will be a regular premium 10-year unit-linked endowment assurance with a maximum guaranteed sum insured of R1 million. Policyholders will be allowed to vary the guaranteed sum insured during the policy term, provided it does not exceed the sum assured selected at the start of the policy. The only charge on the product will be an annual management charge, which will be the same fixed percentage for all policyholders.

Your marketing manager proposes that, because the maximum sum insured is quite low, there should be no initial underwriting on the product besides asking the applicant to state that they are in good health.

i. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the marketing manager's proposal.


The insurer is negotiating an Obligatory/Obligatory reinsurance arrangement.

ii. Outline briefly the advantages and disadvantages to the insurer of entering into this type of reinsurance

arrangement.


Some initial underwriting will be implemented as a condition to the reinsurance arrangement. It has been agreed with the reinsurer that underwriting will be limited to encourage sales.

iii. Describe an initial underwriting programme that would be suitable for this product.


iv. State 4 ways in which the product design could be changed to reduce the risk of poor mortality experience,

other than using initial underwriting.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 3


i.

Advantages


  • No initial underwriting will make the product more attractive and will lead to more sales than if there were initial underwriting.

  • This could allow the company to reach viability quickly, assuming the product is priced correctly.

  • No initial underwriting will reduce the company's up-front costs as it would not need to hire medical underwriters.

  • The risk is also reduced as this is a unit-linked product, and so may be meeting a savings need and not just protection. Disadvantages

  • As there are no medical checks the company opens itself up to anti-selection.

  • The impact will depend on what the market practice is relating to initial underwriting, the risk of anti-selection is higher if other insurers use initial underwriting.

  • Furthermore, people who are sick could fail to disclosure their state of health and take up the policy.

  • Higher than expected claims will lead to losses to the insurer, even though the sum assured is low.

  • Although the company could decline some claims based on the health question, claim rejections may be challenged on grounds of different interpretations of "good health".

  • Declining too many claims will also not be good for the company's reputation. ii. Obligatory/ Obligatory Reinsurance Advantages:

  • The insurer has guaranteed cover for each risk placed.

  • The insurer knows up front what maximum risk that it can accept.

  • The insurer is likely to get more comprehensive service, and better long term pricing, if they give more business to one reinsurer. Disadvantages:

  • The insurer has to cede a certain amount of the risk to the reinsurer.

  • This may mean giving away more profit than they would like to.

  • It is more likely that the treaty reinsurer will have some say in the underwriting and claims management process. iii. Underwriting:

  • For larger sums insured, start by introducing some medical questions into the application form.

  • These could include any pre-existing conditions, current health conditions, family history.

  • If they answer "yes" to any of the questions then they could be asked to do any of the following:

  • Fill in a more detailed questionnaire.

  • Undergo a medical examination with a nurse or doctor.

  • Have blood tests carried out.

  • For the maximum sum insured you could ask for a declaration of income, or proof of debt (if that is the purpose of the cover). iv. Possible changes to the product design:

  • Reduce the maximum guaranteed sum insured.

  • Introduce a waiting period before people become eligible to claim the guaranteed sum insured.

  • Link the product to a specific financial need, e.g. repayment of a housing loan on death.

  • Remove the flexibility to increase the guaranteed sum insured once it has been reduced, to avoid anti-selection.

  • Introduce a mortality charge, to explicitly charge for the sum at risk.

  • This charge can be varied by policyholder mortality risk factors.

SOLUTION 4

i.

Limit on amounts (Proposal A):


  • The proposed regulations place limits on the benefits that insurance companies may offer, which may mean that the reduced benefits may not fully meet financial needs of policyholders.

  • Reduced benefits would mean lower premiums which would make these policies more affordable. Limit on benefit payment term (Proposal B):

  • This limitation is likely to severely impact policyholder needs and resulting unappealing and unmarketable benefits from the perspective of most policyholders.

  • It will have much less impact on policyholders closer to retirement age, and a larger impact on younger policyholders. Limit on guaranteed term (Proposal C):

  • This creates some uncertainty for policyholders who may not be able to afford large unexpected increases in premium rates.

  • Steep increases could lead to policyholders lapsing and being left without cover. ii. Risks and challenges:

  • Products will need to be repriced and there might not be data available on claims and policyholder behaviour under new policy conditions.

  • New product features may be unattractive to customers, leading to reduced sales and premium volumes, which may result in companies not recouping expenses.

  • It is difficult to predict the impact of these changes under different economic conditions. This adds the uncertainty of the impact of these changes.

  • If policyholders do not understand that benefits are governed by legislation, they will blame the companies for poor benefits leading to reputational risks for companies.

  • The indirect impact of these regulatory changes may be lower future product innovation and greater standardisation.

  • Product standardisation could lead to products being mostly differentiated by price and high competition could lead to unsustainably-low premium rates.

  • Changing administrative and other processes may be difficult and costly. iii. Advantages:

  • There may be an improvement in the underwriting experience on these products due to the benefit reducing after six months, as this is likely to encourage some claimants to return to work leading to shorter average claim durations, depending on the length of the deferred period for these products.

  • Limiting benefits to ten years materially reduces the assumption risk for an insurer, as a short projection period improves the reliability of modelling for pricing and reserving purposes.

  • It may also be easier to find investments of suitable matching terms.

  • Limiting rate guarantees to five years also helps as any mispricing or worse than expected experience could be corrected for (at least partially) after a 5-year initial rate guarantee period.

  • Although there are likely to be challenges in implementing premium increases in practice.

SOLUTION 5

i.

Equating policy values method for calculating the revised premium rate for increased sum assured on these contracts.


  • The value of the existing contract will be calculated using prospective or retrospective method.

  • The basis used to calculate the policy value for the existing contract should be between a realistic basis based on actual experience (used to calculate the asset share) and basis used to price the original contract.

  • This will be equated to the policy value for the altered contract using a prospective method.

  • Plus alteration expenses and additional commission for the increase in the sum assured (if applicable).

  • The mortality assumptions will be based on the expected mortality of the policyholder, based on the underwriting applied at the date of the increase in the sum assured.

  • The renewal assumptions will be based expenses and expense inflation at the date of the alteration.

  • The terms and premium basis for the increased sum assured should be consistent with the premium basis and terms for new policies.

  • The premium for the altered policy should not be higher than the premium for a new contract for the same sum assured, to avoid the risk of lapse and re-entry.

  • The choice of the basis used will impact the profit that is being recognised by the insurer and consideration would be given towards fairness of profit recognised between the shareholder and policyholder. ii. Product design change considerations:

  • Ease of explaining the new option - for some target markets it may be too complex.

  • Whether this change adequately meets customer needs, e.g. a CPI-linked annual increase might meet the customer needs better.

  • Affordability of the added option to potential customers.

  • Whether the option should be a voluntary add-on at sale or a required feature.

  • There is likely to be an anti-selection risk as customers in poorer health are more likely to exercise the option than those in better health - the insurer should consider ways to manage and minimise this risk.

  • The difficulties associated with pricing and valuing this option need to be considered.

  • In particular, data needed to estimate the option cost might be limited as this is a new feature.

  • Consider the potential risk of lapse and re-entry and how this can be managed.

  • Any other administrative issues specifically related to administering and engaging with customers to effect the option and to record their decision.

  • Any potential reaction from competitors and how this affects the profitability of the insurer.

  • Consideration should be given to the consistency of the option with other options offered by the insurer as this could simplify the administration effort and also impact lapse and re-entry risk.

  • Any impact on existing reinsurance arrangements and whether or not the additional cover will also be reinsured.

  • In particular, will be insurer be comfortable to underwrite the additional risk without underwriting? iii. Minimising anti-selection risk:

  • Limit the sum assured increases if CPI is likely to fall below 10%. For example, the insurer might consider a min of CPI and the 10% to help keep the option affordable and avoid over-insurance.

  • Some form of financial underwriting might be considered.

  • The timing of exercising the option may be limited, for example:

  • The option might only be exercisable on certain life events (annual salary increase, marriage, divorce or birth of a child).

  • May impose a limited number of exercise dates.

  • May impose a maximum age for the exercise of the option.

  • May impose a maximum duration for the exercise of the option (cover increases after 10 years may require underwriting).

  • Consider imposing a maximum initial sum assured for the option or maximum sum assured after increases.

  • May impose maximum policy term.

  • May need to restrict the option to lives accepted at standard terms.

SOLUTION 6

i.

Description of the model required to calculate the present value of future profits to shareholders:


  • The model would use an appropriate risk discount rate to reflect the level of risk associated with the portfolio of policies.

  • The risk discount rate may be lower than the risk discount rate used in pricing policies because there is less uncertainty relating to existing business.

  • The model should project the expected future cashflows, for example, expected premiums, claims and expense cash flows under the funeral policy book.

  • Future supervisory reserves should also be projected.

  • Proper allowance must be made for guaranteed alteration terms such as benefit increases.

  • Assumptions will be made for mortality, lapses, renewal expenses and expense inflation.

  • The model parameters should reflect the realistic experience expected of the target market.

  • The model should allow for the variation in mortality levels for different lives covered under the policy, for example, grandparents vs children.

  • Allowance should be made for interactions and correlations between different variables.

  • In particular, those that should remain consistent, for example, inflation rates and interest rates.

  • The model will use all the in-force policies.

  • Alternatively, the model should allow for different model points representing various product features and customer profiles.

  • The frequency of cash flow projections must be short enough to produce reliable results, preferably annually.

  • The model will produce the net present value of future profits to shareholders on the basis described above.

  • The model should also allow for the variation of parameters in order to determine the sensitivity of the expected future profits to shareholders to the assumptions. ii. The impact on the value of the shareholders share of net assets:

  • The value of the assets should increase as there is a lower outflow for new business.

  • The value of liabilities for new business should increase as future commission payments will be reserved for.

  • The overall effect may be positive, but it will depend on:

  • Any differences in the value of the initial commission and the total aggregate value of new regular commission payments over the term of the policy.

The impact on the present value of future profits to shareholders:


  • Profit in future years may increase due to the release of the prudent reserves for regular commission payments compared to expected commission payments based on realistic assumptions.

  • Although there may be less prudence in the reserving assumption there is less uncertainty in future commission payments compared to other assumptions. Potential changes in the overall profitability of the policies:

  • If aggregate regular commission payments are lower than the initial commission payments the profitability of the products should increase.

  • If the investment returns on the reserves set aside for future commission payments are higher than the discount rate then the insurer will make a profit.

  • The longer the term of the contract, the higher the impact of the change.

  • Persistency may improve under the new commission regulations which will increase the profitability overall for new policies.

  • Intermediaries selling the product may prefer upfront commission.

  • Possible lower sales volumes may cause an under recovery of expenses with a reduction in profitability of new policies.

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#3 4. External environment 10. The external environment 1. Volume and mix of new business 0.7254

10. The external environment — 1. Volume and mix of new business:

The insurer should consider the expected volume of new business, since this affects profitability, expense recovery, solvency strain and operational capacity.


If volumes are too low, the insurer may not recover fixed costs such as product development, systems, marketing, distribution and regulatory approval costs.


If volumes are too high, the insurer may suffer from new business strain, especially where initial expenses, commission or reserving requirements are high.


The insurer should also consider the expected mix of business, for example by: age, gender, sum assured or benefit level, premium term, policy duration, distribution channel, socio-economic group, underwriting class. A change in business mix may alter the risk profile, capital requirements, claims experience, expense assumptions and profitability of the business.

#4 4. External environment 10.2.1 Distribution channels - Risk to the insurer Impact on risk to the insurer 0.7244

10.2.1 Distribution channels - Risk to the insurer — Impact on risk to the insurer:

The choice of distribution channel introduces several macro risks, primarily related to demographic profile, persistency and anti-selection.

  • Anti-selection: intermediaries are subject to the most stringent underwriting because they represent the client, not the insurer, increasing the potential for anti-selection. Conversely, direct marketing involves the lowest level of underwriting to avoid barriers to sales, but the insurer risks attracting a disproportionate share of high-risk applicants because it appears to have the most relaxed standards in the markets.
  • Withdrawal (Persistency) risk: Channels using aggressive sales approaches or reaching less sophisticated buyers are more likely to see early lapses. Intermediaries typically have the lowest withdrawal rates.
  • Mix of business risk*: Insurers set pricing assumptions based on an expected mix of business. If the volume of a specific channel changes unexpectedly, the overall experience (mortality, morbidity, and expenses) may deviate from the pricing basis.
  • Expense risk: Direct marketing and own sales forces involve high fixed overheads and development costs. If these channels produce low sales volumes, the company may fail to recover the costs, while excessive volume can overstretch capital resources and administrative capacity.
  • Intermediary actions (lapse and re-entry): independent distributors may act in their own interest by encouraging clients to cancel their policies and take out new ones, which can cause significant financial loss to the original insurer. This can be mitigated by exit penalties or commission clawbacks.
#5 14. Guarantees and options 3. Mortality options What are the implications of offering a mortality option? 0.7182

3. Mortality options — What are the implications of offering a mortality option?:

Offering a mortality option such as the right to increase cover or renew a policy without further medical evidence:

  • Anti-selection: The primary risk is selection against the office, where policyholders in poor health are significantly more likely to exercise the option.
  • Financial cost: The cost is the difference between the standard premium charged and the higher premium that would have been charged under full underwriting. $$\{\text{proportion of lives exercising the option}\} \times \{\text{average health of lives exercising the option}\} $$
  • Higher Capital strain: reserving for mortality guarantees must account for both expected higher mortality of those exercising the option and the uncertainty regarding future take up rates.

5.1.4 Income Protection (IP) contracts - Product Variations — Guaranteed and reviewable premium rates:

  • IP premium designs exist at two extremes: A full guarantee of future premiums or no guarantee whatsoever
  • A frequent "middle ground" is to guarantee the premium amount for an initial period, such as the first 5 years, with the insurer gaining the freedom to review and change rates thereafter
  • Reviewable premium structure:
  • Changes are made based on the experience of the entire portfolio of policies, rather than the claims history of the individual policyholder.
  • Reviewable approaches are used because IP risks are influenced by unforeseen economic and social factors, such as unemployment trends and long-term changes in the workplace or medical science

5.1.2 Income Protection (IP) contracts - Features — Over-insurance:

Where a claimant might receive more income while sick than when working will arise if the replacement ratio is too high, which may discourage return to work. Over-insurance can arise from:

  • subsequent over-insurance, through salary not keeping up with benefits (regular reviews, policy conditions)

6.1.1 Critical illness cover - Product structures and benefits — Guarantees and reviewability of premiums and benefits:

  • Competitive pressures: pushed companies to offer guarantees on both benefits (that claim definitions will not change) and premiums.
  • Better estimation of CI risks leads to insurers progressively charging an appropriate price for guarantees.
  • Predicting increases: For reviewable contracts, it is difficult to predict future premium increases because incidence trends for different medical conditions move in different directions.
  • Impact on Reserving and capital: Guaranteed premiums may require capital injections to fund reserves for worsening claims experience.
  • Impact of medical advances
  • Windfall claims: Medical advances may turn a previously "critical" surgery into a minor, low risk procedure. If the benefit criteria is guaranteed, the insurer is forced to pay the full sum assured for that condition.
  • Early diagnosis: Improved screening may detect diseases earlier, triggering "guaranteed" payouts much sooner than insurers originally anticipated.
  • New diseases: insurers often include new diseases at little or no extra cost but new additions must be properly costed.
  • Guaranteed Insurability Options (GIOs): Allow a policyholder to increase their sum insured without providing further medical evidence, triggered by specific life events or specific policy anniversaroes.
#2 14. Guarantees and options 3. Mortality options What are the implications of offering a mortality option? 0.7525

3. Mortality options — What are the implications of offering a mortality option?:

Offering a mortality option such as the right to increase cover or renew a policy without further medical evidence:

  • Anti-selection: The primary risk is selection against the office, where policyholders in poor health are significantly more likely to exercise the option.
  • Financial cost: The cost is the difference between the standard premium charged and the higher premium that would have been charged under full underwriting. $$\{\text{proportion of lives exercising the option}\} \times \{\text{average health of lives exercising the option}\} $$
  • Higher Capital strain: reserving for mortality guarantees must account for both expected higher mortality of those exercising the option and the uncertainty regarding future take up rates.
#3 2. Health and care products 6.1.4 Critical illness cover - Risks to the insurer Morbidity risk 0.7427

6.1.4 Critical illness cover - Risks to the insurer — Morbidity risk:

The primary risk to an insurer issuing Critical Illness (CI) products is the uncertainty regarding incidence rates for the specified conditions

  • Parameter risk: Because these contracts are relatively new to many markets, historical experience data is often limited, unreliable, or non-existent, leading to significant parameter risk.
  • Medical and Technological Advances: Improved screening and medical technology can lead to earlier diagnosis of conditions like cancer, increasing claim frequency sooner than originally priced. Furthermore, advances may turn a previously "critical" surgery into a minor procedure (e.g., angioplasty), resulting in windfall claims.

  • Data Heterogeneity: Because different companies cover different sets of illnesses and use varying medical definitions, industry-wide data is often heterogeneous and can be misleading when used as a basis for a specific insurer’s assumptions.

  • Anti-selection and Selective Withdrawals: There is a significant risk of anti-selection, where individuals who suspect they are at high risk seek out cover. Additionally, selective withdrawals occur when healthy lives lapse their policies, leaving the insurer with a pool of higher-risk individuals.
  • Guarantees: Competitive pressures have forced many insurers to offer guaranteed premiums and benefit definitions. If claims experience worsens or medical advances increase diagnosis rates, the insurer may be legally required to pay claims based on outdated definitions and must fund significant reserve enhancements from shareholder capital or with-profits funds.
  • Tiered Benefit Complexity: Offering tiered benefits based on the severity of a condition introduces additional risks, including the difficulty of finding statistics for transition intensities between severity levels and the potential for claims disputes regarding the exact degree of impairment.
#4 15. Pricing health & care contracts 2. Critical illness How to derive risk premium rates for critical illness contracts? 0.7423

2. Critical illness — How to derive risk premium rates for critical illness contracts?:

The overall incidence rate ($i_x$) is the sum of incidence rates for each defined condition (e.g., heart attack, stroke, cancer, other) minus any interactions between causes.$$i_x = i_x^{hd} + i_x^s + i_x^c + i_x^o - k_x^{hd}i_x^s$$

The final risk premium depends on the policy structure:

  • Standalone CI: The cost is the incidence rate multiplied by the probability of surviving the survival period. $$i_x \times \text{Probability of surviving survival period}$$
  • Accelerated CI: This pays on the earlier of death or diagnosis. The rate combines the CI incidence rate with the mortality rate ($qx$), adjusted for deaths already counted as CI events ($k_xq_x$).$$i_x + (1 - k_x)q_x$$

The final risk premium is found by multiplying $i_x$ by the sum assured $S$.

#5 14. Guarantees and options 4. Valuing Mortality options What are the extra assumptions the insurer would need to make? 0.7373

4. Valuing Mortality options — What are the extra assumptions the insurer would need to make?:

  • Option take-up rates: the probability that the policyholder will exercise the option at each available date
  • Conventional approach: assumes 100% of eligible policyholder will take the maximum benefit
  • Realistic approach: uses percentages based on past experience
  • Mortality of exercisers: Due to anti-selection, those who exercise the option are assumed to have heavier mortality than standard lives. (e.g. 150% of the base table)
  • Mortality of non-exercisers: assume lower than standard mortality so that the weighted average amounts to the original best estimate level.
  • Benefit choice: if the policyholder has a choice of benefit levels, an assumption is made about which level will be chosen (often assume the most expensive option for the insurer)
  • Additional expenses: Allow for the costs of notifying policyholders of their option and the administrative work to process the change.

#1 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7587

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#3 4. External environment 10.6 The tax regime Taxation as a source of risk 0.7266

10.6 The tax regime — Taxation as a source of risk:

The long-term nature of life insurance contracts exposes insurers to taxation risk, as fiscal rules can change over the decades a policy remains in force.


  • Tax Changes: Existing policies are generally not immune to changes in tax methods or rates, meaning an insurer may realize less net profit than anticipated if the fiscal environment worsens after the policy is issued.

  • Parameter Sensitivity: For contracts with fixed, guaranteed benefits, the insurer bears the risk that higher corporate or investment taxes will erode the margins intended for expenses and profit.

  • Asset Share Deductions: In with-profits business, the asset share must explicitly deduct tax on investment income and allow for accrued tax liabilities on unrealized capital gains to ensure fairness between policyholders
#4 4. External environment 10.2.1 Distribution channels - Risk to the insurer Impact on pricing 0.7231

10.2.1 Distribution channels - Risk to the insurer — Impact on pricing:

The distribution channel influences the pricing basis through its effect on expected experience and competitive requirements.

  • Underwriting and claims: The stringency of underwriting usually varies by channel, intermediaries face the most stringent checks, while direct marketing involves the lowest level of underwriting. These differences must be reflected in the mortality and morbidity assumptions used in pricing.
  • Competitiveness: The need for competitive rates is greatest when selling through independent intermediaries, as they directly compare the company's rates against the rest of the market.
  • Expense loading: Remuneration varies across channels, for instance high initial commissions for intermediaries or agents create a large new business strain that must be recouped through higher expense loading in the premium.
  • Weighted assumptions: If an insurer uses multiple channels for the same product, it must use a weighted average of the experience based on the expected mix of business by source. If the actual mix deviates from these assumptions, the company faces a risk to its projected profitability.
#5 4. External environment 10.5 Legal Environment Regulatory requirements 0.7221

10.5 Legal Environment — Regulatory requirements:

Regulators may impose restrictions on life insurance companies, usually with the aim of protecting policyholders.

Common restrictions on:


Product design

  • Contracts types: A restriction on the types of contracts that a life insurance company can offer
  • Premium rates: Restrictions on the premium rates or charges for certain types of contracts
  • Terms and conditions: Requirements relating to the terms and conditions of the contracts
  • Method of sale: Restrictions on the channels through which life insurance can be sold, on sales procedures or on information given at the point of sale.
  • Non-Discrimination: Restrictions on rating factors and the ability to underwrite (e.g. to avoid discrimination)


Capital and reserving

  • Solvency capital requirements: minimum reserving or solvency margin requirements
  • Asset Valuation methods: dictate whether certain assets are valued at market value (active approach) or historic/book value (passive approach), which directly impacts the reported solvency position

Investment strategy

  • limit mismatching liabilities
  • restrict asset types
  • restrict concentration on a single asset type
  • Maximum counterparty exposure
  • Mismatching reserves
  • tax treatment of different asset classes
  • require independent custodians
  • admissible assets
  • liquidity requirement (cash holding)
  • restrict foreign investment
  • prescribe asset classes
  • method of calculating asset values (fair value)

Disclosures

  • Point of sale and marketing materials
  • Projection/illustrations e.g. maturity/surrender values
  • Charging structures
  • Reviewability (yes/no)
  • Risk disclosure (risks to the policyholder)
  • Financial and solvency
  • Published accounts (true and fair view)
  • Supervisory returns (SCR)
  • EV in published accounts
  • Impact of basis changes
  • Market-consistent valuation
  • disclose how stochastic models are calibrated: risk-neutral vs real-world calibration

QUESTION 7


A life insurer in a developing country sells without-profit immediate level annuities. Both single-life and jointlife annuities are offered.

i. Outline the characteristics of the annuity liabilities and hence suggest a suitable matching investment

strategy for these liabilities.


ii. Describe how the matching investment strategy might differ for without-profit immediate annuities

increasing in line with the consumer price index (CPI) of the country.


A director suggests that the insurer should adopt a mismatched investment strategy on its level and CPI increasing annuities to enhance returns for the shareholders.

iii. Discuss the director's suggestion.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 7


i.

Matching investments:


  • A matching strategy should be suitable for the nature, and currency of the liabilities.

  • Nature of the liabilities.

  • The benefits are fixed in money terms.

  • Life office expenses are likely to be real (increasing by a mix of salary and price inflation).

  • Term: this depends on when annuities are purchased - typically purchased at retirement so terms can be long (e.g. 30 years) for single-life, and even longer for joint-life.

  • Currency: expected to be the same as that of the developing country for benefits and expenses.

  • Fixed interest bonds are suitable for most of the liabilities:

  • They match fixed benefits by nature.

  • Bonds of varying terms are usually available, however sufficiently-long bonds for the longest dated liabilities may not be available in the developing country.

  • Government bonds are usually very liquid, even in developing countries, but this may not be true in this country.

  • There should be enough supply of local currency bonds for the insurer's liabilities.

  • If local bonds of suitable term and liquidity are not available, the life office could consider fixed interest bonds in other countries, and manage the currency risk through hedging instruments.

  • However this is only feasible if similar returns are available on foreign bonds, or if annuity pricing reflects foreign bond returns.

  • Inflation-linked bonds could be a reasonable match for expenses:

  • They match the real nature of expenses.

  • However expense inflation might be higher due to wage inflation, however the life company may try to offset this through greater efficiencies.

  • To the extent that index linked bonds are not available in sufficient quantities, the life office may consider using other real assets, such as equities.

  • However equity returns can be very volatile in the short term, making this asset more suitable for longer-term matching of expense liabilities.

  • Cash is liquid and should be held for very short term obligations. ii. Index-linked annuities:

  • The nature of the benefits is real and linked to the CPI index.

  • Local currency CPI-linked index bonds provide an exact match by nature and currency, if these bonds are available.

  • It may be unlikely that bonds of sufficiently long terms are available in the country to match the longest liabilities.

  • If the required bonds are not available, the insurer must consider alternative real assets such as equity and property.

  • This volatility can be offset to a limited extent by selecting a diversified portfolio of very high quality assets generating a reasonably stable and real income stream.

  • A portfolio of direct property is only feasible if the liabilities to be matched are very large, indirect property investments may be considered.

  • Offshore real assets may provide an expected real return in local currency terms if the local currency adjusts as expected by purchasing power parity, however in practice this is unlikely over short terms so the insurer faces significant currency risk.

  • These alternatives to local index-linked bonds are only feasible if the insurer has sufficient free assets to act as a buffer when returns do not match CPI-linked increases in the liabilities. iii. Adopting a mismatched position:

  • In some circumstances, it may be possible to achieve higher returns for shareholders by adopting a mismatched position on the liabilities.

  • Without-profit level annuities, which are mostly matched by fixed interest bonds of suitable term, could be backed by assets with higher expected returns for example. equities.

  • In other circumstances, it may not be possible to achieve higher returns for shareholders by adopting a mismatched position on the liabilities.

  • If without-profit CPI-linked annuities are already backed by equities and property, which provide higher expected returns than other asset classes.

  • Shareholder returns might be enhanced by taking a short-term view on asset classes, however this approach is very risky.

  • While mismatching assets and liabilities can enhance shareholder returns, it also increases risk to the shareholders.

  • Shareholders may not have a high tolerance for risk.

  • This higher risk is likely to result in higher solvency capital requirements (so that returns as a percentage of capital needed may not be higher than a lower risk strategy).

  • The company may not have sufficient free capital to support a higher risk strategy.
