#1 16. Reinsurance 3.2 Retention limits Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve 0.7660

3.2 Retention limits — Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve:

In this approach, insurers aim to minimize the total cost of two components:

  • the cost of obtaining reinsurance and
  • the cost of financing a mortality fluctuations reserve.

The process follows these steps:

1. Set a risk criterion: such as a maximum 1% probability that net losses will exceed a specific amount e.g. 25m

2. Model total costs: for different retention limits, the insurer stochastically models the expected net loss by varying the mortality rates. As the retention limit increases, the cost of reinsurance decreases, but the size of the required fluctuations reserve (and its associated financing cost) increases.

3. Calculate the financing cost: The cost of the reserve ($M$) is calculated as $M \times (j - i)$, where $j$ is the required rate of return on the company's capital and $i$ is the actual investment return earned on the reserve's assets.

4. Optimize: The insurer identifies the specific retention limit where the combined cost of the reserve and reinsurance is lowest while still satisfying the ruin probability target.

#2 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7638

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#3 14. Guarantees and options 4. Valuing Mortality options What are the extra assumptions the insurer would need to make? 0.7608

4. Valuing Mortality options — What are the extra assumptions the insurer would need to make?:

  • Option take-up rates: the probability that the policyholder will exercise the option at each available date
  • Conventional approach: assumes 100% of eligible policyholder will take the maximum benefit
  • Realistic approach: uses percentages based on past experience
  • Mortality of exercisers: Due to anti-selection, those who exercise the option are assumed to have heavier mortality than standard lives. (e.g. 150% of the base table)
  • Mortality of non-exercisers: assume lower than standard mortality so that the weighted average amounts to the original best estimate level.
  • Benefit choice: if the policyholder has a choice of benefit levels, an assumption is made about which level will be chosen (often assume the most expensive option for the insurer)
  • Additional expenses: Allow for the costs of notifying policyholders of their option and the administrative work to process the change.
#4 9. Assumptions 15.5 Investment return assumptions Using the 5-step framework for setting the investment assumption 0.7499

15.5 Investment return assumptions — Using the 5-step framework for setting the investment assumption:

  • Identify importance: because the contracts build up large reserves and involve a fixed monetary guarantee at maturity, the investment return assumption is very important.
  • Asset choice: typically government or corporate fixed interest securities will be selected to match the liabilities.
  • Best estimate: The actuary uses the concept of discounted mean term (duration) to select assets whose proceeds will align with the expected timing of liability outgo. The starting point is the current weighted average redemption yield available on matching securities in the market.
  • Future changes: For a regular premium contract and/or coupon paying bonds, there is a need to account for the fact that future premiums and coupon payments will be received at various points and must be invested at unknown future interest rates.
  • Taxation: if the company is taxed on investment income, it must net the investment return for taxation to reflect the actual investment return it will receive.
  • Balancing credibility and judgement: The actuary will have to balance the amount of weight that they place on historical experience and expected changes. The final estimate is a weighted adjustment of the best estimate parameter and expected changes.
  • Margins for prudence: to protect the company against the risk that future yields are lower than anticipated, a margin is deducted from the established expected investment return.
#5 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7455

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

F102_NOVEMBER_2022_Papergeneral_Q2

2022 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 2


i. Regulatory restrictions:

• There may be restrictions placed on premium rates or charges for certain

contracts.

• There may be restrictions on the types of contracts that may be offered.

• There may be restrictions on the terms and conditions placed on certain contracts,

e.g. restrictions on surrender value terms.

• There may be enhanced disclosure requirements.

• There may be restrictions on underwriting.

• There may be higher minimum requirements for statutory reserves, or there may

be restrictions on the amount of new business written through minimum solvency

requirements.


• There may be restrictions placed on the types of assets which may be held.

ii. Investments for the funeral business:

• The insurer will first consider the investments that match the liabilities by nature,

term and currency.

• The benefits are without-profits, making the nature of liabilities fixed in monetary

terms (whether level or fixed annual increases).

➢ Fixed interest bonds of suitable term are suitable for matching these liabilities.

➢ Government bonds are lowest risk, while corporate bonds may provide a

higher expected return for higher default and liquidity risk.

• Local currency assets are suitable for matching local currency liabilities.

• Funeral cover is usually short-medium term cover, and it should be possible to

find bonds of suitable matching term.

• Some liabilities will relate to the management expenses for this business, which

are mostly salary-related and therefore inflation-linked.

➢ Investments that produce expected real returns such as index-linked bonds

and perhaps equities and property may be suitable for these liabilities.

• Cash should be held as working capital and to meet short-term expenses and claim

payments.

• The extent to which investments can mismatch liabilities depends to a large extent

on the level of free assets of the insurer.

➢ The larger the level of free assets, the more investment freedom the company

has.

➢ Mismatching could be by nature, term, and/or currency, in order to maximise

returns for shareholders.

iii. Impact on sales volumes:

• Sales volumes of the savings contracts may drop as investors divert money to less

risky investment structures in the short term, such as bank deposits.

• To the extent that economic conditions deteriorate as a result of higher interest

rates, and result in higher unemployment, sales of most products, and in particular

savings type products, will suffer as premiums become unaffordable.

• The volumes of with-profits contracts may reduce by less than the volumes of

unit-linked savings contracts in the short term as the company will have the ability

to smooth bonus rates through volatile market cycles.

• The impact on the volumes of funeral insurance contracts should be negligible,

however, it depends on how employment levels are affected.

Impact on product profitability:

• A drop in the asset values of unit-linked contracts will reduce the fund-based fee

revenue of the company and therefore the product profitability.

• Sustained poor investment returns may lead to an increase in lapses for the unit-

linked contracts, reducing product profitability.


• Higher unemployment will most likely lead to higher lapses and lower sales,

impacting profitability negatively.

• Depending on the degree of matching and reserving methodology, a sudden drop

in the asset values may lead to reserves decreasing by less on some contracts, e.g.

whole life contracts, leading to losses.

• As funeral contracts have lower sums assured and require smaller reserves, the

impact on the profitability of these products should be negligible.

• As profits and losses are shared with policyholders of with-profits contracts, the

impact on the short term profitability of these products to the company is expected

to be muted.

iv. Risks:

• The internet-based distribution platform will sell to a different target market than

the adviser channels.

• The target market is likely to have a different underwriting experience, for which

the company may not have experience data.

• This data may be available through local reinsurers in the foreign market.

➢ However, the reinsurance terms may not be attractive, impacting product

margins.

• Clients purchasing insurance products through an internet-based platform are

likely to be much more price sensitive, reducing product margins.

• The company should consider what the competitor offerings look like through

similar channels in the developed country and how competitive their product

offering would be as this would impact product volumes and margins.

• The Life & Invest brand will not be well recognised in the new market, which

may negatively impact sales volumes, especially those of savings products.

➢ Higher costs may thus be incurred to market effectively and build credibility.

This could increase premiums and negatively impact sales.

• An internet-based sales channel may not be suitable for the company’s full range

of products, negatively affecting sales volumes

➢ It may be well suited to simpler products such as funeral products and with-

profits endowment products.

➢ It will not be suitable for whole of life products as the ability to underwrite

will be negatively impacted, leading to reduced margins through worse

experience.

➢ Savings products with complex charging structures or complex underlying

investment structures, such as unit-linked contracts typically sell better

through advised channels, where there is a better opportunity to explain terms

face-to-face for an investor.

Part (i) was a bookwork question and was well answered by most candidates.

Part (ii) was well answered by most candidates. A number, however, mistakenly indicated that

funeral liabilities would be long term and thus that bonds of a suitable term would not be

available.


Part (iii) was poorly answered by most candidates. Very few candidates referenced a diversion

of new business flows to competing banking products or recognised the fact that with-profits

policies would be mostly unaffected due to smoothing of returns and bonus levels.

Part (iv) was poorly answered by most candidates, as most were distracted by potential

administration issues or technical challenges that an internet platform may face, as opposed to

evaluating the basic risk factors associated with an insurance product.

#1 4. External environment 10.5 Legal Environment Regulatory requirements 0.7680

10.5 Legal Environment — Regulatory requirements:

Regulators may impose restrictions on life insurance companies, usually with the aim of protecting policyholders.

Common restrictions on:


Product design

  • Contracts types: A restriction on the types of contracts that a life insurance company can offer
  • Premium rates: Restrictions on the premium rates or charges for certain types of contracts
  • Terms and conditions: Requirements relating to the terms and conditions of the contracts
  • Method of sale: Restrictions on the channels through which life insurance can be sold, on sales procedures or on information given at the point of sale.
  • Non-Discrimination: Restrictions on rating factors and the ability to underwrite (e.g. to avoid discrimination)


Capital and reserving

  • Solvency capital requirements: minimum reserving or solvency margin requirements
  • Asset Valuation methods: dictate whether certain assets are valued at market value (active approach) or historic/book value (passive approach), which directly impacts the reported solvency position

Investment strategy

  • limit mismatching liabilities
  • restrict asset types
  • restrict concentration on a single asset type
  • Maximum counterparty exposure
  • Mismatching reserves
  • tax treatment of different asset classes
  • require independent custodians
  • admissible assets
  • liquidity requirement (cash holding)
  • restrict foreign investment
  • prescribe asset classes
  • method of calculating asset values (fair value)

Disclosures

  • Point of sale and marketing materials
  • Projection/illustrations e.g. maturity/surrender values
  • Charging structures
  • Reviewability (yes/no)
  • Risk disclosure (risks to the policyholder)
  • Financial and solvency
  • Published accounts (true and fair view)
  • Supervisory returns (SCR)
  • EV in published accounts
  • Impact of basis changes
  • Market-consistent valuation
  • disclose how stochastic models are calibrated: risk-neutral vs real-world calibration

The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#3 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7319

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#4 1. Life insurance contracts 3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer Investment risk 0.7157

3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer — Investment risk:

  • The insurer must invest the single premium to cover regular outgo over an unknown timeframe.
  • This risk can be mitigated by matching liabilities with fixed-interest securities with redemption dates matching the amounts being paid each year.
  • In a perfectly matched strategy, assuming that annuitants die exactly as expected, the insurance company should not need to buy or sell any of its assets during the term of the contract because the cash needed is provided by the coupons and redemption amounts.
  • This removes interest rate volatility risk and yield uncertainty because the cashflows and yields are locked in at the time when the contract was priced.
  • This scenario is impractical because:
  • Timing: The term of the annuity payments uncertain
  • Availability: Assets with perfectly matching terms may not be available (reinvestment risk)
#5 16. Reinsurance 3.2 Retention limits Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve 0.7138

3.2 Retention limits — Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve:

In this approach, insurers aim to minimize the total cost of two components:

  • the cost of obtaining reinsurance and
  • the cost of financing a mortality fluctuations reserve.

The process follows these steps:

1. Set a risk criterion: such as a maximum 1% probability that net losses will exceed a specific amount e.g. 25m

2. Model total costs: for different retention limits, the insurer stochastically models the expected net loss by varying the mortality rates. As the retention limit increases, the cost of reinsurance decreases, but the size of the required fluctuations reserve (and its associated financing cost) increases.

3. Calculate the financing cost: The cost of the reserve ($M$) is calculated as $M \times (j - i)$, where $j$ is the required rate of return on the company's capital and $i$ is the actual investment return earned on the reserve's assets.

4. Optimize: The insurer identifies the specific retention limit where the combined cost of the reserve and reinsurance is lowest while still satisfying the ruin probability target.

2022 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 3


i. Factors:

• The model points should be chosen in such a way that they represent the mix of

expected whole life assurance business accurately.

• Specifically, you would want to ensure that there are model points from each of

the age bands shown in the product design.

• Each model point should represent a group of policies with similar features and

characteristics of the expected whole life assurance book.

➢ E.g. age of policyholder, sum assured applicable, different premium levels.

• Different model points would specifically be chosen, to allow for variations in

factors that directly affect capital requirements.

➢ E.g. mortality levels which differ by age and other underwriting factors such

as gender, smoking status, health status etc.

ii. Advantages of using a deterministic model for profit testing:

• The model should be relatively easy and quick to run for different premium levels

to assess the impact on our profit criteria.

• Different parameters can also be sensitivity tested/scenarios tested by re-running

the model to understand the sensitivity of profit towards different key assumptions

thereby getting a clear understanding of which parameters/assumptions cause

more risks to the profitability of the product.

• The time to build the model should be relatively quick compared to a stochastic

approach.

• Modelling mortality deterministically also makes sense as it is normally not

subject to large fluctuations as would be the case for say investment returns.

• A deterministic model would allow easier iteration to allow us to understand the

parameters better. (We could use this over time to test and calibrate a stochastic

model with less chance of then having a spurious outcome from a sensitive

parameter.)

iii. Description of model:

• The model would project all expected cashflows associated with a single policy

or model point up to some terminal age, for example 100.

• Cashflows should be projected on a monthly or annual basis.


• To calculate expected cashflows, allowance would need to be made for the

different decrements that could influence a potential policyholder, for example,

death, cancellation of policy or making it paid-up etc.

• Specific care should be taken at the ages when large changes occur for example

at ages 35 and 50 where a possible spike in cancellations could occur.

• The model should allow for all potential cashflows, such as:

➢ Premiums charged and the changes in premium rates over time (by age)

depending on the nature of the premium pattern/escalation pattern selected.

➢ Specifically, the premium levels would need to be flexible enough to adjust

in line with the sum assured changes if that is the intended design.

➢ Expenses associated with the product for example initial commission, upfront

distribution expenses, policy administration, premium collections, ongoing

client communication expenses etc.

• The model would need to be able to accommodate different premium levels for

which a profit metric is produced.

• The model output should align with the profitability metric decided upon, for

example, net present value of expected profit or internal rate of return, etc.

• A suitable risk discount rate will be used when calculating the net present value

of profit which considers the riskiness of the product, assumptions and the capital

requirements of shareholders.

• The model should allow for the build-up of reserves over time and capital

requirements including solvency capital and allow for a suitable cost of capital as

an outflow item.

• The model would then be run for the different model points that represent the

future expected new business sales for the company to produce a projected

income statement and balance sheet for the business.

iv. Premium pattern:

• If a level premium or fixed increasing premium is used:

➢ The premiums would need to be quite high initially (relative to the initial sum

assured) as large reserves will have to be built up.

➢ This might make the product appear expensive and unattractive to potential

policyholders.

• If premiums change in proportional to the sum assured:

➢ This might be difficult to explain to policyholders.

➢ This might result in high lapses, particularly at age 36.

• If premiums are age-rated with some link to sum assured:

➢ This would be even more complicated for policyholders to understand.

Part (i) was reasonably well answered. However, many students focussed on selecting model

points for conducting a valuation on existing business rather than for pricing a new product.

In part (ii) many candidates only focussed on the generic comparison of a deterministic model

versus a stochastic model and did not specifically apply their knowledge to the case at hand.

Only a few mentioned that the main variable impacting the price would be the mortality rates

which are relatively stable and hence a deterministic approach is sensible.


In part (iii) the candidates who described the cashflow model did fairly well. Many went into

lots of detail discussing how the assumptions would be set rather than describing the model

workings.

Only a few candidates scored well in part (iv). The majority focused their discussion on the

level of premium rather than the premium pattern.

#2 7. Modelling 13.2 Model components Model components 0.7700

13.2 Model components — Model components:

To satisfy these requirements, the components of the model must allow for all those features of the business being modelled that could significantly affect the advice being given:

  • Model points: These are data records representing homogeneous groups of policies chosen to reflect the distribution of the business without needing to model every individual policy.
  • Parameters: A parameter must be included in the model if the decision reached would alter for different values of that parameter e.g. interest rates.
  • Time period (frequency) of cashflow projection must be short enough to produce reliable results while being cost-effective.
  • Future Cashflows: inclusion of all material cashflows, including premiums, investment income, benefit payments, expenses that are relevant to the business being modelled.
  • Dynamic correlations: The ability to model interactions between assets and liabilities, such as bonus declarations moving in line with investment performance.
  • Reserving cashflows: Allowance for the notional cashflows arising from setting up supervisory reserves and required solvency margins. The investment income from the supervisory reserve should also be included as a positive contribution to the profit flow.
  • Stochastic capability: For products with financial guarantees or options, the model may need to use stochastic simulation (Monte Carlo methods) rather than deterministic approaches.

#5 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Assessing solvency 0.7400

13.5 Model uses — Assessing solvency:

This assessment involves comparing the value of the company's assets against its liabilities using either supervisory (regulatory) or economic capital requirements.

17. Static vs dynamic: static solvency testing only measures a company's financial position at a single point in time, dynamic solvency testing uses a full model office to project the revenue account and balance sheet forward for 3 to 5 years.

  • Assesses the company's resilience to changes in the external economic environment.
  • Identify is the company's surplus assets might be likely to run out or become negative in the near future.
  • Provide management with enough time to adjust strategies - such as changing investment strategy, reduce bonus distributions, or alter marketing plans - to reduce the risk of insolvency/

18. Deterministic vs stochastic: actuaries use deterministic projections to test the impact on solvency, of specific scenarios, such as a gradual fall in investment returns or faster-than-expected mortality improvements on. Regulators may specify which deterministic scenarios must be tested. Stochastic projections uses Monte Carlo simulations to generate thousands of potential future paths for variables like in the balance sheet and revenue account. This allows the actuary to quantify the probability of ruin.

19. Modelling challenges: When projecting solvency stochastically, a major computational challenge is nested simulations, where the projected balance sheet for a future year itself requires thousands of simulations to value complex features like financial guarantees or options. Closed-form approximations (such as the Black-Scholes formula) or proxy models can be used to estimate these values efficiently.

20. Probability of absolute ruin: for a closed fund (no new business), an actuary may project just the revenue account until the very last contract expires. If the accumulated net cashflow up to that time is positive, company is solvent for that run. The proportion of simulations where the company runs out of assets is the estimated probability of absolute ruin.

21. Solvency capital requirements (risk margin): Models are used to determine the level of required solvency capital, which acts as a protective cushion. Under risk-based regimes like Value-at-Risk (VaR), models subject the balance sheet to extreme "shocks" (such as a 1-in-200-year event) to ensure the company remains solvency over a defined period, usually over one year. This requires the model to account for the benefits of diversification within its portfolio as it is unlikely that all extreme risks will happen at the same time.

QUESTION 4


i. Benefits for the company:

• May bring the product in line with those of competitors or make it more appealing

in the market.

➢ This may lead to increased sales and profits for the company. As it could result

in designing a more appealing or easier understood solution to clients or

advisers,

➢ This would reduce the likelihood of new business volumes being insufficient

to cover the company’s initial expenses.

• The company may be able to implement charges that are more easily reviewable

• It may also be able to formulate new (and easier to achieve) policyholder

reasonable expectations.

• The company may be able to implement a more capital efficient product.

➢ E.g. reduce guarantees; or implement higher initial charges.

• The unitised with-profits product may increase operational efficiency

➢ E.g. The current administration systems, distribution and other processes for

unit-linked business may only require minor changes to cater for the new

product range.

Benefits to new policyholders:

• The new product is easier to understand and more transparent than the conventional

product.

➢ As fees are explicit and bonuses may be more easily understood in terms of

value of units

• There is usually less smoothing in unitised with-profits business, so it may be more

equitable to different cohorts of policyholders

• The company may be able to offer more choice, e.g. by level of risk/return trade-

off and level of guarantees.

• The lower level of guarantees compared to the conventional product may provide

greater investment freedom to pursue higher expected return investments leading

to better returns for policyholders.

Benefits to existing policyholders:

• Any accumulated surplus won’t be shared with new policyholders.


➢ This would result in a more equitable distribution to existing clients who

contributed to the surplus.

ii. Investigations and associated action:

• Investigate whether any mistakes were made in the initial analysis to determine the

actual expenses per policy (e.g. data used is all correct).

➢ E.g. Initial expenses misclassed as renewal expenses.

• Check for once-off items.

➢ If this is causing a distortion no remedial action may be required.

➢ However, anticipated once-off expenses should be accounted for in the

charging structure or bonuses.

• Check whether the deviation is significant in terms of absolute size.

➢ For a small book, no immediate action may be taken.

• Check whether higher expenses per policy are due to expenses exceeding the

expected level, or due to lower than expected business volumes, or both.

➢ Past budgets and business plans may be useful sources for comparing against

actual experience (expenses and business volumes).

➢ Higher-than-expected expenses should be investigated to identify specific

drivers and sources, and whether these can be managed in future, e.g. through

cost-cutting exercises.

➢ If business volumes are lower-than-expected then causes for this should be

investigated and whether this trend is likely to continue.

▪ E.g. higher than expected withdrawals or lower than expected new

business may have led to lower overall volumes.

• If the expense over-run is significant and costs cannot be reduced or volumes

increased:

➢ Pricing assumptions and charges will need to be updated.

➢ For new business and for existing business (if charges are reviewable).

➢ Valuation assumptions will be adjusted as necessary.

This question was generally poorly answered.

In part (i) many candidates used the terms unitised with-profits and unit-linked

interchangeably, without demonstrating an understanding of the difference between them.

Furthermore, some weaker candidates assumed that “closed to new business” meant that the

product was closed, and that the insurer had the right to use the surplus as it wished. Some

candidates incorrectly focussed on risks rather than the benefits of the company’s decision.

Often points made were too generic to gain credit.

In part (ii) only the stronger candidates used the context well, structuring enough points to

answer the question whereas weaker candidates either only listed (often incorrectly) the steps

in an expense investigation, or provided management actions not related to the pricing or

valuation bases (and often to elements like mortality or investment risk).

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#3 4. External environment 10. The external environment 1. Volume and mix of new business 0.7156

10. The external environment — 1. Volume and mix of new business:

The insurer should consider the expected volume of new business, since this affects profitability, expense recovery, solvency strain and operational capacity.


If volumes are too low, the insurer may not recover fixed costs such as product development, systems, marketing, distribution and regulatory approval costs.


If volumes are too high, the insurer may suffer from new business strain, especially where initial expenses, commission or reserving requirements are high.


The insurer should also consider the expected mix of business, for example by: age, gender, sum assured or benefit level, premium term, policy duration, distribution channel, socio-economic group, underwriting class. A change in business mix may alter the risk profile, capital requirements, claims experience, expense assumptions and profitability of the business.

#4 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.5 Summary comparison of Surplus Distribution Systems Business Objectives 0.7096

9.1.5 Summary comparison of Surplus Distribution Systems — Business Objectives:

A primary business objective is to maximize profit distribution to policyholders to improve the company's competitive position. Competitive pressure encourages high bonus rates to attract new business. However, this creates a conflict during financial instability:


• Reductions in bonus rates can injure a company's competitive standing and reduce new business volumes.


• Management must balance this against the need to ensure solvency or reflect "financial reality," which may necessitate reducing rates.


• The level of control over this risk varies by method; for example, the conventional additions to benefits method allows the actuary to smooth rates to manage short-term anomalous results, whereas the revalorisation method offers no such discretion

  • Growth vs. Yield: If the objective is rapid growth, the company might pay higher bonuses to improve marketability and attract new business. 📈

  • Proprietary vs. Mutual: In a proprietary company, a portion of the distributed surplus (often 1/9th of the bonus) is transferred to shareholders, creating a conflict between policyholder returns and shareholder dividends. 🏛️
#5 8. Product design 14.4 Competitiveness The profit-volume relationship 0.7077

14.4 Competitiveness — The profit-volume relationship:

The primary objective is to maximize total contributions to the firms fixed overheads and profit from the product as a whole not per single policy. $$[total \ contribution] = [per \ policy \ contribution] \times [number \ of \ policies \ sold]$$


Where the per-policy contribution is the profit from a single policy net of marginal costs (ignoring overhead costs).


The company's total profit is then:

$$[Total \ profit] = \left\{ \sum\limits_{all \ products} [total \ contributions] \right\} - [overheads] $$


In highly competitive markets, an insurer may choose a design with lower per-policy contributions to ensure high sales volume, thereby maximizing the total contribution.

QUESTION 5


i. Actuarial funding:

• This is the method that a life insurance company can use to reduce the size of the

“unit reserves” it needs to hold in respect of its unit-linked business.

• The company effectively capitalizes some or all of the unit-related charges it

expects to receive from the units it has nominally allocated, with the funding then

being repaid from these future charges as they are received.

• When associated with appropriate surrender penalties it enables the company to:

➢ reduce its financing requirements because initial expenses are matched in terms

of time and nature.

ii. Surrender values should:

• Take into account policyholder’s reasonable expectations.

• At early durations, not appear too low compared with premiums paid (taking into

account any projections given at new business stage).

• At later durations, be consistent with projected maturity values.

• Not exceed earned asset share, in aggregate, over a reasonable time period.

➢ Make an appropriate contribution to profit, if possible (and consistent with the

other objectives).

• Take account of surrender values offered by competitors.

• Not be subject to

➢ frequent change, unless dictated by financial conditions.

➢ discontinuities over the duration of a policy.

• Not be excessively complicated to calculate, taking into account the computing

powers available nor explain to policyholders.

• Be capable of being documented clearly.

• Avoid selection against the insurer, including lapse and re-entry risks.

• Take account of auction values that may be available.

• Comply with regulatory and professional requirements.

• Appropriately allow for the cost of administering the surrender.

iii. a. Impact on ability to actuarially fund:

• Both designs include unit-related penalties, which will allow the company to

actuarially fund units.

• Under both designs the maximum rate that can be used in the funding-factor is

0.2% (the fund management charge in respect of initial expenses).

• Under B, the actuarial funding factors will be limited to a maximum term of

10 years.

• Therefore actuarial funding will have a larger effect for A.


b. Fairness:

• To policyholders that surrender:

➢ Both surrender penalties reduce over time (as a percentage of fund value),

which is reasonable as initial expenses are being repaid over time.

➢ Under A, the surrender penalty is approximately equal to the future

management charges (in respect of the initial expenses) the company will not

receive, which seems fair.

➢ Under B, there is a relatively large penalty at early durations, which may not

be viewed as fair to early leavers.

➢ Under B, no surrender penalty at later durations may be overly generous to

policyholders that lapse at these durations.

➢ However, this may be appropriate as the insurer would have likely recovered a

large portion of the initial expenses incurred.

• To policyholders that do not surrender:

➢ Under A, the initial expenses are recovered, and therefore policyholders that

do not lapse should largely be unaffected by surrenders.

➢ Under B there is an under-recovery for late surrenders.

▪ If these losses are passed on to other policyholders through higher policy

charges (compared to A), this may not be seen as fair.

• To shareholders :

➢ Under A, shareholders are not compensated for the loss of future profits. This

may be viewed as unfair.

➢ Under B:

▪ Shareholders would receive some profit on surrender on very early

surrenders.

▪ e.g. 0.4% × 10 = 4% of fund value > 0.2% × 15 = 3% of fund value.

▪ Shareholders would not be compensated for (some of) the lost future

charges, which could be unfair.

➢ Under B, there is a cross-subsidy between policyholders that surrender early

and those that surrender later.

▪ B therefore exposes the shareholder to more risk, (due to it being less capital

efficient and the cross-subsidy risk).

▪ It is not clear that this design compensates the shareholder for that risk,

which could be viewed as unfair.

Parts (i) and (ii) were generally answered well

For part (iii) most candidates compared the two designs, rather than discussing the two designs

and giving reasons why each design impacted the ability to use actuarial funding and or why

the design is fair (or not).

In addition, many candidates considered the surrender penalty to decide on the maximum

discount rate that can be considered for actuarial funding. While the surrender penalty protects

the company when policyholders surrender, it is not available for those that remain in-force.

#1 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding example 0.7903

12.2 Actuarial funding — example:

The setup:

  • Single premium: R10 000 (purchasing 10 000 units at R1 each)
  • Annual FMC: 5 (levied only on units physically held)
  • Discount rate for funding $(i)$: 4%
  • Policy term: 5 years
  • Age ($x$): 40 year old
  • Investment return $(g)$: 7%
  • Actuarial funding factor ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$): A multiplier that determines the required reserve based on the 4% and the probability of the contingent events (death or maturity)

----

Year 0: Inception

At the start, the insurer calculates the actuarially funded unit reserve instead of holding the full R10 000.

  • Funding factor ($A_{40:\overline{5|}}$): $0.8219$ (based on 4% discount over 5 years)
  • Reserve physically held: $$V_0 = R 10,000 * 0.8219 = R 8,219$$
  • Cashflow to non-unit fund: $R10,000 - R8,219$
  • This positive cashflow is used to pay for initial expenses like commission and underwriting.
  • The insurer is now missing $1,781$ units that it must buy back later.

---

#2 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor 0.7835

12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:

Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.

  • Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be

$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$

  • Where:
  • $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
  • $x$ is the entry age
  • $n$ is the policy term
  • Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.
#3 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding Conditions for use 0.7634

12.2 Actuarial funding — Conditions for use:

For actuarial funding to be viable and prudent, the following conditions must be met:

  • High management charges: There must be a substantial level of regular management charges to "buy back" the missing units over the policy term.
  • Higher management charges can be charged on all units, provided there is a sizeable quantity of FMC's to make the pre-funding worthwhile.
  • In the early years allocated premiums would be used to buy capital units which have higher charges and accumulation units. - this practice is no longer popular due to transparency issues.
  • Surrender penalties: It is not prudent to hold a reserve lower than what would be paid if the policyholder surrendered. Therefore, the funded reserve must not be less than the surrender value (bid value minus surrender penalty)
  • Positive Future Cashflows: Projections must show that future net cashflows to the insurer remain positive even after the management charges are reduced to rebuild the reserve.
  • Contingency: The benefit must be payable in a contingent event e.g. death or sickness
#4 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding Absence of investment risk 0.7492

12.2 Actuarial funding — Absence of investment risk:

The expected return on the unit fund is irrelevant to the discount rate because there is no investment risk in the buy-back process.

  • The liability ($l$) (the missing units) is denoted in units: $l = (n-x)* UnitPrice$
  • The source of funding (management charge) is a fixed percentage of the units. $FMC=percentagexUnitPrice$
  • Therefore: $l \approx FMC$

If the unit fund doubles in value due to high investment returns, the monetary cost of buying the missing units also doubles. However, because the management charge is a percentage of that fund, the amount of money to buy those units also doubles. Because both the cost of the units and the funding source (the management charges) move in direct proportion to the unit price. The insurer effectively "borrows" units rather than cash, and since the "repayments" are also unit-linked, the investment risk is eliminated from the buy-back process

#5 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding Purpose and rationale 0.7411

12.2 Actuarial funding — Purpose and rationale:

Unit-linked contracts often incur very high initial expenses (such as commission and medical underwriting) that exceed the first premium, resulting in a large initial capital strain.


The practice of funding initial expenses through lower allocation rates during the early policy years is no longer common and lower premium allocation rates are not consistent with PRE.


The expenses are usually recouped gradually via future fund management charges, this creates a mismatch in timing and nature between the immediate cash outgo and the gradual investment-linked income.


Actuarial funding addresses this by allowing the company to hold a smaller unit reserve at inception than the actual value of the units purchased by the premium. The company essentially "takes credit" in advance for a portion of the future management charges to cover its up-front costs.

QUESTION 6


i. Factors:

• The risks faced by the insurer.

➢ The greater the risks faced by the company related to the new product the

greater will be the extent of reinsurance needed.

➢ The larger the benefits offered and/or replacement ratios, the greater will be

the need for some form of reinsurance.

➢ A high degree of future benefit increases can result in significant risk, and

therefore a greater amount of reinsurance will likely be required.

➢ If the insurer is planning on entering a particularly risky target market, a greater

amount of reinsurance will be required.

• The experience of the insurer.

➢ As this is a new product the company is likely to need reinsurance as it will

have limited experience to draw on.

➢ If it has similar products this may reduce the need for reinsurance as it may

have relevant experience data to draw on.

➢ The extent of technical pricing assistance available from the reinsurer could

play a role.

➢ The more competent and experienced the insurer’s underwriting staff, the less

the need for reinsurance or technical assistance

• Reinsurance available in the market for this type of product.

➢ If there is nothing suitable available, it is a moot point.

• The cost of reinsurance.

➢ If the reinsurer wants to charge significantly more than the insurer’s estimate

of the underlying risk cost, hence making the product unmarketable, it may not

be able to use reinsurance.

➢ If reinsurance is perceived to be cheap the insurer may put more reinsurance in

place.

• Level of free reserves.

➢ The larger the free reserves the less need there may be for reinsurance.

• The insurer’s risk appetite.

➢ The more risk averse the insurer is, the more reinsurance will be required.

• The impact of reinsurance on solvency capital requirements.

➢ If reinsurance results in a significant reduction in solvency capital

requirements, the insurer may seek out a larger amount of reinsurance.

• The terms of reinsurance on offer.

➢ The more onerous the terms and conditions, the less likely the insurer will be

to take up reinsurance.

• Regulation may place requirements/limits on the amount of reinsurance to be used.

ii. Reinsurance programme:

• This will depend on the factors mentioned above.

• Quota share reinsurance as this will protect the insurer against parameter risk.

• Surplus reinsurance will protect the insurer from claims on the larger policies.


• Stop loss reinsurance (if available) could protect the insurer from overall poor

experience on the portfolio.

• Catastrophe cover could help protect the company from multiple claims arising

from a single event.

• The insurer may need to reinsure more than it would ideally like (quota share rather

than surplus, say) to get access to technical assistance from the reinsurer.

ii. Information from a standard application form:

• Height and weight;

• smoking and drinking habits;

• current health and details of any current treatment being received;

• personal medical history (any major illnesses or operations);

• family medical history (hereditary ailments like heart disease);

• occupation;

• potentially dangerous pastimes/hobbies;

• income; and

• assets and liabilities.

Part (i) was generally well answered by most candidates. Candidates scored well if they

identified which factors would have an impact on the amount of reinsurance sought out, as

well as identifying whether more or less reinsurance would be bought based on the factors

identified.

Candidates scored well in part (ii) if they were able to name the specific reinsurance

arrangements which would be appropriate.

Part (iii) was well answered by most candidates.

#1 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.8060

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#2 4. External environment 10. The external environment 11. Reinsurance availability 0.7820

10. The external environment — 11. Reinsurance availability:

The insurer should consider whether reinsurance is available and whether it is needed.


Reinsurance may help with: reducing volatility, managing large claims, reducing capital requirements, accessing specialist underwriting or claims expertise, supporting new product development.


However, reinsurance introduces counterparty risk and may reduce retained profits. The cost and terms of reinsurance may also affect the viability of the product.

#3 16. Reinsurance 3. Considerations before reinsuring What are the considerations before reinsuring? 0.7776

3. Considerations before reinsuring — What are the considerations before reinsuring?:

Before deciding whether and how to reinsure, an insurer evaluates several strategic and financial factors:

  • Type of reinsurance: The type of reinsurance (whether it is OTR, Risk premiums or excess of loss or Fin Re), will depend will depend on:
  • The reason the insurance company is using reinsurance
  • The reinsurance cost
  • The type of insurance business for which the reinsurance is to be arranged
  • Cost of Reinsurance: Because reinsurers include their own profit margins and expenses, which reduce the insurer's absolute profit level. the insurer must balance security versus return. It must determine if the reduction in volatility justifies the reduced expected return.
  • Retention Limits must be set by considering the company's risk appetite, its level of free assets, and the distribution of sum assured across its portfolio. A company with higher free assets can generally afford a higher retention limit.
  • Counterparty (Credit) Risk: The insurer retains liability according to the contract, to pay benefits even if the reinsurer cannot meet claim payments (becomes insolvent)
  • Alternatives, such as holding a mortality fluctuation reserve may be more cost-effective than purchasing reinsurance.
  • Legal Risks: Finally the company should consider legal risk by ensuring treaties are legally watertight.
#4 16. Reinsurance 3.1 Cost of reinsurance How does the cost of the reinsurance affect decisions about reinsurance arrangements? 0.7576

3.1 Cost of reinsurance — How does the cost of the reinsurance affect decisions about reinsurance arrangements?:

  • Reinsurance comes at a cost, these costs reduce the expected profit for the cedant
  • The reinsurance adds profit margins to its risk premiums.
  • The reinsurer may insist on more stringent risk management than the insurer would like e.g. stricter underwriting or claims processes
  • The reinsurance processes may result in a slower service offering to the policyholder (facultative, claims, delays)
  • The insurer will have increased counterparty risk, as it is exposed to the risk of the reinsurer failing to meet its obligations.
  • The direct writer must balance the cost of reinsurance against the risk of loss from adverse experience if less reinsurance were to be used.

However, the risk reduction caused by reinsurance could leverage up the return or risk-adjusted return on capital

#5 4. External environment 10. The external environment 6. Legal and regulatory environment 0.7500

10. The external environment — 6. Legal and regulatory environment:

The insurer should consider current and future legal and regulatory requirements.


These may affect: product design, policy wording, disclosure requirements, underwriting, claims handling, treating customers fairly, commission and remuneration structures, reserving, solvency capital requirements, reporting requirements.


Regulatory changes may increase costs or require product redesign. There is also a risk that the insurer may need to hold additional reserves or capital if the regulator considers the product to have significant guarantees or uncertain future cashflows.

QUESTION 7


i. Conditions may include:

• The sum of the unit and non-unit reserves for a policy should not be less than any

guaranteed surrender value.

• The future profits arising on a policy with a negative non-unit reserve need to

emerge in time to repay the “loan”.

• After taking account of the future non-unit reserves, there are no future negative

cashflows for the policy i.e. there should be no future valuation strain.

• In aggregate, the sum of all non-unit reserves (including from other business)

should not be negative.

• Negative non-unit reserves cannot be used to offset unit reserves.

• Assumptions must be prudent (i.e. they should lead to larger reserves) in order to

ensure that the negative non-unit reserve is not too aggressive resulting in

upfronting of profit recognition.


ii. Accounting information:

Revenue account:

• Premium income

• Investment income

• Charges collected (from premiums and unit-linked)

• Claims outgo (death, maturity, surrender)

• Expenses outgo (commissions, life office costs)

• Tax outgo

Balance sheet:

• Asset values (including current assets)

• Accounting provisions (including current liabilities)

Fund management information:

Overall and per fund if more than one fund:

• Asset values for the fund (including a breakdown of holdings and their values)

• Investment income (e.g. dividends, interest, rental)

• Capital gains (realised and unrealised)

• Net cashflows received for investment or paid out (e.g. to meet claims)

• Transaction costs paid from fund assets

iii. Data checks:

Accounts versus Fund manager information

• Fund manager net cashflows compared to cashflows from the accounts e.g. net

cashflow ~ premiums received – claims – expenses – tax (from accounts).

• Fund manager investment income compared to investment income shown in the

accounts should be consistent.

Accounts versus data extracts

• Assets (from accounts) ~ number of units (in force) x unit price at valuation date.

• Accounts death benefit outgo ≥ sum of unit values for deaths (in movements file).

➢ And/or accounts death outgo ~ number of deaths (movements file) x average

death benefit (taken as max of SA and unit value; from in-force file).

• Accounts maturity benefit outgo ≥ sum of unit values for maturities (in movements

file).

➢ And/or accounts maturity outgo ~ number of maturities (movements file) x

Fund manager information versus data extract files

iv. Possible reasons:

• A positive non-unit reserve implies that future expected charges are not sufficient

to meet expected non-unit fund outgo (including expenses and benefits in excess

of the unit fund).

likely have occurred due to unfavourable experience.

➢ This leads to lower fund values, which in turn leads to lower fund-related

➢ This increases the value of future expenses to be paid from the non-unit fund

➢ Proportionately more surrenders of large policies occur where charges

fund policies.

➢ New business comprises more of the smaller and less-profitable policies.

Parts (i) and (ii) were bookwork questions and were generally well answered.

#1 10. Reserving 4. Negative non-unit reserves What is the algorithm for calculating negative non-unit reserves? 0.8247

4. Negative non-unit reserves — What is the algorithm for calculating negative non-unit reserves?:

1. Project future cashflows:

  • Project the expected future non-unit cashflows for the policy, income less outgo (expenses and benefits in excess of the unit fund)

2. Identify the last cashflow:

  • Locate the last projected cashflow, regardless of whether it is positive or negative

3. Set the initial reserve:

  • Determine the amount needed to meet that final cashflow at that specific point in time. If the cashflow is positive, the reserve is set as a negative amount

4. Apply the surrender value floor:

  • Check that the total reserve (the sum of the unit and non-unit reserves) is not less than the guaranteed surrender value (unit reserve minus surrender penalty)

5. Iterate backward:

  • Move back to the next previous cashflow (t-1). Discount the current reserve to that point and subtract the cashflow at that time period. Repeat the surrender value floor check (Step 4).

6. Repeat the process:

  • Repeat these steps working backward through each time period until reaching the valuation date.

7. Establish the final reserve:

  • The result at the valuation date is the required non-unit reserve
#2 10. Reserving 4. Negative non-unit reserves No future valuation strain 0.8209

4. Negative non-unit reserves — No future valuation strain:

The negative reserve must be calculated such that there are no future negative cashflows for that policy. This ensures there is no future valuation strain, meaning the company will not be forced to suddenly find more capital at a later date because it took too much credit for profit today.

#3 10. Reserving 3. Non-unit reserves How is the non-unit reserve calculated in a Prudential valuation? 0.7923

3. Non-unit reserves — How is the non-unit reserve calculated in a Prudential valuation?:

The non-unit reserve is defined as the amount required to ensure that the company is able to pay claims and expenses without needing further financing.


The company projects forwards its year-by-year non-unit cashflows on the reserving basis and works backwards from the end of the policy term.

1. Project cashflows

2. Identify the last negative cashflow

3. Zeroise the shortfall by holding the required money at the start of that period and allowing for investment returns during the year.

4. Deduct from the cashflow at end of the previous period.

5. Repeat backward.


At the end of the zeroization process (valuation date), if the discounted adjusted cashflow is negative then a non-unit reserve is set up equal to the absolute value of that negative amount. In a prudential valuation if the discounted adjusted cashflow is non-negative the non-unit reserve is typically set to zero.

#4 10. Reserving 4. Negative non-unit reserves What is a negative non-unit reserve? 0.7908

4. Negative non-unit reserves — What is a negative non-unit reserve?:

A negative non-unit reserve arises when the value of future positive cashflows outweighs the value of the negative cashflows. The can occur for unit contracts if future charges are expected to exceed future expenses and other costs.


If a contract has a negative reserve it means that we a treating the contract as an asset. By holding a negative reserve, the company effectively takes advance credit for future profits to reduce initial capital strain and improve the capital efficiency of the product

#5 10. Reserving 3. Non-unit reserves What is a non-unit reserve? 0.7850

3. Non-unit reserves — What is a non-unit reserve?:

Due to the complexity of unit linked-contracts a cashflow approach is necessary. We refer to the gross premium cashflow reserve of a unit-linked contract as the non-unit reserve.

$$\text{Non-unit reserve} = \text{EPV[Non-unit Outgo]} - \text{EPV[Non-unit Income]}$$

Where:

  • Non-unit outgo: includes future costs, such as administration expenses, benefit outgo in excess of the unit fund.
  • Non-unit income: includes unallocated premiums, fund management charges, risk charges and bid-offer spreads
