#1 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7480

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#2 14. Guarantees and options 3. Mortality options What are the implications of offering a mortality option? 0.7351

3. Mortality options — What are the implications of offering a mortality option?:

Offering a mortality option such as the right to increase cover or renew a policy without further medical evidence:

  • Anti-selection: The primary risk is selection against the office, where policyholders in poor health are significantly more likely to exercise the option.
  • Financial cost: The cost is the difference between the standard premium charged and the higher premium that would have been charged under full underwriting. $$\{\text{proportion of lives exercising the option}\} \times \{\text{average health of lives exercising the option}\} $$
  • Higher Capital strain: reserving for mortality guarantees must account for both expected higher mortality of those exercising the option and the uncertainty regarding future take up rates.
#3 5. Risks 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk Influences on model and parameter uncertainty 0.7328

11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Influences on model and parameter uncertainty:

Insurers must constantly update their assumptions, but several factors make this process risky:

  • Medical advances
  • Data inadequacy
  • Expanding funnel of doubt
  • Capital and reserving impact
#4 5. Risks 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk Directions of mortality risk 0.7312

11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Directions of mortality risk:

The impact of mortality depends on the nature of the insurance contract:

  • Mortality: For life insurance products like term assurance, the risk is that deaths are higher than expected, leading to a reduction in profit or capital shortfall. The risk is most significant at the start of a contract when the sum at risk is at its highest.
  • Longevity: For survival-contingent products like immediate annuities, the risk is that policyholders live longer than expected. In this scenario, the insurer risks paying out more income than they had initially priced for through the initial single premium and reserved for.

See mortality question example: Question 13.3

#5 5. Risks 11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk Components of mortality/morbidity risk 0.7305

11.2 Mortality and morbidity risk — Components of mortality/morbidity risk:

There are three risks associated with mortality/ASSA/F102 Life Insurance Principles/Definitions/morbidity assumptions:

  • Model risk: the assumed probability distribution could be inappropriate e.g assuming policyholders are i.i.d, with $Bin(n, p)$. The failure of these assumptions about the population i.e. independent, identical and the type of distribution with respect to mortality would increase the risk.
  • Parameter risk: the specific model parameter estimates e.g. $p$ used in the model may not reflect actual population parameters even though the underlying model is appropriate.
  • Random fluctuations: unpredictable variations due to sample size (too low for the law of large numbers to apply).

The likelihood of our assumptions for the future being correct depends on the quality, credibility and relevance of the data available.

F102_NOVEMBER_2023_Paper1_Q1

2023 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 1


An insurance company sells regular premium 10-year conventional with-profits endowment assurance policies. It offers guaranteed minimum maturity values and surrender values on these policies equal to a return of premiums paid accumulated at 10% per annum.

i. Outline how option pricing techniques can be used to determine the cost of the guaranteed

minimum maturity and surrender values.


The company operates in a developing economy with a limited set of bonds and stocks available in the local market.

ii. Explain the difficulties associated with pricing these guarantees using option pricing

techniques.


The company is considering expanding its sales to a different country.

iii. Discuss the main taxation considerations that the company should take into account in making

this decision.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 1


i. The cost of the guarantee can be determined as follows:


  • The company would project the asset shares of the endowment portfolio, and the level of future bonuses given the company's bonus philosophy.

  • The company would also project the accumulated value of premiums at 10% p.a. as the minimum level of benefits guaranteed.

  • While the guarantee is based on sum assured and bonuses, market-traded options are based on the price of assets, which in this case could be taken as the level or price of the assets backing the asset shares.

  • The cost of the minimum guarantees could be determined using the cost of markettraded put options applied to the projection of asset shares: ➢ The cost of the minimum maturity value could be determined by referencing the cost of European style put options to sell the assets underlying the assets shares at the maturity date, at the required strike price to match the minimum guaranteed benefit. ➢ The cost of the minimum surrender value could be determined by referencing the cost of American style put options to sell the underlying assets at the required price to match the guarantee, at any time during the term of the policy.

ii. Difficulties:


  • Given the limited set of stocks and bonds available, there may not be options available for the full range of instruments required.

  • The limited markets may lead to liquidity issues for the assets. ➢ This will increase the cost of the relevant option and make the insurance product pricing uncompetitive.

  • Given the market limitations, the pricing of options may not yet be accurate. ➢ This may lead to mispricing of the insurance policies.

  • There could be difficulty in deciding on the extent to which any margins included in option prices should be reflected in the insurer's pricing.

  • Option prices may be volatile or experience short-term anomalies in a developing market. ➢ This may result in the pricing of the insurance contracts being volatile.

iii. Main considerations


  • The main considerations for the company would be to understand how the taxation basis of the new country and market works and how this compares to the current country of operation as this could influence various aspects of their strategy.

  • This affects both the company tax and tax in the hands of the policyholders.

  • Company tax may be levied on: ➢ annual profits; ➢ investment income less expenses in policyholders' funds; or ➢ both of the above.

  • Taxation can lead to advantages (or restrictions) during the different stages of the policy. ➢ If premiums are fully or partially deductible from the individual's taxable income, or other tax incentives are offered, it can create a strong selling point for the insurer. Conversely, a premium tax may add an extra cost layer, affecting both pricing strategy and consumer appeal. ➢ Understanding how funds are taxed during the contract's term is crucial and it can impact the investment strategy of the insurer. ➢ The eventual taxation of policy benefits may influence the attractiveness too. If the benefits are subject to heavy taxation, it could deter potential policyholders, while favourable tax treatment could be marketed as a key advantage.

  • The taxation basis would also affect pricing.

  • Restrictive tax laws might limit innovation and flexibility in contract design. This question was not well answered by most candidates. Many candidates did not know their bookwork on option pricing techniques well enough. Candidates who were able to think through the product cycle and the tax considerations at each stage were able to score well in part (iii).

#1 14. Guarantees and options 2. Valuing an investment guarantee How are investment guarantees valued using stochastic simulation? 0.7636

2. Valuing an investment guarantee — How are investment guarantees valued using stochastic simulation?:

  • Identify the underlying assets
  • Project asset values: use a stochastic model to simulate future asset prices or returns based on a chosen probability distribution (e.g. mean and variance) for the underlying assets
  • Model Policyholder behaviour: Incorporate assumptions about when policyholders are likely to exercise the option (when it is in the money).
  • Identify shortfalls: In each simulation, compare the projected fund value against the guaranteed amount. If the fund is lower, the difference is the cost of the guarantee for that specific scenario. For paths where the fund value is above the guarantee, the cost is recorded as zero.
  • Discounting: Discount the cost of each individual path back to the valuation date e.g. using the risk-free rate under market consistent frameworks
  • Expected cost: Take the average of the simulated costs across all runs, which provides the expected present value for the guarantee,
#2 12. Surrender values 2. Methods of calculation Explain the prospective method 0.7503

2. Methods of calculation — Explain the prospective method:

The discounted value of future benefits and expenses, net of future premiums using best estimate assumptions.

  • ensures the surrender value progresses smoothly into the maturity value
  • allows the company to capitalize future profits
  • used primarily after the initial early stage of the policy.
  • It is very sensitive to future assumptions, particularly the interest rate assumption

Example: $$SV = SA \cdot A_{x+t} + e \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t} + f \cdot A_{x+t} - G \cdot \ddot{a}^{(m)}_{x+t} - C$$

#3 10. Reserving 9. Cost of capital approach The Three-Step Calculation Process 0.7497

9. Cost of capital approach — The Three-Step Calculation Process:

1. Project Required Capital: The insurer projects the future capital required to be held $(C_t​)$ for each period during the "run-off" of the business. (this is the SCR)

2. Apply Cost of Capital Rate: These projected capital amounts are multiplied by a cost of capital rate (e.g., 6% per annum).

3. Discount to Present Value: The resulting annual costs are discounted back to the valuation date using risk-free (market-consistent) interest rates to produce the total risk margin. $$\text{Risk margin} = \displaystyle{\sum_t \dfrac{k_tC_t}{(1 + r_t)^t}}$$

#4 16. Reinsurance 3.2 Retention limits Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve 0.7482

3.2 Retention limits — Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve:

In this approach, insurers aim to minimize the total cost of two components:

  • the cost of obtaining reinsurance and
  • the cost of financing a mortality fluctuations reserve.

The process follows these steps:

1. Set a risk criterion: such as a maximum 1% probability that net losses will exceed a specific amount e.g. 25m

2. Model total costs: for different retention limits, the insurer stochastically models the expected net loss by varying the mortality rates. As the retention limit increases, the cost of reinsurance decreases, but the size of the required fluctuations reserve (and its associated financing cost) increases.

3. Calculate the financing cost: The cost of the reserve ($M$) is calculated as $M \times (j - i)$, where $j$ is the required rate of return on the company's capital and $i$ is the actual investment return earned on the reserve's assets.

4. Optimize: The insurer identifies the specific retention limit where the combined cost of the reserve and reinsurance is lowest while still satisfying the ruin probability target.

#5 14. Guarantees and options 2. Valuing an investment guarantee How are option pricing techniques used to value guarantees? 0.7427

2. Valuing an investment guarantee — How are option pricing techniques used to value guarantees?:

This approach treats insurance guarantees as analogous to market-traded derivatives. In these scenarios the insurer is seen as a seller of the option to the policyholder (in exchange for a premium), who can then exercise it to limit their downside own risk.

  • Maturity guarantees: valued as European-style put options.
  • Surrender guarantees: valued as American-style put options.
  • Guaranteed annuity rates: valued as call options on bonds or swaps option (to swap floating rate returns for fixed rate returns)

Under market-consistent valuations, if suitable options exists in the market that replicates the cashflows from the guarantee, the market prices of those are taken as the value of the option (Market-to-market)


Formulas for option values like Black-Scholes are also used to calculate the values of the options efficiently. They are helpful for avoiding nested simulations.

Question

QUESTION 2


An actuarial student proposes using the "equating policy values" method when policyholders request altering their conventional without-profits whole life assurance policy to a conventional without-profits term assurance policy with the same sum assured. The policy value before the alteration would be set equal to 90% of the policy's asset share as at the date of alteration. The policy value after alteration would be calculated using the current pricing basis for new products.

Discuss the considerations that you would take into account in evaluating this proposal.

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 2


Considerations:


  • It is unlikely that there is a significant risk of anti-selection for this type of alteration.

  • Offering the alteration protects the company against the risk of lapse-and-reentry and therefore incurring new business costs again.

  • Boundary conditions: ➢ Surrendering the existing policy and buying a new term assurance policy is a boundary condition. ➢ Using the current pricing basis ensures that premiums are consistent with new business premiums. ➢ However, consistency of the premiums is dependent on the surrender value that is available for the whole life policy (under the boundary condition alternative above).

  • Policyholder's reasonable expectations: ➢ If the alteration is consistent with the boundary condition, it is likely that policyholder's expectations are likely to be met.

➢ If the policy value before alteration is larger than the prospective reserve on the original pricing basis, the company will not retain all of the historic margins included in the original pricing basis. ➢ If the policy value before alteration is less than the prospective reserve on the original pricing basis, then the company will also extract some of the future profit it would have made on the original policy (in addition to the historic margins). ➢ If the policy value before alteration is equal to the prospective reserve on a realistic basis, then the company will extract the full profit it would have made on the original policy. ➢ Using the current pricing basis for the policy value after alteration ensures that the company will make future profit that is consistent with the current new business margins. ➢ This proposal does not make any allowance for the cost of the alteration, which could be deducted from the policy value before alteration. ➢ The initial expenses included in the current pricing basis should be removed to avoid charging the policyholder again.


  • At very early durations the asset share is likely to be negative. Including a negative value in the alteration is appropriate because it means that the initial costs of the original policy have not been recovered.

  • However, using only 90% of the asset share when it is negative, means that the company would not be recovering some of the initial costs incurred on the original policy.

  • Fairness - the company needs to consider: ➢ Fairness to the policyholders that alter their policies and those that don't. ➢ Fairness to shareholders. ➢ If the policy value before alteration broadly extracts historic margins (only), then it could be argued that this alteration is fair to the three parties. ➢ For very short policy terms under the new Term Assurance policy, the policy value before alteration may be in excess of what is required to cover benefits and expenses (without any further premiums being paid). ➢ It would thus be sensible for the company to specify a minimum term for the term assurance policy in order to ensure reasonable value for money for the policyholder.

  • The surrender value before the alteration will not be consistent with that after the alteration, as the term assurance is not likely to offer a surrender value.

  • Stability over time and duration: ➢ Even though the new business pricing basis should not change frequently, this method is unlikely to be stable over time as the asset share is dependent on the actual experience (which may be volatile).

  • Competition: ➢ The company needs to consider whether this alteration is consistent with similar alterations offered by competitors.

  • Legislative/professional requirements: ➢ This alteration would almost certainly be allowed in terms of regulation or professional guidance.

➢ If the term of the new term assurance policy is very long, then the premium should be consistent with (and slightly lower than) the premium under the whole life assurance policy


  • Easy to explain: ➢ Equating policy values will be difficult to explain to policyholders, who are unlikely to be familiar with present value calculations or asset share calculations.

  • Easy to document and administer: ➢ Calculating asset shares could be challenging to document and administer as the historical experience must be captured. ➢ New business terms are readily available This, fairly straightforward, question was generally poorly answered. Answers were too generic, with generally insufficient application. Most candidates knew the theory reasonably well and scored marks for the various headings (boundary conditions, affordability, etc.), but few candidates could apply these to the question scenario and make specific comments under these headings. Very few candidates commented on the relationship between the policy value before alteration and the reserve on the original pricing basis and the impact thereof on profit extraction. Many candidates incorrectly indicated that using the asset share as basis for the policy value before alteration would mean that the insurer made no profit at the date of the alteration seeming to ignore the fact that only 90% of the asset share was used as the policy value before the alteration.. Many candidates incorrectly indicated that the amendment would cause selection against the insurer and recommended underwriting to avoid this happening. The following principles were not relevant to the scenario in the question and therefore did not gain any credit: Consistency with premium at start; consistency with maturity values at end; consistency with auction values.

#1 13. Alterations 3. Methods of calculation example 0.7739

3. Methods of calculation — example:

For a whole life assurance at duration $t$, the equation of value is:


$$(PUSA)_t \cdot A_{x+t} + e \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t} + f \cdot A_{x+t} = (SV)_t$$


Components


  • $(PUSA)_t$: The new, reduced paid-up sum assured.
  • $(SV)_t$: The surrender value (or prospective reserve) at the time of alteration.
  • $A_{x+t}$: The present value of 1 payable on death at the attained age.
  • $e$: Level annual renewal administration expenses (note that renewal commission is removed since no further premiums are paid).
  • $\ddot{a}_{x+t}$: The present value of a life annuity of 1 per annum.
  • $f$: The cost of processing the final claim.

If a specific administrative alteration expense ($C$) is charged, it is typically subtracted from the value before alteration.

#2 13. Alterations 3. Methods of calculation Equating policy values 0.7701

3. Methods of calculation — Equating policy values:

Use for all types of alterations: $$\text{Value before alteration} = \text{Prospective value after alteration}$$

#3 12. Surrender values 2. Methods of calculation Explain the prospective method 0.7570

2. Methods of calculation — Explain the prospective method:

The discounted value of future benefits and expenses, net of future premiums using best estimate assumptions.

  • ensures the surrender value progresses smoothly into the maturity value
  • allows the company to capitalize future profits
  • used primarily after the initial early stage of the policy.
  • It is very sensitive to future assumptions, particularly the interest rate assumption

Example: $$SV = SA \cdot A_{x+t} + e \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t} + f \cdot A_{x+t} - G \cdot \ddot{a}^{(m)}_{x+t} - C$$

#4 12. Surrender values 3. Retention of profit on surrender How does the choice of surrender basis influence how much future profit is extracted/capitalized? 0.7461

3. Retention of profit on surrender — How does the choice of surrender basis influence how much future profit is extracted/capitalized?:

The profit on surrender is equal to the Asset share per policy less the surrender benefit paid.

The profit on surrender is zero when the surrender benefit is equal to the earned asset share.


The capitalized value of future profit arises from the differences between the premium rate assumptions and the surrender values assumptions.

  • Best estimate basis: If the insurer uses realistic, best estimate assumptions for calculating the surrender value, it effectively retains the same total profit it would have made if the contract stayed in force until the end
  • Premium basis: If the insurer uses the original premium basis (with margins), it only retains the profit made up to date.
  • Blended basis: Capitalising future profits may be considered unfair to surrendering policyholders so many companies use a "blended" approach, which is a basis between the realistic basis and the premium basis
#5 13. Alterations 2. Principles of alterations How are boundary conditions used to assess proposals for alterations? 0.7453

2. Principles of alterations — How are boundary conditions used to assess proposals for alterations?:

Boundary conditions act as limits or tests to verify that proposed changes are fair and don't allow policyholders to exploit inconsistencies in the company's pricing and terms.

  • Surrender: A reduction in a policy's term to zero should produce a value consistent with the cash surrender value
  • Paid-up status: A reduction in sum assured should be consistent with a paid-up calculation
  • New policy: For an increase in benefits, the additional premium should be consistent with what the company would charge for taking out a new policy of that size.
  • Alteration to itself: reflecting a minor change

QUESTION 3


A well-established life insurance company that sells conventional without-profits business only is considering changing its distribution model, from being mainly through independent intermediaries to an internet-based direct selling model.

i. Outline the considerations and actions required by the company prior to implementing this

change.


ii. Outline the reasons why it would be preferable for the company to sell term assurances, rather

than whole life assurances, through direct selling.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 3


i. Target market:


  • Need to analyse which demographics are reached by the current model and how to target them directly.

  • How to implement new advertising and promotional strategies tailored to reach the same audience without intermediaries.

Technology infrastructure:


  • Need to build or upgrade an online platform to facilitate direct sales and customer service.

  • Need to Implement robust cybersecurity protocols to protect customer information and financial transactions. Regulatory compliance:

  • Careful review of existing regulations related to direct sales and ensure compliance.

  • Engage legal expertise to monitor and adapt to potential changes in regulation that might affect the new model. Product complexity:

  • Assess current product offerings to determine necessary simplifications for direct sales.

  • Balance simplicity with a diverse product range to meet various customer needs and preferences. Brand perception:

  • Craft communication strategies to mitigate any perception of reduced personal touch.

  • Establish strong brand guidelines and customer service protocols to maintain brand reputation. Training and development:

  • Develop a comprehensive training program for sales and support staff to adapt to the direct sales model.

  • Offer continuous development opportunities to ensure the team stays up-to-date with relevant skills. Competition analysis:

  • Research competitors' strategies in direct sales to identify opportunities and threats.

  • Tailor the direct sales approach to maintain or enhance competitive positioning. Transition costs:

  • Plan the financial aspects of the transition, including potential one-time costs and ongoing investments.

Risk management:


  • Create detailed risk assessments for new vulnerabilities introduced by direct interactions with customers.

  • Establish controls and continuous monitoring to minimize exposure to identified risks. Customer service:

  • Design customer service protocols that ensure quick and personalised responses in the absence of intermediaries.

  • Leverage technology such as chatbots or AI-based support systems, while maintaining human interaction where needed. Pricing strategy:

  • Analyse the impact of removing intermediary commissions on pricing.

  • Revise pricing strategies to ensure competitiveness while maintaining profitability. Data management:

  • Employ advanced analytics to make informed decisions using collected customer data.

  • Ensure compliance with data protection regulations and ethical standards. Market research:

  • Conduct in-depth research to understand the preferences of the target market segment for direct sales.

  • Adapt products, marketing, and overall strategy based on research insights. Communication Strategy:

  • Plan clear and transparent communication with existing policyholders, intermediaries and other stakeholders about the changes.

  • Create a feedback mechanism to address concerns and build trust. Sales targets and performance metrics:

  • Set realistic sales targets that reflect the changes in the distribution model.

  • Monitor performance regularly and adapt strategies as needed for continuous improvement. Channel integration:

  • Invest in technology that ensures consistent information and service across channels. Strategic partnerships:

  • Identify potential partnerships with tech companies to enhance the direct sales model.

  • Manage the transition with existing intermediaries to mitigate conflicts or legal challenges. Reputational risk:

  • Identify potential reputational risks associated with the change and craft strategies to mitigate them.

  • Implement crisis communication plans to respond quickly if issues arise. Long-term strategy alignment:

  • Evaluate how the change aligns with long-term business goals and market trends.

  • Periodically review the approach to ensure it stays aligned with the evolving business landscape. Impact on existing policyholders:

  • Carefully assess the potential effects of the shift on existing policyholders and tailor strategies to ensure a smooth transition.

  • Maintain open communication with existing policyholders and offer incentives or assurances to foster retention.

ii. Reasons why selling term assurances would be preferable:


  • Term assurance contracts are generally simpler and easier to understand. ➢ This could appeal to a broader customer base than whole life assurance. ➢ A lower risk of misunderstanding leads to a lower risk of mis-selling and reputational damage.

  • Term assurances would have lower costs. ➢ There should be lower underwriting costs than with whole life. ➢ Administration expenses should also be lower due, for example, to there being no surrender values. ➢ This aligns well with the direct sales model, where cost reduction is often a primary goal.

  • Selling a simple and low-cost term assurance (rather than potentially more complex and costly whole life) can foster transparency and trust, contributing to customer retention.

  • Term assurance contracts may present a more predictable risk profile.

  • Term assurance can be more easily tailored to specific customer needs, such as young families.

  • Term assurance premiums are generally lower, potentially leading to higher sales volumes.

  • As the end of the term of cover approaches, there will be opportunities to cross-sell other products to policyholders.

  • Term assurance contracts can align well with the direct sales model, where efficiency and streamlined processes are key. ➢ This strategic fit can enhance the overall success of the new distribution strategy. Candidates performed well in part (i). Those that underperformed generally did not cover a broad enough spectrum of considerations. Part (ii) was generally not well answered. Many candidates focussed on generic reasons why a direct sales strategy has benefits and thus did not answer the question, which related to why it would be preferable for the company to sell term assurances rather than whole life assurances using a direct sales approach.

#1 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7503

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#2 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7351

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#3 4. External environment 10.2.2 Distribution channels - Actuarial control cycle Using the control cycle to manage distribution channels 0.7348

10.2.2 Distribution channels - Actuarial control cycle — Using the control cycle to manage distribution channels:

The Actuarial Control Cycle can be used at a macro level to specify the problem by helping a company decide which distribution channels such as independent intermediaries, tied agents, an own sales force, or direct marketing, should be used to achieve future profitability while maintaining an acceptable level of risk.


This involves analyzing the general commercial environment and competitors to identify successful methods that align with the company's strategic goals.


In the developing the solution stage, the choice of distribution channel serves as a critical input for projection models, as it dictates assumptions regarding the volume, type, and mix of new business, average policy size, and demographic factors like mortality, morbidity, and withdrawal rates. These models must be used to test the impact of variations from central assumptions, particularly for highly uncertain elements like future new business levels, before a specific strategy is adopted.


The monitoring and feedback phase requires the company to continually analyze actual experience to see if the type and quality of business coming onto the books materializes as expected in the models. If actual experience deviates from the assumed parameters, the actuary must update the model assumptions, which may lead to revised management decisions.


At a micro level, the control cycle helps manage the distribution by evaluating the performance of individual channels, such as specific brokers or agents, to identify and improve areas of poor performance through better training, administration, or sales information.


Furthermore, the element of professionalism within the cycle ensures that the sales strategy is ethical and aligned with consumer interests, requiring the insurer to identify and rectify poor practices while fostering good ones. Overall, the control cycle ensures the distribution strategy is sound and sustainable.

#4 4. External environment 10.2.1 Distribution channels - Risk to the insurer Impact on risk to the insurer 0.7266

10.2.1 Distribution channels - Risk to the insurer — Impact on risk to the insurer:

The choice of distribution channel introduces several macro risks, primarily related to demographic profile, persistency and anti-selection.

  • Anti-selection: intermediaries are subject to the most stringent underwriting because they represent the client, not the insurer, increasing the potential for anti-selection. Conversely, direct marketing involves the lowest level of underwriting to avoid barriers to sales, but the insurer risks attracting a disproportionate share of high-risk applicants because it appears to have the most relaxed standards in the markets.
  • Withdrawal (Persistency) risk: Channels using aggressive sales approaches or reaching less sophisticated buyers are more likely to see early lapses. Intermediaries typically have the lowest withdrawal rates.
  • Mix of business risk*: Insurers set pricing assumptions based on an expected mix of business. If the volume of a specific channel changes unexpectedly, the overall experience (mortality, morbidity, and expenses) may deviate from the pricing basis.
  • Expense risk: Direct marketing and own sales forces involve high fixed overheads and development costs. If these channels produce low sales volumes, the company may fail to recover the costs, while excessive volume can overstretch capital resources and administrative capacity.
  • Intermediary actions (lapse and re-entry): independent distributors may act in their own interest by encouraging clients to cancel their policies and take out new ones, which can cause significant financial loss to the original insurer. This can be mitigated by exit penalties or commission clawbacks.
#5 4. External environment 10. The external environment 3. Distribution channel and distributor behaviour 0.7217

10. The external environment — 3. Distribution channel and distributor behaviour:

The insurer should consider how the product will be distributed and whether the distribution channel is appropriate for the target market.


Distribution factors include: whether the sales force has sufficient training, whether distributors understand the product, whether customers receive adequate disclosure, whether advice is suitable, whether sales incentives encourage good customer outcomes.


Commission structures may create conflicts of interest. For example, high upfront commission may encourage excessive sales, poor-quality business, policy churning or mis-selling. The insurer should monitor persistency, complaints and claims disputes by distribution channel.

CY 2022 CY 2023

R millions R millions Sums assured from new policies 550 600 Sums assured lapsed 150 75 Sums assured paid out 300 250

QUESTION 4

  • Benefits: ➢ Benefits paid rate = paid SA / start of year SA ➢ For 2022: R 300m / R2200m =13.6% ➢ For 2023: R 250m / R2300m = 10.9%

  • New business: ➢ New business rate = new business SA / start of year SA ➢ For 2022: R 550m / R2200m =25.0% ➢ For 2023: R 600m / R2300m = 26.1%

9. Cost of capital approach — The Three-Step Calculation Process:

1. Project Required Capital: The insurer projects the future capital required to be held $(C_t​)$ for each period during the "run-off" of the business. (this is the SCR)

2. Apply Cost of Capital Rate: These projected capital amounts are multiplied by a cost of capital rate (e.g., 6% per annum).

3. Discount to Present Value: The resulting annual costs are discounted back to the valuation date using risk-free (market-consistent) interest rates to produce the total risk margin. $$\text{Risk margin} = \displaystyle{\sum_t \dfrac{k_tC_t}{(1 + r_t)^t}}$$

#2 2. Health and care products 6.1.5 Critical illness cover - Capital requirements Capital requirements for Critical Illness (CI) cover 0.7404

6.1.5 Critical illness cover - Capital requirements — Capital requirements for Critical Illness (CI) cover:

The following factors affect capital requirements for CI contracts:


  • Contract Design (High): Unit-linked or reviewable designs are more capital-efficient than non-linked or guaranteed products. Reviewable premiums allow the insurer to adjust for worsening experience, reducing the need for massive initial contingency loadings.
  • Premium Frequency (High): Regular premiums require significantly more initial capital than single premiums. Regular premium contracts often have negative initial cash flow (new business strain) because initial expenses exceed the first premium.
  • Reserving vs. Pricing Basis (Significant): Capital requirements increase as the difference between the pricing basis and the supervisory reserving basis grows. If the reserving basis is stronger than the pricing basis, capital must be provided to set up the required reserves at the outset.
  • Initial Expenses (Significant): High acquisition costs, such as commissions and complex medical underwriting, increase the initial capital strain. CI requires multi-disciplinary teams to assess medical and financial data, leading to heavy up-front expenses.
  • Solvency Capital Requirement (Significant): Supervisory authorities require a capital cushion to cover the unpredictability of diagnosis rates, which are less stable than mortality rates. CI involves higher prudent margins and risk-based capital to withstand extreme adverse scenarios.
  • Guarantees (High): Offering guaranteed premiums or benefit definitions increases the risk of needing significant reserve enhancements if experience worsens. Medical advances can lead to earlier diagnosis or windfall claims, forcing insurers to find additional capital.
  • Late Claim Notification (Relevant): Insurers must maintain reserves for late notified claims, which can arise up to ten years after the initial incidence. This increases the duration for which capital must be held and managed.
#3 2. Health and care products 6.1.1 Critical illness cover - Product structures and benefits Guarantees and reviewability of premiums and benefits 0.7401

6.1.1 Critical illness cover - Product structures and benefits — Guarantees and reviewability of premiums and benefits:

  • Competitive pressures: pushed companies to offer guarantees on both benefits (that claim definitions will not change) and premiums.
  • Better estimation of CI risks leads to insurers progressively charging an appropriate price for guarantees.
  • Predicting increases: For reviewable contracts, it is difficult to predict future premium increases because incidence trends for different medical conditions move in different directions.
  • Impact on Reserving and capital: Guaranteed premiums may require capital injections to fund reserves for worsening claims experience.
  • Impact of medical advances
  • Windfall claims: Medical advances may turn a previously "critical" surgery into a minor, low risk procedure. If the benefit criteria is guaranteed, the insurer is forced to pay the full sum assured for that condition.
  • Early diagnosis: Improved screening may detect diseases earlier, triggering "guaranteed" payouts much sooner than insurers originally anticipated.
  • New diseases: insurers often include new diseases at little or no extra cost but new additions must be properly costed.
  • Guaranteed Insurability Options (GIOs): Allow a policyholder to increase their sum insured without providing further medical evidence, triggered by specific life events or specific policy anniversaroes.

  • Cashflow to non-unit fund: $R10,000 - R8,219$
  • This positive cashflow is used to pay for initial expenses like commission and underwriting.
  • The insurer is now missing $1,781$ units that it must buy back later.

---

#5 15. Pricing health & care contracts 2. Critical illness How to derive risk premium rates for critical illness contracts? 0.7365

2. Critical illness — How to derive risk premium rates for critical illness contracts?:

The overall incidence rate ($i_x$) is the sum of incidence rates for each defined condition (e.g., heart attack, stroke, cancer, other) minus any interactions between causes.$$i_x = i_x^{hd} + i_x^s + i_x^c + i_x^o - k_x^{hd}i_x^s$$

The final risk premium depends on the policy structure:

  • Standalone CI: The cost is the incidence rate multiplied by the probability of surviving the survival period. $$i_x \times \text{Probability of surviving survival period}$$
  • Accelerated CI: This pays on the earlier of death or diagnosis. The rate combines the CI incidence rate with the mortality rate ($qx$), adjusted for deaths already counted as CI events ($k_xq_x$).$$i_x + (1 - k_x)q_x$$

The final risk premium is found by multiplying $i_x$ by the sum assured $S$.

F102_NOVEMBER_2023_Paper1_Q5

2023 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 5


A large life insurance company in a developed economy has been successfully selling conventional without-profits annuity business for many years but sales have declined in recent months. The company is considering launching a conventional with-profits annuity as an alternative to boost sales.

i. Discuss the key factors that need to be considered in the design of the with-profits annuity

product.


ii. Describe how the company could go about setting its mortality assumption for the with-profits

annuity. A description of experience investigations is not required.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 5


i. Design considerations:

Meeting customers' needs


  • The insurer should consider how the product would meet customers' needs differently to the without-profits annuity.

Profitability


  • A company will want to ensure that the rates charged will be sufficient to cover the benefits to be provided and the expenses in most foreseeable circumstances, as well as providing a profit margin.

  • The profitability of the with-profits annuity should be similar to that of the without-profits annuity, or material differences should be justifiable.

  • Consideration should be given to the key influences on the sensitivity of profit to changes in experience. Marketability and competitiveness

  • The benefits offered need to be attractive to the market in which the contract will be sold. The with-profits feature may make the contracts more attractive.

  • This needs to be balanced against the complexity of with-profits business and how well customers will understand this product.

  • The annuity market is typically very competitive and so the design, price and bonus rates of competitors are key influences.

  • Consider marketing material in terms of projections of bonus distributions and whether this may result in unmet policyholder expectations in the future.

  • Consider whether any guarantees should be offered to improve marketability. Financing requirement and guarantees.

  • With-profits annuity business should have low financing requirements.

  • However, the design and communication need to consider how the insurer will manage the bonuses and guarantees.

  • The level of any regulatory or internal solvency capital required should be considered.

  • Consider how the bonus philosophy chosen will impact on the capital requirements of the insurer. Risk characteristics

  • Consideration will need to be given to the acceptability of the level of risk associated with the proposed product.

  • The level of risk that may be acceptable will depend upon the company's risk appetite and risk management approach.

  • A key risk is that bonus declarations do not meet PRE resulting in reputational risk. Extent of cross-subsidies

Administration systems


  • Some development of administration systems and other processes (such as bonus declarations) may be required.

  • Any development costs will need to be recouped in some way. Consistency with other products

  • Differences to the existing without-profits annuity should be justifiable and marketable. Meeting regulatory requirements

  • The design should consider the need to adhere to any regulatory requirements. ➢ E.g. such as treating customers fairly. Sustainability of investment options

  • A company needs to consider Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) issues and the sustainability of the investment options.

  • This may be constrained by the availability of suitable assets. Distribution channel

  • The insurer should consider the distribution channel that it will use to sell the new with-profits policies.

  • Sales representatives need to be trained in selling with-profits annuities so as to avoid mis-selling. Bonus distribution philosophy

  • The insurer should consider what types of bonuses will be awarded.

  • It will need to consider how profit deferral might be allowed for - if at all.

  • It will need to determine how frequently bonus declarations will take place.

  • It will need to consider how profits will be split between policyholders and shareholders.

  • It will need to consider its bonus smoothing philosophy. Investment strategy

  • The insurer should consider its investment strategy to enable it to provide a reasonable level of bonuses in future.

  • The level of free assets will determine to what extent the insurer is able to invest in riskier asset classes in search of high returns.

ii. Determining mortality assumption:


  • An assumption is required for both the base mortality and the mortality trend.

  • For base mortality, the company's recent experience of the without-profits annuity would be a starting point. ➢ Since the insurer is large, and the market developed, this experience should be credible. ➢ However, this should be compared to any relevant industry or possibly reinsurer tables.

  • Adjustments will be required to allow for differences between the lives for which the assumptions are being set and the lives from which the data is obtained. ➢ There may be differences in the target market or distribution channel for example.

  • An allowance should also be made for expected changes in mortality rates over time, that is the mortality trend, using a combination of: ➢ Expectation approaches, involving expert opinion and subjective judgment to specify a range of future scenarios; ➢ Extrapolation approaches based on projecting historical trends in mortality into the future; and ➢ Explanatory approaches which attempt to model trends in mortality rates from a bio-medical perspective.

  • Deterministic projections might allow for different mortality improvement rates according to year of birth cohort (as well as by age and gender).

  • Alternatively, stochastic mortality projections can be used, such as the Lee-Carter or P-spline method, although these may be challenging to calibrate.

  • The assumptions should consider any applicable actuarial professional guidance. Candidates typically performed fairly well in part (i). Strong candidates were able to consider a wide range of product design considerations applicable to the scenario presented. In part (ii) the candidates who clearly presented how the company would set both the base mortality assumption as well as the mortality trend assumption performed well.

#1 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7615

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#2 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7607

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#3 1. Life insurance contracts 3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer Investment risk 0.7273

3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer — Investment risk:

  • The insurer must invest the single premium to cover regular outgo over an unknown timeframe.
  • This risk can be mitigated by matching liabilities with fixed-interest securities with redemption dates matching the amounts being paid each year.
  • In a perfectly matched strategy, assuming that annuitants die exactly as expected, the insurance company should not need to buy or sell any of its assets during the term of the contract because the cash needed is provided by the coupons and redemption amounts.
  • This removes interest rate volatility risk and yield uncertainty because the cashflows and yields are locked in at the time when the contract was priced.
  • This scenario is impractical because:
  • Timing: The term of the annuity payments uncertain
  • Availability: Assets with perfectly matching terms may not be available (reinvestment risk)
#4 16. Reinsurance 3.2 Retention limits Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve 0.7023

3.2 Retention limits — Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve:

In this approach, insurers aim to minimize the total cost of two components:

  • the cost of obtaining reinsurance and
  • the cost of financing a mortality fluctuations reserve.

The process follows these steps:

1. Set a risk criterion: such as a maximum 1% probability that net losses will exceed a specific amount e.g. 25m

2. Model total costs: for different retention limits, the insurer stochastically models the expected net loss by varying the mortality rates. As the retention limit increases, the cost of reinsurance decreases, but the size of the required fluctuations reserve (and its associated financing cost) increases.

3. Calculate the financing cost: The cost of the reserve ($M$) is calculated as $M \times (j - i)$, where $j$ is the required rate of return on the company's capital and $i$ is the actual investment return earned on the reserve's assets.

4. Optimize: The insurer identifies the specific retention limit where the combined cost of the reserve and reinsurance is lowest while still satisfying the ruin probability target.

#5 4. External environment 10.5 Legal Environment Regulatory requirements 0.7018

10.5 Legal Environment — Regulatory requirements:

Regulators may impose restrictions on life insurance companies, usually with the aim of protecting policyholders.

Common restrictions on:


Product design

  • Contracts types: A restriction on the types of contracts that a life insurance company can offer
  • Premium rates: Restrictions on the premium rates or charges for certain types of contracts
  • Terms and conditions: Requirements relating to the terms and conditions of the contracts
  • Method of sale: Restrictions on the channels through which life insurance can be sold, on sales procedures or on information given at the point of sale.
  • Non-Discrimination: Restrictions on rating factors and the ability to underwrite (e.g. to avoid discrimination)


Capital and reserving

  • Solvency capital requirements: minimum reserving or solvency margin requirements
  • Asset Valuation methods: dictate whether certain assets are valued at market value (active approach) or historic/book value (passive approach), which directly impacts the reported solvency position

Investment strategy

  • limit mismatching liabilities
  • restrict asset types
  • restrict concentration on a single asset type
  • Maximum counterparty exposure
  • Mismatching reserves
  • tax treatment of different asset classes
  • require independent custodians
  • admissible assets
  • liquidity requirement (cash holding)
  • restrict foreign investment
  • prescribe asset classes
  • method of calculating asset values (fair value)

Disclosures

  • Point of sale and marketing materials
  • Projection/illustrations e.g. maturity/surrender values
  • Charging structures
  • Reviewability (yes/no)
  • Risk disclosure (risks to the policyholder)
  • Financial and solvency
  • Published accounts (true and fair view)
  • Supervisory returns (SCR)
  • EV in published accounts
  • Impact of basis changes
  • Market-consistent valuation
  • disclose how stochastic models are calibrated: risk-neutral vs real-world calibration

Question

QUESTION 6


A medium-sized life insurance company in a developing market offers a wide range of unit-linked life insurance products. Recent changes in regulations allow life insurers to invest overseas, which had previously not been allowed. The office is planning to expand its range of products by launching a new (regular premium) unit-linked endowment assurance product with the following characteristics:


  • Policy benefits:

  • The death benefit will be the bid value of units.

  • Surrender values will be equal to the bid value of units less a surrender penalty. However, on each 5th policy anniversary there will be a guaranteed minimum surrender value equal to a return of 75% of premiums paid.

  • There will be a guaranteed minimum maturity value equal to a return of premiums.

  • The unit fund to be offered will invest only in overseas equities.

  • The only charge to be levied will be an annual management charge. The charge will be fixed at 6% p.a. for units issued in the first year and 1% p.a. on units issued thereafter.

i. Outline briefly the customer needs met by this product.


ii. Outline the risks that offering this product exposes the insurer to in respect of:

a. investment performance; b. expenses; and

c. withdrawals.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 6


i. Customer needs met:


  • Can provide a savings benefit, with exposure to the overseas equity market which may provide attractive returns.

  • The overseas investment can offer diversification from local investments.

  • The guaranteed maturity value, albeit only a return of premiums, can protect against poor investment performance at maturity .

  • The guaranteed minimum surrender values can protect against poor investment returns during the term of the contract and may allow surrender on financially favourable terms at those points.

  • Although the benefit may vary depending on market returns, it allows for a benefit on death of the policyholder that may be more than the sum of the premiums.

ii. a. Investment performance:


  • The office will need to be able to meet the investment guarantees if overseas equities perform poorly in local currency terms. ➢ As this risk will be difficult to match, the insurer may hold a provision for the investment guarantee, but the risk is that this provision is inadequate.

  • The risk is significant as the guarantees apply during the policy term in addition to applying at maturity.

  • There is an indirect impact on profitability as poor returns will lead to lower management charges than anticipated, possibly resulting in expenses not being recouped.

  • As all charges are unit related, the risk could be significant (as the charges may be vital for profitability).

  • Poor investment performance will lead to unhappy policyholders and bad publicity and a competitive disadvantage. b. Expenses:

  • The risk is that the expenses are higher than anticipated and not covered by the management charge.

  • The risk is exacerbated by the fact that there is a mismatch in nature, timing and currency between the charges and the expenses. ➢ There is a risk that initial expenses might not be recouped if fund growth is not as expected.

  • This is exacerbated due to the fact that the level of charges is fixed and not variable at the discretion of the insurer.

  • The company is also exposed to the risk of inflation being higher than expected on the administration and overhead expenses over the term of the policies: ➢ The extent of this risk will depend on how closely matched investment growth is to expense inflation. ➢ Charges are fund-related and so might be expected to produce amounts which beat inflation.

  • The level of expenses will be uncertain because the office is launching a new product (admin. costs, development costs, investment costs, marketing campaign costs). ➢ In particular, the costs relating to overseas investment may be difficult for the insurer to estimate, never having invested overseas before.

  • Lower than expected new business volumes, which is a significant risk with this new product unfamiliar to the market, may mean fixed expenses may not be adequately recouped.

  • More withdrawals than expected may result in overhead expenses not being covered. ➢ However, the surrender penalty may reduce this risk.

c. Withdrawals:


  • There is a risk of higher withdrawals than expected at early durations, before initial expenses have been recouped.

  • Other than at the guaranteed surrender value points, the surrender penalties should provide the insurer with some protection against withdrawals being higher than expected.

  • There may be financial selection against the company at the guaranteed surrender value dates if unit performance has been poor. Part (i) was generally well answered, with better solutions outlining needs met by each of the key features of the product. Part (ii) was not as well answered. Only stronger candidates provided well-structured points for each of (a),( b) and (c), taking account of the context and the specifics of the product benefits. Aside from a shortage of distinct points, weaker candidates made several errors, often writing much content for little marks. Some of the content not scoring marks included listing generic risks not relevant to the product (such as high guaranteed death benefits, or mismatching assets and liabilities), giving mitigations (which were not asked for in the question), rewriting the same points in different ways, providing generic difficulties with offshore investment, or providing aspects they believed were not risks for the given product.

#1 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor 0.7526

12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:

Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.

  • Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be

$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$

  • Where:
  • $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
  • $x$ is the entry age
  • $n$ is the policy term
  • Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.

  • Poor unit-linked investment returns relative to competitors, resulting in selective withdrawals
  • If the insurer provides non-unit-linked guarantees (such as a minimum sum assured on death), and the unit fund falls below the guaranteed level, the insurer must meet the shortfall

F102_NOVEMBER_2023_Paper1_Q7

2023 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 7


i. List the 4 main types of underwriting.


A large life insurance company has a well-established book of risk business that is sold mainly through independent intermediaries. The company writes a significant number of policies on lives considered as non-standard risks with appropriate loadings to the premium rates. The loadings are also applied to the modelled mortality rate in the valuation.

ii. Outline the reasons that the company would accept non-standard risks.


iii. Outline the ways the company could monitor and manage the mortality risk associated with

such non-standard risks, other than through alternative underwriting decisions such as imposing exclusions.


The company recently performed a valuation of these policies. Upon investigation, an error was identified whereby the loadings for premiums and mortality were not applied and the standard rates for both were used in the valuation. The actual premiums being paid by sub-standard lives are correct.

iv. Outline how this error would have impacted the valuation results.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 7


i. Forms of underwriting:


  • Medical underwriting

  • Financial underwriting

  • Lifestyle underwriting

  • Claims underwriting

ii. Reasons why the company may accept non-standard risks:


  • Since the company has a well-established book of risk business, the company might have the experience and appetite to take on the additional risk.

➢ This could be based on a gap in the market that the company identified and decided to target this market.


  • It may create bad publicity were the company not to accept such risks.

  • The company will allow for the additional risk in the premium it charges to policyholders that are considered non-standard. If the charges are appropriate, the company is likely to make a profit from these policyholders.

  • This will be in line with the objectives of the company which would be to make profits for the shareholders.

iii. The company could manage the risk through:

Experience investigations:


  • The experience investigation will be a key control to ensure that the experience is tracking in line with expectation.

  • This will be used as part of the pricing basis as well as the valuation basis.

  • If the experience is not tracking in line with expectation, the company can change the rates to ensure that the loadings are still appropriate. Analysis of Surplus

  • This will identify sources of profits or losses over a reporting period from these non-standard policies.

  • Certain risks might have volatile experience or continuously result in losses. This will help the company identify which non-standard risk might not be worth selling.

  • This will also link back to the experience investigation and might provide areas where the company needs to place more focus on assessing experience. Reinsurance

  • Reinsurance will also be a useful tool in managing the risks associated with the non-standard policies.

  • Since the company is large and well established, it might not want to share the parameter risk with the reinsurer through a quota share arrangement.

  • However, the insurer might provide cover for large sums assured and therefore, a surplus / excess of loss arrangement might be quite useful.

  • Some form of aggregate or catastrophe cover may be suitable, for example to protect against adverse experience caused by a pandemic (as non-standard lives may be more susceptible than standard lives).

  • Reinsurance rates may also provide an indication of the adequacy of the insurer's pricing in combination with its underwriting practices. If reinsurers are not willing to provide cover at reasonable rates this may indicate that the insurer is not adequately pricing for these non-standard risks. Other

  • It would be important to continuously feedback the results from the above items into the actuarial control cycle.

  • If experience turns out to deviate, the company should take proactive action to correct this.

iv. Impact on the valuation:


  • The loadings are used to determine the premium rates and the mortality rates.

  • This would have resulted in the present value (PV) of premiums being understated (the modelled premiums would have been lower than the premiums actually charged).

  • The PV of mortality payments would have also been understated (the expected number of deaths would have been understated due to a lower modelled mortality assumption).

  • The net impact would depend on how the loadings on premiums compare to those used in the modelling.

  • The impact on profits emerging between valuation dates depends on whether the same error was made in the valuation at the start of the period.

  • There would have also been second order impacts on expense, reinsurance and capital modelling, which would have mainly been a function of the number of policies in-force and the mortality outgo. Stronger candidates managed to generate more valid points, and also considered the context in which the company was operating. Many candidates simply listed the general underwriting decisions from the notes, which did not score any marks. Part (iv) also had a broad range of answers. Many candidates did not read the question or did not answer how the valuation results were impacted. Candidates that considered the present value of premiums and benefits scored well.
