#2 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.1 Unit pricing Appropriation and expropriation prices 0.7799

12.1 Unit pricing — Appropriation and expropriation prices:

To maintain this equity, insurers distinguish between the price at which units are created and the price at which they are cancelled.

  • Appropriation price: this is the price at which the company creates a unit. It is calculated on an offer basis, i.e. using the market's "offer price" for the underlying assets plus purchases expenses, taxes and accrued income.
  • This represents the amount of money of money that must be put into the fund for the creation of a unit
  • Expropriation price: this is the price at which the company cancels a unit. It is calculated on a bid basis, i.e. using the market's "bid price" (the proceeds from selling the assets minus sale expenses)

#4 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor 0.7557

12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:

Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.

  • Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be

$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$

  • Where:
  • $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
  • $x$ is the entry age
  • $n$ is the policy term
  • Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.
#5 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding Absence of investment risk 0.7503

12.2 Actuarial funding — Absence of investment risk:

The expected return on the unit fund is irrelevant to the discount rate because there is no investment risk in the buy-back process.

  • The liability ($l$) (the missing units) is denoted in units: $l = (n-x)* UnitPrice$
  • The source of funding (management charge) is a fixed percentage of the units. $FMC=percentagexUnitPrice$
  • Therefore: $l \approx FMC$

If the unit fund doubles in value due to high investment returns, the monetary cost of buying the missing units also doubles. However, because the management charge is a percentage of that fund, the amount of money to buy those units also doubles. Because both the cost of the units and the funding source (the management charges) move in direct proportion to the unit price. The insurer effectively "borrows" units rather than cash, and since the "repayments" are also unit-linked, the investment risk is eliminated from the buy-back process

QUESTION 1


i. Differences:

• Term assurance product (through the internet):

➢ The target market is any person who has a specific need that can be met by a

term assurance product.

➢ Term assurance products are typically used for a specific purpose, such as

paying off a loan

➢ Since the product is sold through the internet, there is likely to be limited

underwriting.

➢ The sum assured will also likely be capped.

➢ It therefore makes the product suited for the lower- and middle-income

households, who might not have need for high sums assured.

➢ Because of the limited underwriting, the product might be slightly cheaper

(compared to the fully underwritten version), which therefore makes it more

suitable for a target market that does not have a significant amount of

disposable income.

• Income Protection (independent intermediaries):

➢ People that make use of brokers, may have a higher level of financial

sophistication than people who make use of direct underwriting methods.

➢ This product is likely targeted at the middle to upper income classes.

➢ The products sold through independent intermediaries also tend to be more

expensive (the intermediary needs to be paid) and there is normally more

rigorous underwriting involved.

➢ Income protection products tend to have more complicated definitions and

nuances compared to a simple term assurance product and therefore require a

higher level of financial understanding (this is where the intermediary assists).

➢ This product is therefore suitable for a target market that has more disposable

income and higher financial literacy (or access to an intermediary who can

assist).

ii. Product Design Factors:

• Meeting customers’ needs:

➢ Both products need to meet the customer needs of their respective target

markets. (If not, the company will battle to sell policies and not recoup the

expenses invested in designing the products.)

• Profitability:

➢ Both products will have to meet specific profit criteria.

➢ The new income protection product might have a higher profitability

requirement if the company is taking on more risk with this product. This will

have to be agreed by the company’s Board and pricing team.

• Marketability:

➢ Both products need to be marketable through their respective distribution

channels. It is therefore important that these products meet customer needs and

provide value for money.


• Competitiveness:

➢ The products need to be competitive in their respective markets. The income

protection product will be subject to more scrutiny. Independent intermediaries

are expected to find the best value for money for their clients.

➢ The level of competitiveness will also be dependent on the market and what

other competitors are offering. It might be that the competition for term

assurance is low and for income protection products the competition is high.

The company will have to do proper research for the new product.

• Financing requirements:

➢ The new product might have more upfront costs than the existing term

assurance. This will be driven by higher underwriting costs as well as

remuneration for the financial advisors.

➢ The new product will likely result in more new business strain than the existing

product.

➢ It is therefore important to consider the company’s free asset position as well

as the impact of writing new business for the new product.

• Risk Characteristics:

➢ The new product introduces new risks related to disability.

➢ The target markets (and products) are also completely different, so the

company may also experience different lapse rates.

➢ The company will need to consider what level of risk it is comfortable with for

the new product, given that it has little experience in managing the new risks.

➢ The company may consider a reinsurer to help manage the new risks.

• Onerousness of any guarantees:

➢ The company should consider the impact of any guarantees offered on the

products. The question did not state any guarantees (like premium guarantees),

and it is therefore likely that the company is not offering any guarantees on

these products.

• Sensitivity of profit:

➢ The company would have sensitivity tested the term assurance product to

mortality, lapses and expenses under various scenarios.

➢ The company will have to do sensitivity tests for the new product as well. This

will include morbidity, lapses and expenses.

➢ The company will need to determine if the new product remains profitable and

feasible under various circumstances.

➢ Income protection generally has a wider range of outcomes as disability rates

vary more with economic circumstances than mortality.

• Extent of cross-subsidies:

➢ The company will determine whether there will be any cross-subsidies for the

new product – large policies cross-subsidising small policies.

➢ The company may consider the existing approach on the term product.

➢ It is important that the different products don’t cross-subsidise each other.

➢ However, the company may have some economies of scale by adding more

policies on its books and these should be spread appropriately across the

different products.

• Administration systems:

➢ The existing system is unlikely to cater for the new, more complicated product.


➢ The company would need to build a new system with added capacity to manage

the new product.

➢ However, the company can leverage their existing knowledge to help with

ensuring that the new system is adequate and fit for purpose.

• Consistency with other products:

➢ These products are quite different, so it would be difficult to compare them for

consistency.

• Meeting Regulatory Requirements

➢ The company will need to meet all the regulatory requirements for both

products. The company would need to understand the requirements of the new

product.

➢ There might be additional requirements for using standardised or industry

definitions for various disability or incapacity criteria.

handled the first part on target markets reasonably well, many wasted time on unnecessary

meets the needs of the clients while overlooking all the other design factors. A structured

comparison was explicitly required. Candidates are reminded to carefully read questions, focus

on relevance, and structure their answers effectively to maximize marks.

Lastly time management is as always critical – there was ample evidence of poor time

management in this question with some candidates going into significant detail on some of the

factors while only mentioning others without any discussion.

The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#2 4. External environment 10. The external environment 2. Target market and customer demand 0.7377

10. The external environment — 2. Target market and customer demand:

The insurer should consider whether there is sufficient demand for the product in the intended target market.


This includes considering: customers' need for the product, affordability of premiums, financial literacy and product understanding, cultural or social attitudes towards insurance, customer trust in insurers, whether the product meets policyholder reasonable expectations.


If customers do not understand the product, there is a risk of poor take-up, mis-selling, complaints, reputational damage and regulatory intervention.

#3 4. External environment 10.2.1 Distribution channels - Risk to the insurer Impact on risk to the insurer 0.7314

10.2.1 Distribution channels - Risk to the insurer — Impact on risk to the insurer:

The choice of distribution channel introduces several macro risks, primarily related to demographic profile, persistency and anti-selection.

  • Anti-selection: intermediaries are subject to the most stringent underwriting because they represent the client, not the insurer, increasing the potential for anti-selection. Conversely, direct marketing involves the lowest level of underwriting to avoid barriers to sales, but the insurer risks attracting a disproportionate share of high-risk applicants because it appears to have the most relaxed standards in the markets.
  • Withdrawal (Persistency) risk: Channels using aggressive sales approaches or reaching less sophisticated buyers are more likely to see early lapses. Intermediaries typically have the lowest withdrawal rates.
  • Mix of business risk*: Insurers set pricing assumptions based on an expected mix of business. If the volume of a specific channel changes unexpectedly, the overall experience (mortality, morbidity, and expenses) may deviate from the pricing basis.
  • Expense risk: Direct marketing and own sales forces involve high fixed overheads and development costs. If these channels produce low sales volumes, the company may fail to recover the costs, while excessive volume can overstretch capital resources and administrative capacity.
  • Intermediary actions (lapse and re-entry): independent distributors may act in their own interest by encouraging clients to cancel their policies and take out new ones, which can cause significant financial loss to the original insurer. This can be mitigated by exit penalties or commission clawbacks.
#4 4. External environment 10.1 Consumer propensity To buy or not to buy? 0.7247

10.1 Consumer propensity — To buy or not to buy?:

  • Lack of awareness: Many consumers are simply unaware that they need a life insurance product until its too late, or they operate under the belief that negative events won't happen to them.
  • Information imbalance: Insurers possess full information regarding charges and competitiveness, while consumers have very little.
  • Usefulness of benefits: in the long run a life insurer will run a risk to profit if it does not sell product with useful benefits to consumers
  • Need for education: consumers need to be educated and informed about the benefits of life insurance and the company's products
#5 2. Health and care products 5.1.4 Income Protection (IP) contracts - Product Variations Guaranteed and reviewable premium rates 0.7219

5.1.4 Income Protection (IP) contracts - Product Variations — Guaranteed and reviewable premium rates:

  • IP premium designs exist at two extremes: A full guarantee of future premiums or no guarantee whatsoever
  • A frequent "middle ground" is to guarantee the premium amount for an initial period, such as the first 5 years, with the insurer gaining the freedom to review and change rates thereafter
  • Reviewable premium structure:
  • Changes are made based on the experience of the entire portfolio of policies, rather than the claims history of the individual policyholder.
  • Reviewable approaches are used because IP risks are influenced by unforeseen economic and social factors, such as unemployment trends and long-term changes in the workplace or medical science
  • Insurers with reviewable policies face the risk of selective withdrawal, where healthy individuals leave the portfolio following a premium increase, leaving the pool with sub-standard lives who are more likely to claim.

  • Guaranteed premiums
  • Generally more expenses because they require a substantial contingency loading to protect the insurer against the high uncertainty of future claims experience.

QUESTION 2


Considerations:


  • Affordability: ➢ The company should assess whether the alteration is supportable by the asset share (i.e. the policy value before the alteration does not exceed the asset share on average, over time). ➢ The difference between the asset share and the policy value before alteration on the current premium basis, represents the accumulated value of historical profit to the date of alteration. ➢ This could be argued to be an appropriate amount of profit for the risk the company has been exposed to, to date. ➢ The policy value after alteration is calculated using the current premium basis, which means that the future profits expected from the altered policy is consistent with profit expected on the new without-profits policies with the critical illness (CI) accelerator. ➢ The actuary should also consider whether the allowance for initial expenses in the current pricing basis is appropriate:

  • The allowance for underwriting costs in the current pricing basis will still be relevant.

  • However, other initial expenses that are incurred on new business may not be appropriate. ➢ As the altered policy will lead to a premium increase,

  • The cost of additional commission payable should also be included. ➢ The cost of the alteration should be included, for example by adding it to the policy value after the alteration.

  • There is a risk of anti-selection from existing policyholders. ➢ Additional underwriting is therefore required. ➢ An exclusion for pre-existing conditions would be required. ➢ It is likely that this option is only available to policyholders younger than a certain age (e.g. 60).

  • Offering this option would assist in avoiding the potential problem of lapse and re-entry. ➢ As the policy value after alteration is calculated on the current premium basis, the premium on the altered policy should be consistent with the premium on new policies.

  • Surrendering the existing policy and buying a new policy is a boundary condition. ➢ There is still a lapse-and-re-entry risk if the surrender value offered on the whole life policy is very generous.

  • The company should consider whether surrender values before and after the alteration are consistent.

➢ Could also only offer as a "once-off", which would limit the problem.


  • The company will have to consider alteration terms used by competitors. ➢ This may affect policyholders' reasonable expectations.

  • Small alterations. ➢ There is likely to be a minimum sum assured for the CI benefit, so it is not necessary to assess the impact of "small alterations" to the policy.

  • Easy to document/administer. ➢ It may be difficult to administer and document because the original pricing basis may no longer be available.

  • Easy to explain. ➢ Could be difficult to explain to policyholders, who are unlikely to be familiar with present value calculations.

#2 12. Surrender values 2. Methods of calculation Explain the prospective method 0.7280

2. Methods of calculation — Explain the prospective method:

The discounted value of future benefits and expenses, net of future premiums using best estimate assumptions.

  • ensures the surrender value progresses smoothly into the maturity value
  • allows the company to capitalize future profits
  • used primarily after the initial early stage of the policy.
  • It is very sensitive to future assumptions, particularly the interest rate assumption

Example: $$SV = SA \cdot A_{x+t} + e \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t} + f \cdot A_{x+t} - G \cdot \ddot{a}^{(m)}_{x+t} - C$$

#3 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7236

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#4 13. Alterations 3. Methods of calculation example 0.7234

3. Methods of calculation — example:

For a whole life assurance at duration $t$, the equation of value is:


$$(PUSA)_t \cdot A_{x+t} + e \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t} + f \cdot A_{x+t} = (SV)_t$$


Components


  • $(PUSA)_t$: The new, reduced paid-up sum assured.
  • $(SV)_t$: The surrender value (or prospective reserve) at the time of alteration.
  • $A_{x+t}$: The present value of 1 payable on death at the attained age.
  • $e$: Level annual renewal administration expenses (note that renewal commission is removed since no further premiums are paid).
  • $\ddot{a}_{x+t}$: The present value of a life annuity of 1 per annum.
  • $f$: The cost of processing the final claim.

If a specific administrative alteration expense ($C$) is charged, it is typically subtracted from the value before alteration.

Question

QUESTION 3


i. Reasons for monitoring experience:

• To develop earned asset shares.

• To update assumptions as to future experience

➢ For both pricing and reserving.

• To monitor any adverse trends in experience to take corrective actions.

• To provide management information.

ii. Possible reasons for losses:

• A key reason for losses could be that the outgo from company expenses allocated

to the unit-linked endowments exceeds the income from policy charges.

• Usually this arises when expenses are relatively fixed whereas policy charges are

variable.

• This can be due to various reasons, such as:

➢ Poor investment returns reducing the fund-based charges received.

➢ Lower new business volumes than expected, leading to less income relative to

fixed acquisition expenses.

➢ Higher exits than expected (such as surrenders).

➢ Overly generous surrender values (or insufficient surrender charges).

➢ Higher than expected expense inflation.

➢ Unexpected once-off costs.

➢ Higher than expected dealing costs.

• If unitised with profits, where the insurer shares in the investment profits, then

lower than expected investment returns will give rise to losses.

• Losses from new business (due to new business strain) could exceed profits from

existing business (e.g. if the book is relatively young).

• There may be too many expenses allocated to the product, e.g. due to an error in

the analysis.

• The pricing may have been aggressive (low charges), in order to attract business.

• If there are high levels of sums assured, there could be mortality losses, for

example due to:

➢ Inadequate risk charges.

➢ Higher than expected deaths (for various reasons including pandemics and

catastrophes).

• Default of a reinsurer (if reinsured).

• There could be an error in the analysis.

• Cross-subsidies assumed in pricing between bigger and smaller policies not

coming to fruition.

iii. Different expense types:

• Initial/acquisition costs (other than commission) if such costs are spread over

some period after sale.


• Renewal/maintenance.

• Investment.

• Claims (of all kinds).

iv. Expense investigation process:

• Get total company expenses over a past recent period, say the last 12 months or

previous financial year.

• Remove any expenses deemed not relevant, such as once-off costs or shareholder-

only costs.

• Sub-divide the expenses by type:

➢ Initial.

➢ Renewal.

➢ Termination.

➢ Investment.

➢ Overheads.

• Further sub-divide or allocate each of the above into the different product

groupings, specifically the unit-linked endowments.

• If deemed necessary, these can be further split between single and regular

premium contracts.

• Consider if any of the resulting ‘cells’ of expenses are too small to be credible.

➢ If so, group these small cells pragmatically with other cells.

• Expenses are allocated to ‘cells’ based on an analysis of expenses by department

or function:

➢ Staff expenses may need to be subdivided between cells by the use of

timesheets.

➢ Property expenses can be allowed for by charging a notional rent to each

department in proportion to the floorspace occupied, and then allocated to the

different cells in proportion to the department’s salary costs.

➢ New computer costs can be spread over their future expected lifetimes and then

allocated to departments in proportion to usage.

➢ Investment costs would be subdivided by asset class and usually allowed for

by a reduction in yield for each class.

➢ One off capital costs would be spread over the expected future lifetime of the

item, then treated as an overhead.

➢ Pragmatically allocate overheads e.g. in proportion to the split of direct

expenses.

• Check that all expenses are accounted for, that is nothing relevant lost in the above

process.

• Calculate per-unit expenses by dividing the monetary amount of expenses in each

cell by the relevant denominator (such as number of policies or total sum assured

or total unit funds), eg:

➢ Per policy for initial and renewal.

➢ Per unit sum assured for underwriting expenses (e.g. if material and not

included in initial).

➢ Termination expenses may be per policy or percentage of unit fund value.

➢ Percentage of unit fund value (or funds under management) for investment.


• Consider the expected future per-unit expenses given the insurer’s plans over the

business planning horizon, and adjust the above as necessary (other than for

inflation).

• These best estimates may need to be adjusted to include a margin for prudence.

➢ The size of any margin incorporated will depend on the legislation and

accounting principles governing the preparation of those accounts in the

country concerned, and the degree of risk associated with the parameter.

Examiner Comments

This question was largely bookwork and was answered well by most candidates. Candidates

that did not know their bookwork well, were unable to score well.

Part (ii) of the question was answered well by candidates who were able to apply their

knowledge of a unit linked product in suggesting potential sources of experience loss.

Weaker candidates tended to produce vague and unstructured answers for part (iv).

#3 20. Monitoring experience 3. Analysis of experience What is the process for conducting an investment return experience investigation? 0.7556

3. Analysis of experience — What is the process for conducting an investment return experience investigation?:

The process focuses on the actual investment returns achieved on the company's assets to provide feedback for the actuarial control cycle.

  • Purpose determines valuation basis: The choice of basis depends on the purpose of the investigation:
  • With-profit surplus distribution: if the goal is to determine the surplus to be distributed via the revalorisation methods, use partially written-up book values
  • For unit-linked performance: use market values
  • For pricing and valuation: use actual returns and compare them with the interest rate assumptions used in premium/reserving basis
  • Subdivide the experience by
  • main asset types
  • fund (policyholder vs shareholder assets)
  • Unit-linked investment funds
  • return components (interest/dividend vs capital gains)
  • Investment expenses: the analysis should be performed both on gross and net of investment expenses (duties and commissions)
  • Benchmarking and comparison: common benchmarks include
  • Internal assumptions used in models
  • Investment indices
  • Competitor performance
  • Feeding results back into the control cycle
  • Change investment strategy to better match liabilities
  • Update with profit surplus distribution strategy
  • Adjust pricing for new business
  • Change reserving interest rate assumptions.

2. Principles of investment — Issues with matching equity-index linked liabilities:

  • The assets should be invested to match or replicate the equity index
  • Index replication requires holdings in the correct weights
  • Tracking the index requires monitoring and rebalancing
  • purchasing every stock in the index may be impractical
  • transaction costs from frequent trading may reduce returns below the required index-linked return
  • buying and selling at the same time as other index trackers may move prices
  • inflows and outflows must be invest/disinvested in line with the index, this may be difficult for small cashflows
  • the insurer may use specialist index-tracking strategies
  • proxy portfolios or quantitative replication techniques may be used

#5 16. Reinsurance 3. Considerations before reinsuring What are the considerations before reinsuring? 0.7419

3. Considerations before reinsuring — What are the considerations before reinsuring?:

Before deciding whether and how to reinsure, an insurer evaluates several strategic and financial factors:

  • Type of reinsurance: The type of reinsurance (whether it is OTR, Risk premiums or excess of loss or Fin Re), will depend will depend on:
  • The reason the insurance company is using reinsurance
  • The reinsurance cost
  • The type of insurance business for which the reinsurance is to be arranged
  • Cost of Reinsurance: Because reinsurers include their own profit margins and expenses, which reduce the insurer's absolute profit level. the insurer must balance security versus return. It must determine if the reduction in volatility justifies the reduced expected return.
  • Retention Limits must be set by considering the company's risk appetite, its level of free assets, and the distribution of sum assured across its portfolio. A company with higher free assets can generally afford a higher retention limit.
  • Counterparty (Credit) Risk: The insurer retains liability according to the contract, to pay benefits even if the reinsurer cannot meet claim payments (becomes insolvent)
  • Alternatives, such as holding a mortality fluctuation reserve may be more cost-effective than purchasing reinsurance.
  • Legal Risks: Finally the company should consider legal risk by ensuring treaties are legally watertight.

F102_NOVEMBER_2024_Papergeneral_Q4

2024 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 4


For part (i) many candidates could not generate enough points to score well. Too many

candidates treated this question as an assumption setting question, instead of describing how

the market consistent value of the endowments would be calculated.

Candidates also missed easy marks on the risk margin – the compensation that a third party

would require for taking on the uncertainty in these liabilities.

In part (ii) plenty of candidates missed that the illiquidity premium would be the difference in

the discount rate. Candidates that picked this up and described that annuity cash flows are

longer dated and more predictable than endowment cash flows, scored quite well.

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 4


i Market-consistent valuation


  • To determine a market-consistent liability value of the without-profits endowment assurance book of business, future unknown parameter values and cashflows are set to be consistent with the market values ➢ where a corresponding market exists.

  • Market values are also used for the assets backing these liabilities, if a market price exists.

  • One method would be to determine the market price of a portfolio of assets whose cashflows exactly replicate the expected cashflows on the endowment assurance.

  • The current market price of this replicating portfolio would then be taken as the market-consistent value of the liabilities.

  • It may be difficult to determine a portfolio of assets which exactly replicate the expected cashflows of the endowment assurance.

  • An alternative method would be to discount the expected liability cashflows ➢ at current risk-free rates of interest.

  • Future investment returns are based on a risk-free rate of return, ➢ irrespective of the type of asset actually held, and the discount rates are also based on risk-free rates.

  • The risk-free rates may be determined based on government bond yields ➢ or on swap rates.

  • It would be most appropriate to use different discount rates for different durations to reflect a yield curve.

  • It would only be appropriate to use swap rates if there is a sufficiently deep and liquid swap market in the country where the insurer operates.

  • It may be appropriate to make a deduction to allow for credit risk.

  • It is unlikely to be appropriate to add an illiquidity premium to the risk-free rate, ➢ as the insurer would be exposed to price volatility on the bonds backing the liabilities if the insurer has to sell the bonds to pay surrender values during the term of the endowment assurance.

  • It may be difficult to obtain market-consistent assumptions for some elements of the basis, such as mortality, persistency or expenses, ➢ for which there is not a sufficiently deep and liquid market in which to trade or hedge such risks.

  • For these assumptions the insurer will start with best estimate assumptions. ➢ A risk margin would then be added to the best estimate liability.

  • The risk margin would reflect the compensation required by the market in return for taking on the uncertain aspects of the liability cashflows.

  • The risk margin can be allowed for by adding an explicit margin to each assumption.

  • The insurer may be able to invest in corporate bonds to maturity which exactly replicate the some of the expected cashflows on the book of immediate annuities.

  • The insurer would therefore not be exposed to the liquidity risk due to price volatility on the bonds, as the bonds will be held to maturity.

  • Corporate bonds typically have a higher yield than risk-free bonds due to the relative illiquidity of these assets.

  • It may therefore be possible for the insurer to take credit for the illiquidity premium on the corporate bond yields and thereby discount liabilities at a higher yield than risk-free.

#1 14. Guarantees and options 2. Valuing an investment guarantee How are investment guarantees valued using stochastic simulation? 0.7533

2. Valuing an investment guarantee — How are investment guarantees valued using stochastic simulation?:

  • Identify the underlying assets
  • Project asset values: use a stochastic model to simulate future asset prices or returns based on a chosen probability distribution (e.g. mean and variance) for the underlying assets
  • Model Policyholder behaviour: Incorporate assumptions about when policyholders are likely to exercise the option (when it is in the money).
  • Identify shortfalls: In each simulation, compare the projected fund value against the guaranteed amount. If the fund is lower, the difference is the cost of the guarantee for that specific scenario. For paths where the fund value is above the guarantee, the cost is recorded as zero.
  • Discounting: Discount the cost of each individual path back to the valuation date e.g. using the risk-free rate under market consistent frameworks
  • Expected cost: Take the average of the simulated costs across all runs, which provides the expected present value for the guarantee,
#2 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor 0.7430

12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:

Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.

  • Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be

$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$

  • Where:
  • $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
  • $x$ is the entry age
  • $n$ is the policy term
  • Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.
#3 10. Reserving 9. Cost of capital approach The Three-Step Calculation Process 0.7372

9. Cost of capital approach — The Three-Step Calculation Process:

1. Project Required Capital: The insurer projects the future capital required to be held $(C_t​)$ for each period during the "run-off" of the business. (this is the SCR)

2. Apply Cost of Capital Rate: These projected capital amounts are multiplied by a cost of capital rate (e.g., 6% per annum).

3. Discount to Present Value: The resulting annual costs are discounted back to the valuation date using risk-free (market-consistent) interest rates to produce the total risk margin. $$\text{Risk margin} = \displaystyle{\sum_t \dfrac{k_tC_t}{(1 + r_t)^t}}$$

#4 1. Life insurance contracts 3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer Investment risk 0.7362

3.1.3 Immediate annuity - Risks to the insurer — Investment risk:

  • The insurer must invest the single premium to cover regular outgo over an unknown timeframe.
  • This risk can be mitigated by matching liabilities with fixed-interest securities with redemption dates matching the amounts being paid each year.
  • In a perfectly matched strategy, assuming that annuitants die exactly as expected, the insurance company should not need to buy or sell any of its assets during the term of the contract because the cash needed is provided by the coupons and redemption amounts.
  • This removes interest rate volatility risk and yield uncertainty because the cashflows and yields are locked in at the time when the contract was priced.
  • This scenario is impractical because:
  • Timing: The term of the annuity payments uncertain
  • Availability: Assets with perfectly matching terms may not be available (reinvestment risk)
#5 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7351

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

F102_NOVEMBER_2024_Papergeneral_Q5

2024 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 5


Part (i) required candidates to distinguish between the savings profit and insurance profit

given their different treatment.

For part (ii) some candidates confused the question and instead wrote about why the insurer

should have chosen the additions to benefit method.

For parts (iii)-(v) the candidates that did well were those that generated more points specific

to the circumstances (product, developing country etc.) whilst candidates who performed less

well made very generic points and did not discuss the situations when equity investment

would/would not be appropriate.

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 5


i. Revalorisation method features:


  • The profit, or surplus, to be awarded to a particular contract is expressed as a percentage (r% say) of that contract's supervisory reserve. ➢ The benefit (sum insured) under the contract and the premium payable by the policyholder are then increased by the same percentage (r%). ➢ In practice the premium might remain level (and the benefit increases by less than r%).

  • The profit is normally divided into a "savings" profit and an "insurance" profit. ➢ The "savings" profit represents the profit from the assets and can be distributed in whole or in part under the revalorisation method. ➢ The minimum proportion of savings profit distributed is normally specified in policy conditions and is an important marketing and competitive aspect of the product. ➢ The "insurance" profit is that arising from all sources other than return on the assets and is normally retained for the shareholders as reward for pure insurance risks borne.

ii. Reasons for choosing this method:


  • The method codifies exactly how a company should distribute its profits - it usually requires very little judgement compared to the additions to benefits method. ➢ This makes the method simple to apply, and ➢ cheaper to administer.

  • Some policyholders may prefer this approach: ➢ It may be more understandable and thus appealing to policyholders; ➢ Bonuses are more stable and predictable under this approach as it discourages equity investment - it appeals to more risk averse policyholders (e.g. older policyholders).

  • The company may wish to differentiate itself from competitors.

iii. Investment risk:


  • The initial sum assured is a guaranteed benefit - if the insurer earns a lower investment return than that required to meet this guarantee (i.e. the assumption in pricing), the insurer will experience a financial loss (all else being equal).

  • The company may struggle to find sufficient and adequate assets to match its guarantees and bonus expectations in a developing country.

  • The company could face default risk (higher in developing countries) on some of its assets.

  • This method is not compatible with profit deferral and equity investment: ➢ Investment returns (and bonuses) may be disappointing (and not even match inflation) compared to competitors who can include equity investments under additions to benefits, causing higher withdrawal risk and reputational damage.

iv. Suitability of the asset split:


  • A large part of the liabilities will relate to guaranteed benefits (sum insured) and this must be matched as closely as possible: ➢ By term, currency (local), and nature (fixed). ➢ Local FI government bonds of suitable terms should offer a good match for these liabilities.

  • For future bonuses the insurer needs to be certain that it can earn a return that exceeds its valuation interest rate in each period for it to be able to declare bonuses

  • FI bonds are suitable for providing this certainty.

  • Some liabilities will relate to the insurer's own expenses in administering this business, and these will be real in nature as they mainly relate to staff and IT costs: ➢ Ideally real assets should be used to match these liabilities; ➢ To the extent that these liabilities are small and inflation is not expected to differ much from implied levels priced into bonds, the insurer could invest in FI bonds and cash as it has done, although ILB would be better (if available).

  • Cash holdings may be needed to meet claims and expense outgo expected in the short term.

  • Overall the asset split does not appear to be unreasonable, provided it is aligned with policyholder expectations and pricing basis.

v. Comments on the suggestion:


  • The merit of the suggestion will depend on the reason for it, for example: ➢ To the extent that the insurer has large free reserves and large risk appetite, it could decide to adopt a mismatched position (to pursue higher returns for shareholders and policyholders). ➢ The equity holdings may be suitable for matching the insurer's expenses in administering this business.

Examiner Comments Question 5 was generally not well answered.

Part (i) required candidates to distinguish between the savings profit and insurance profit given their different treatment.

For part (ii) some candidates confused the question and instead wrote about why the insurer should have chosen the additions to benefit method.

For parts (iii)-(v) the candidates that did well were those that generated more points specific to the circumstances (product, developing country etc.) whilst candidates who performed less well made very generic points and did not discuss the situations when equity investment would/would not be appropriate.

#1 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.3 Revalorisation Revalorisation Method 0.7636

9.1.3 Revalorisation — Revalorisation Method:

Under this method, the benefits are increased each year by a proportion of the investment income earned on the assets backing the policies.


  • Source of Profit: It is primarily based on the investment income earned on the assets backing the life fund. 💰

  • Allocation: A high percentage (e.g., 85%–90%) of the actual investment return is legally or contractually required to be allocated to policyholders.

  • The Technical Rate: Policies have a guaranteed minimum interest rate. The "Revalorisation" is the excess return above this rate. 📈
  • Guarantees: There is usually a minimum guaranteed interest rate (the technical rate). If the actual investment return is higher, the "excess" is used to provide the revalorisation. 📈If the actual investment is lower than the technical rate the insurer would have to bear the costs of the shortfall.

More transparent but less flexible for the insurer. The insurer is fully exposed to mortality and expense overruns without being able to offset them by adjusting profit distributions.

F102_NOVEMBER_2024_Papergeneral_Q6

2024 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 6


i. Reasons for analysing surplus:

• To show the financial effect of divergences between the valuation assumptions

and the actual experience, exposing which assumptions are the more financially

significant.

• To show the financial effect of writing new business.

• To provide a check on the valuation data and process, if carried out independently

• To identify non-recurring components of surplus, thus enabling appropriate

decisions to be made about the distribution of surplus to with-profits

policyholders.

• To give management information on trends in the experience of the company.

• To comply with regulatory requirements.

ii. Possible reasons for mortality profit:

• Mortality profit arises when the actual mortality experience over the period is

better than that expected in the assumptions used at the start of the period.

• We would expect to see a mortality profit when the assumptions are prudent, such

as in supervisory reserves.

• The sophisticated underwriting could be particularly effective in rating

individuals and minimising anti-selection, whereas the valuation assumptions do

not reflect this.

➢ For example the valuation assumptions could be at a more aggregate or prudent

level.

➢ Or the assumptions could ignore the selective effect of the underwriting.

➢ Or the class of lives that are attracted to this product are better (in terms of

mortality) than assumed.

• The insurer's dynamic pricing model could incentivize policyholders to maintain

healthier lifestyles, and this could lead to lower claims than expected and a

subsequent profit.

• There could have been overall improvement to underlying mortality not yet

reflected in adjusted premiums.

• It could be due to random fluctuations or seasonality (particularly if the period of

investigation is very short).

• There could be an error in the analysis of surplus.

• Efficient claims management practices could also contribute to a mortality profit.

More thorough investigation of claims and effective fraud detection than allowed

for could result in fewer illegitimate claims paid out than anticipated.

iii. Data required for mortality investigation:

• Benefit start date.

• Benefit cease date (if applicable).

• Date of birth or age at entry.


• Count of actual death claims reported in the period.

• Can use either, or both, of benefit count or sum assured for the above.

➢ If using the sum assured, then this would be needed at each date if this

potentially varies over time.

• Identifiers in order to group the data into relevant homogeneous groups, typically

the rating factors applied in the pricing.

➢ In particular whether standard or non-standard.

iv. Factors to consider when reviewing valuation mortality assumptions:

• The insurer may not adjust its valuation assumptions, for example if:

➢ The period over which the analysis of surplus was too short.

➢ The amount of surplus was small.

➢ The mortality investigation revealed no material change to underlying

mortality.

➢ The financial effect of changing the assumptions is not material.

• The insurer would consider the results of the mortality investigation, assuming

this covers an appropriate time interval and gives credible results.

➢ In particular, how the experience has changed compared to the current

mortality basis.

• Consider whether to create its own mortality tables or to adjust standard tables.

➢ Given the niche nature and the techniques used, it would seem unlikely that

standard tables could even be suitably adjusted.

• Expected future mortality experience over the valuation projection period.

➢ May consider trends if the projection period is particularly long, or if the trends

show worsening mortality.

➢ Would typically ignore mortality improvements in term assurance valuation.

• Consider if there are any regulatory requirements or accounting standards that

apply, such as the inclusion of margins.

• May consider mortality experience from reinsurers or industry, although these are

less likely to be applicable given the nature of this insurer.

Examiner Comments

Part (i) was generally well answered.

Part (ii) was reasonably answered. A common issue was that candidates did not relate their

comments to the specific scenario in the question. Many candidates also commented that the

company was selecting good lives as a result of the underwriting process. While this may well

be true, they will only make a profit if the lives selected are better than expected.

The marks for part (iii) were generally good, but too many candidates did not consider that

for a mortality investigation the deaths and the exposed to risk are required. A list of rating

factors only received limited credit.


Part (iv) was poorly answered. Many candidates listed the factors that need to be considered

when setting an assumption. Few candidates considered the situation given where there is

already an assumption and an investigation in place.

#3 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7407

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

F102_NOVEMBER_2024_Papergeneral_Q7

2024 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 7


i Why use a cash flow approach:

• The cashflow approach will allow for the complexity of the product, e.g.:

➢ multiple lives insured;

➢ multiple projected decrements (death and withdrawal).

• In particular it will also allow the company to investigate the sensitivity to profit

due to:

➢ mortality variance;

➢ variations in average numbers of children insured; and

➢ children’s ages.

• A cashflow approach allows the measurement of the expected return that the

providers of capital will receive.

• A cashflow approach will allow for the projection of both statutory reserves and

capital requirements.

• A cashflow approach will allow flexibility to model country A and X together or

separately.

➢ The cashflow method may be easier to allow for the different mortality in the

two countries.

➢ The cashflow method can allow more easily for different lapse rates in the two

countries.

• The company may wish to allow for stochastic decrements or decrements that may

vary over time.

➢ It is unlikely that stochastic investment returns will be required since this is a

protection policy.

➢ However, mortality could be projected stochastically.

➢ Similarly for lapses which will impact per policy expenses.

• A cashflow method allows the modelling of interdependencies between variables

➢ and the link between the variables and economic conditions.

• A cashflow method will allow the company to model projected birth rates since

newborns are automatically insured.

➢ It will also allow this to be varied with factors such as the economy if the

company wants to model it.

• The risk discount rate can take account of the term structure of interest rates.

• Tax and reinsurance will be easier to allow for.

ii Setting model points:

• The data from Country X may not be useful for the model point data and the

company may need to use risk factors to determine model points.

• They may approach the government /reinsurer /census bureau in Country A to

determine birthrates and family dynamics to estimate the likely spread of the

number of children to be covered.

• For the areas which do not have high child mortality in Country A the experience

from Country X may be useful to set model points with appropriate adjustments.


• For mortality the company could use groupings by:

➢ number of children ;

➢ age of children,

➢ sex of children;

➢ policyholder’s ages;

➢ region.

• Allow for likely volumes of sales and expected birth rates.

Overall candidates did not score well on this question.

For part (i) some candidates described the kind of assumptions needed for a cashflow model

rather than why the company should use a cashflow method. Some candidates wasted time

explaining how to build a cashflow model which did not score marks.

For part (ii) many candidates followed a standard bookwork approach which generated some

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 7


i Why use a cash flow approach:


  • The cashflow approach will allow for the complexity of the product, e.g.: ➢ multiple lives insured; ➢ multiple projected decrements (death and withdrawal).

  • In particular it will also allow the company to investigate the sensitivity to profit due to: ➢ mortality variance; ➢ variations in average numbers of children insured; and ➢ children's ages.

  • A cashflow approach allows the measurement of the expected return that the providers of capital will receive.

  • A cashflow approach will allow for the projection of both statutory reserves and capital requirements.

  • A cashflow approach will allow flexibility to model country A and X together or separately. ➢ The cashflow method may be easier to allow for the different mortality in the two countries. ➢ The cashflow method can allow more easily for different lapse rates in the two countries.

  • The company may wish to allow for stochastic decrements or decrements that may vary over time. ➢ It is unlikely that stochastic investment returns will be required since this is a protection policy. ➢ However, mortality could be projected stochastically. ➢ Similarly for lapses which will impact per policy expenses.

  • A cashflow method allows the modelling of interdependencies between variables ➢ and the link between the variables and economic conditions.

  • A cashflow method will allow the company to model projected birth rates since newborns are automatically insured. ➢ It will also allow this to be varied with factors such as the economy if the company wants to model it.

  • The risk discount rate can take account of the term structure of interest rates.

  • Tax and reinsurance will be easier to allow for. ii Setting model points:

  • The data from Country X may not be useful for the model point data and the company may need to use risk factors to determine model points.

  • They may approach the government /reinsurer /census bureau in Country A to determine birthrates and family dynamics to estimate the likely spread of the number of children to be covered.

  • For mortality the company could use groupings by: ➢ number of children ; ➢ age of children, ➢ sex of children; ➢ policyholder's ages; ➢ region.

#1 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7826

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#2 7. Modelling 13.7 Allowing for risk Risk discount rate 0.7465

13.7 Allowing for risk — Risk discount rate:

The most common way to allow for the statistical risk associated with parameter values (assumptions) in cashflow modelling is by using a risk discount rate that includes a risk premium over the risk-free rate of return.



  • Prudential margins in assumptions: such as using higher-expected mortality rates for life insurance products or lower than expected interest rates for savings products
  • Stochastic modelling: assigning probability distributions to unknown parameters rather than a single value.
  • the main difficulty is what probability distribution to assign and how to parameterize it, sensitivity analysis is a more pragmatic and transparent way to handle parameter risk without the risk of spurious accuracy caused by deciding upon some arbitrary probability distribution.
#3 7. Modelling 13.2 Model components Model components 0.7417

13.2 Model components — Model components:

To satisfy these requirements, the components of the model must allow for all those features of the business being modelled that could significantly affect the advice being given:

  • Model points: These are data records representing homogeneous groups of policies chosen to reflect the distribution of the business without needing to model every individual policy.
  • Parameters: A parameter must be included in the model if the decision reached would alter for different values of that parameter e.g. interest rates.
  • Time period (frequency) of cashflow projection must be short enough to produce reliable results while being cost-effective.
  • Future Cashflows: inclusion of all material cashflows, including premiums, investment income, benefit payments, expenses that are relevant to the business being modelled.
  • Dynamic correlations: The ability to model interactions between assets and liabilities, such as bonus declarations moving in line with investment performance.
  • Reserving cashflows: Allowance for the notional cashflows arising from setting up supervisory reserves and required solvency margins. The investment income from the supervisory reserve should also be included as a positive contribution to the profit flow.
  • Stochastic capability: For products with financial guarantees or options, the model may need to use stochastic simulation (Monte Carlo methods) rather than deterministic approaches.
#4 9. Assumptions 15.9 Allowing for risk Stochastic approach 0.7386

15.9 Allowing for risk — Stochastic approach:

This method uses probability distributions and simulations to quantify risk and determine appropriate safety levels

1. Assign probability distributions to unknown future parameters (like investment returns) e.g. probability density functions.

2. Generate simulations: Use Monte Carlo simulation to run thousands of "sample paths" (e.g. 5k to 10k) for the parameters.

3. Project cashflows: for each individual simulation, calculate the resulting profit or shortfall based on the generated parameter values

4. Determine the margin: Analyse the results to find a specific percentile (such as the 99.5% confidence level) that ensures the company can meet its obligations under all scenarios.

#5 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7359

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#1 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.1 Unit pricing Unit pricing 0.8120

12.1 Unit pricing — Unit pricing:

1. The appropriation price is the price at which a unit would be created determined as:

  • the net asset value of the fund on an offer basis
  • divided by the number of existing units at the time of the calculation

2. The net asset value of the fund on an offer basis is calculated as:

1. The market value of the assets obtained from the exchange (mark-to-market)

2. If some assets do not have an observable market value, e.g. property a professional valuation may be needed

3. Alternatively, a mark-to-model approach may be used. A model may project expected cashflows using financial economic assumptions and the cashflows are discounted.

4. Any expenses involved in purchasing additional assets must be added (incl. stamp duty)

5. Current assets must be added (e.g. cash on deposit)

6. Current liabilities must be deducted (e.g. investments purchased but not yet settled)

7. Accrued income must be added (e.g. interest income on deposits) net of any outgo (e.g. charges)

8. Accrued tax must be deducted

#2 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.1 Unit pricing Appropriation and expropriation prices 0.7859

12.1 Unit pricing — Appropriation and expropriation prices:

To maintain this equity, insurers distinguish between the price at which units are created and the price at which they are cancelled.

  • Appropriation price: this is the price at which the company creates a unit. It is calculated on an offer basis, i.e. using the market's "offer price" for the underlying assets plus purchases expenses, taxes and accrued income.
  • This represents the amount of money of money that must be put into the fund for the creation of a unit
  • Expropriation price: this is the price at which the company cancels a unit. It is calculated on a bid basis, i.e. using the market's "bid price" (the proceeds from selling the assets minus sale expenses)
#3 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding example 0.7318

12.2 Actuarial funding — example:

The setup:

  • Single premium: R10 000 (purchasing 10 000 units at R1 each)
  • Annual FMC: 5 (levied only on units physically held)
  • Discount rate for funding $(i)$: 4%
  • Policy term: 5 years
  • Age ($x$): 40 year old
  • Investment return $(g)$: 7%
  • Actuarial funding factor ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$): A multiplier that determines the required reserve based on the 4% and the probability of the contingent events (death or maturity)

----

Year 0: Inception

At the start, the insurer calculates the actuarially funded unit reserve instead of holding the full R10 000.

  • Funding factor ($A_{40:\overline{5|}}$): $0.8219$ (based on 4% discount over 5 years)
  • Reserve physically held: $$V_0 = R 10,000 * 0.8219 = R 8,219$$
  • Cashflow to non-unit fund: $R10,000 - R8,219$
  • This positive cashflow is used to pay for initial expenses like commission and underwriting.
  • The insurer is now missing $1,781$ units that it must buy back later.

---

#4 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding Absence of investment risk 0.7218

12.2 Actuarial funding — Absence of investment risk:

The expected return on the unit fund is irrelevant to the discount rate because there is no investment risk in the buy-back process.

  • The liability ($l$) (the missing units) is denoted in units: $l = (n-x)* UnitPrice$
  • The source of funding (management charge) is a fixed percentage of the units. $FMC=percentagexUnitPrice$
  • Therefore: $l \approx FMC$

If the unit fund doubles in value due to high investment returns, the monetary cost of buying the missing units also doubles. However, because the management charge is a percentage of that fund, the amount of money to buy those units also doubles. Because both the cost of the units and the funding source (the management charges) move in direct proportion to the unit price. The insurer effectively "borrows" units rather than cash, and since the "repayments" are also unit-linked, the investment risk is eliminated from the buy-back process

#5 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor 0.7181

12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:

Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.

  • Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be

$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$

  • Where:
  • $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
  • $x$ is the entry age
  • $n$ is the policy term
  • Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.

QUESTION 1


A life insurance company writes conventional with profits endowment assurances.

i. Outline briefly the risks to the policyholder of purchasing one of these contracts.


ii. Describe how you would calculate the asset share for this type of contract.


iii. Outline how asset shares could be used to set appropriate amounts for maturity values and

amounts payable on death before maturity.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 1


i. Risks to the policyholder:


  • The main risk borne by the policyholder is that the amount of benefit provided is lower than expected, on surrender, death and on maturity. ➢ This is caused by reversionary and/or terminal bonuses being lower than expected.

  • Although these with-profits contracts should provide some protection against inflation, this might not be the case in the event of poor investment returns and poor resulting bonuses.

  • The policyholder is exposed to the risks that final bonuses are lower than expected due for example to: ➢ investment returns being lower than expected ➢ expenses being higher than expected ➢ other surpluses being lower than expected (e.g. higher than expected guaranteed mortality payments)

  • The policyholder carries some risk of the insurer becoming insolvent.

  • The policyholder is exposed to the risk of being unable to maintain premiums due to accident, sickness, redundancy, or other loss of income. ➢ The benefit received if the policy is surrendered or made paid-up may not appear to be good value for money.

  • There is the risk that the policyholder does not understand the policy; and therefore it may not meet their needs. ➢ For example, if the policy was taken out to repay a mortgage on a house and the risks not explained.

  • There is a risk that changes in taxation may reduce the value from the policy.

ii. Calculation of asset share


  • The asset share is the accumulation of premiums less deductions associated with the contract ➢ This is accumulated at the actual rate of return earned on investments.

  • An allocation of profits on any without profits business written in the with-profits fund will also be allocated to the asset share.

➢ a contribution to the free assets, to support the smoothing of bonuses and the ability to exercise greater investment flexibility.


  • The asset share can be calculated recursively on a year-to-year basis.

  • The asset share can be calculated for an individual policy or a group of policies.

iii. How the asset share could be used to set an amount for:


  • Both maturity and death benefits may be subject to a guaranteed minimum (e.g. initial sum assured plus vested bonuses subject to a minimum). ➢ Thus asset share has no impact if the guaranteed minimum bites. ➢ This is most likely for death early in the policy term.

  • The maturity value will be based on average asset share over time.

  • It will depend heavily on the smoothing policy and so a particular maturity value may be above or below its asset share.

  • The bonus rates are likely to be based on the asset share for an average policy, rather than each individual policy.

  • If death occurs close to the maturity date, the insurer may wish for the death benefit to reflect the asset share more closely for consistency reasons Examiner's Comments Part (i) and Part (ii) were generally well answered. It was evident that some candidates did not know the theory, in which case they scored substantially worse than others. Some candidates wrote lost marks writing about accumulating with-profits and others wasted time writing about various bonus distribution methods. Part (iii) was generally not answered well and it reflected weak understanding of how an asset share is used. Candidates did not focus on the average asset share for a cohort of policies or in the case of minimum guaranteed benefits, that the asset share would have no impact on the death or maturity benefits. Many candidates thought that the maturity value must always be the same as the asset share, some suggested it must always be less otherwise the insurer makes a loss, and others thought it must always exceed the asset share.
