#1 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 8.3 Asset share calculation The recursive formula 0.7548

8.3 Asset share calculation — The recursive formula:

Asset shares are typically calculated recursively on a year to year basis, starting from an initial value of zero at policy inception. Because asset shares are expressed per policy in force, the calculation must account for the proportion of policyholders who survive each year.


The calculation identifies all actual income and expenditure associated with the contract over its lifetime to date.


The recursive formula for an individual policy is: $$AS_{t+1} = \frac{(AS_t + P - E)(1 + i) - q'_{x+t} \cdot S}{1 - q'_{x+t}}$$

Where:

  • $AS_t$: Asset share at the start of the year.
  • $P$: Premium paid.
  • $E$: Per-policy expenses.
  • $i$: Actual investment return achieved during the year.
  • $S$: Death benefit sum assured.
  • $q'_{x+t}$: Actual mortality rate experienced during the year.

The formula assumes that claims are paid at the end of the year. Therefore the cost of the death strain is not rolled up with interest.

#4 1. Life insurance contracts 1.6 Endowment Assurances - Risks to the insurer Investment Risk 0.7348

1.6 Endowment Assurances - Risks to the insurer — Investment Risk:

The savings nature of the contract exposes the insure to investment risk, the extend of which depends on the structure.

  • Without profits: the insurer bears most risk because benefits are fully guaranteed.
  • With-profits: the risk is lower because the company can mitigate poor investment performance by reducing future bonus declarations, though they must still meet initial guarantees and manage policyholder's reasonable expectations.
  • Unit-linked: the policyholder bears most of the risk, but the insurer faces a secondary risk. If fund values fall, the insurer's fund management charges will decrease.
#5 4. External environment 10.6 The tax regime Taxation as a source of risk 0.7341

10.6 The tax regime — Taxation as a source of risk:

The long-term nature of life insurance contracts exposes insurers to taxation risk, as fiscal rules can change over the decades a policy remains in force.


  • Tax Changes: Existing policies are generally not immune to changes in tax methods or rates, meaning an insurer may realize less net profit than anticipated if the fiscal environment worsens after the policy is issued.

  • Parameter Sensitivity: For contracts with fixed, guaranteed benefits, the insurer bears the risk that higher corporate or investment taxes will erode the margins intended for expenses and profit.

  • Asset Share Deductions: In with-profits business, the asset share must explicitly deduct tax on investment income and allow for accrued tax liabilities on unrealized capital gains to ensure fairness between policyholders

Question

QUESTION 2


A life insurance company currently offers a single premium unit-linked whole life policy sold online.

The product includes the following features:


  • Death benefit: Higher of bid value of units and 101% of premiums paid.

  • Surrender value: Bid value of units, with surrender penalties reducing to zero over 10 years.

  • Investment funds: Choice of five externally managed funds ranging from cautious to aggressive.

  • Initial underwriting: Online health declaration only; no medical tests for sums assured below a threshold.

  • Charging structure:

  • Initial charge: 3% of premium.

  • Annual fund management charge: 1.2% p.a.

  • Monthly policy fee: R50, deducted from the unit fund. Due to increasing competitive pressure, the company is considering the following product changes:

1. Introduce a guaranteed minimum death benefit of 110% of the premium for the first 15 years.

2. Allow annual withdrawals of up to 10% of the fund value without penalties.

3. Replace upfront charges with a 0.75% p.a. annual fund management charge increase to recover

acquisition costs over time.

4. Launch a "guided fund selector" robo-advice tool to assist policyholders in selecting

appropriate funds.

5. Outsource policy administration to a third-party service provider.

i. Describe the increased risks to the insurer associated with the proposed changes.


ii. Suggest how the insurer could manage the risks identified in part (i).


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 2


i. Increased risks:

Expense risk


  • The replacement of upfront charges with an increased fund-based charge delays expense recovery, especially for acquisition costs. ➢ This creates a cashflow mismatch and may result in significant new business strain.

  • The pricing and profitability of the new structure depends on assumptions about withdrawals, mortality, investment returns, and premium sizes. ➢ If any of these are mis-estimated, the insurer could face losses.

  • The new charging structure is more dependent on fund value, as there are more ongoing charges linked to fund value than initial charges. ➢ Lower than expected investment performance would reduce the fee income, even if expenses remain fixed, leading to the risk of insufficient charges to cover expenses. Investment risk

  • More policyholders than expected may opt to invest in the more aggressive fund choices. ➢ This would result in more volatility in fund values and hence in charges than expected.

  • There may be some reputational damage if an aggressive fund performs very poorly

  • the insurer may be seen as partly to blame due to it making that fund choice available to policyholders. Mortality risk

  • The introduction of the guaranteed minimum death benefit increases the insurer's liability on death. ➢ This is particularly so at early durations where the unit fund may be lower than the guaranteed amount.

  • Since only a basic health declaration is required, this introduces increased antiselection risk, as individuals with known health issues may be more likely to buy cover.

  • If this increased anti-selection risk is not adequately allowed for in the mortality assumptions, it may lead to losses for the insurer.

  • Mortality claims at early durations may cause a strain since insufficient charges have been collected to recoup upfront expenses.

  • Past mortality experience on which assumptions have likely been based may no longer reflect the revised product's risk profile ➢ This would be particularly so if the new features attract different segments of the market. Withdrawal risk

  • Introducing partial withdrawals may encourage earlier and more frequent fund outflows, which may result in smaller charges than expected to cover expenses.

  • Such withdrawals may also be anti-selective by those in poor health

  • The revised structure may be based on optimistic assumptions about new business growth. If actual sales are lower, fixed costs may not be recouped.

  • High sales volumes may place a significant strain on administrative processes.

  • Competitors may undercut the insurer or offer more attractive terms, reducing the expected take-up and profitability of the revised product. Robo-advice tool risk

  • The robo-tool may recommend inappropriate funds, leading to poor outcomes for policyholders and potential complaints ➢ or reputational damage for the insurer.

  • Policyholders may misunderstand the nature of the tool and assume it provides regulated advice, leading to liability in the event of losses.

  • The algorithm may have biases or flaws not detected in development, leading to misallocation of customers to funds. Outsourcing and operational risk

  • Outsourced administration introduces risk of service delays, errors, or poor customer experience. ➢ This could potentially affect the insurer's reputation and persistency experience.

  • Problems during the migration of the administration to a third party can lead to errors, delays and data issues.

  • There is counterparty risk related to the possibility of the third-party provider failing, which could result in the insurer having to take back the administration function at a high cost.

  • Transferring customer data to an external provider increases the risk of breaches or regulatory issues under data privacy laws.

  • The administrator may increase their fees over time, and if the company is unable to review their charges then there is a risk of losses the company.

ii. Ways to manage risks:

Expense risk


  • The insurer can consider making use of actuarial funding or the use of negative non-unit reserves, if allowed, to recover acquisition costs from future charges and reduce new business strain.

  • Introduce reviewable charges to allow the insurer to adjust charges periodically if experience deviates significantly from assumptions.

  • Introduce waiting periods or exclusions, for example, only cover accidental death for the first 6 months to deter anti-selective purchases.

  • Obtain reinsurance cover for the guaranteed minimum death benefit, especially in the early years, to help smooth claims volatility and protect capital.

  • Monitor emerging experience, particularly for the guaranteed minimum death benefit, to update valuation and pricing assumptions if adverse trends emerge.

  • Narrow the fund options or use the robo-tool to steer customers towards the safer fund choices to achieve more predictable investment outcomes.

  • Reduce the sum assured threshold above which more detailed underwriting is required, to reduce the risk of anti-selection.

  • Introduce a risk charge on the unit fund to cover the cost of the mortality guarantee. Withdrawal risks

  • Limit partial withdrawals to once every few years, say 3 years, or delay eligibility of partial withdrawals to reduce the risk of early depletion of the fund value.

  • Increase the surrender penalties on full withdrawals or introduce surrender penalties on partial withdrawals to discourage early lapses. Robo-tool risks

  • Validate and test the robo-tool thoroughly, including expert oversight, independent reviews and scenario testing to ensure recommendations are suitable.

  • Provide clear disclaimers clarifying that the tool is guidance, not regulated advice, to limit legal liability. Third-party risks

  • Define clear performance metrics and penalties for the outsourced admin provider to ensure accountability.

Candidates who tried to combine parts i and ii of the question into a single solution did not score well.

Candidates needed to consider the additional risks arising from each of the proposed changes, as well as practical methods of managing these risks.

#1 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7495

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#2 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding example 0.7383

12.2 Actuarial funding — example:

The setup:

  • Single premium: R10 000 (purchasing 10 000 units at R1 each)
  • Annual FMC: 5 (levied only on units physically held)
  • Discount rate for funding $(i)$: 4%
  • Policy term: 5 years
  • Age ($x$): 40 year old
  • Investment return $(g)$: 7%
  • Actuarial funding factor ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$): A multiplier that determines the required reserve based on the 4% and the probability of the contingent events (death or maturity)

----

Year 0: Inception

At the start, the insurer calculates the actuarially funded unit reserve instead of holding the full R10 000.

  • Funding factor ($A_{40:\overline{5|}}$): $0.8219$ (based on 4% discount over 5 years)
  • Reserve physically held: $$V_0 = R 10,000 * 0.8219 = R 8,219$$
  • Cashflow to non-unit fund: $R10,000 - R8,219$
  • This positive cashflow is used to pay for initial expenses like commission and underwriting.
  • The insurer is now missing $1,781$ units that it must buy back later.

#3 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor 0.7383

12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:

Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.

  • Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be

$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$

  • Where:
  • $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
  • $x$ is the entry age
  • $n$ is the policy term
  • Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.
#4 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7322

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#5 14. Guarantees and options 3. Mortality options What are the implications of offering a mortality option? 0.7183

3. Mortality options — What are the implications of offering a mortality option?:

Offering a mortality option such as the right to increase cover or renew a policy without further medical evidence:

  • Anti-selection: The primary risk is selection against the office, where policyholders in poor health are significantly more likely to exercise the option.
  • Financial cost: The cost is the difference between the standard premium charged and the higher premium that would have been charged under full underwriting. $$\{\text{proportion of lives exercising the option}\} \times \{\text{average health of lives exercising the option}\} $$
  • Higher Capital strain: reserving for mortality guarantees must account for both expected higher mortality of those exercising the option and the uncertainty regarding future take up rates.

F102_NOVEMBER_2025_Paper1_Q3

2025 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 3


A life insurance company sells a regular premium unit-linked endowment assurance policy with the following features:


  • The benefit payable on maturity is the value of the unit fund (if positive).

  • The benefit payable on death is the value of the unit fund (if positive), subject to a minimum guaranteed sum assured specified at inception by the policyholder.

  • The surrender value is equal to the bid value of units less a surrender penalty (if positive).

  • The policyholder may select from several local and overseas investment portfolios.

  • The only product charges are a risk charge and fund management charge, both of which are deducted monthly from the unit fund.

  • The policyholder can specify the monthly premium at inception, but it is subject to a minimum premium specific to each policy.

i. Outline briefly the main client needs that are met by this product.


ii. Explain briefly why the insurance company would specify minimum premiums.


iii. Outline briefly how the insurer would calculate an expropriation price of a unit.


iv. Describe 2 examples which demonstrate how the calculation of unit prices may affect equity

between different generations of policyholders. Assume there are no calculation errors.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 3


i. Main needs met:


  • The benefit on maturity allows the policyholder to save for a specific purpose ➢ The range of investment portfolios meet the need for diversification

  • The death benefit meets the need of providing for the policyholder's dependents or liabilities due on death (e.g. paying back a loan). ➢ As the policyholder can specify the sum assured, the product can be tailored to be more of a risk product (a relatively large sum assured, for a given premium) or a savings product (a relatively small sum assured, for a given premium). ➢ The death benefit is also a way of passing wealth to the next generation in a tax-efficient way

  • The surrender benefit could provide funds in the case of a financial emergency.

  • The charging structure is relatively simple and therefore easy to understand.

  • The policyholder can specify the premium and therefore meet the need of affordability. ➢ Premiums are also payable monthly, which again makes the product more affordable than a single premium product, for example.

  • As the product is unit-linked, the policyholder carries some risk (e.g. investment risk) which means this product is possibly more cost effective relative to a nonlinked version of the contract.

ii. Reasons for a minimum premium:


  • Each policy must contribute adequately to the company's expenses and profit. ➢ The minimum premium ensures that the fund management charge will be sufficient, on average over the duration of the policy, to adequately meet these expenses and profit contribution. ➢ There may be some cross-subsidies in this regard, with larger policies contributing relatively more than smaller policies.

  • The premium needs to be sufficient to meet the cost of cover. ➢ As the policyholder can select the sum assured, the minimum premium will need to be at least sufficient to meet the cost of cover.

  • Attracting a specific target market. ➢ Higher premiums should lead to a higher income/wealth client profile which may be the preferred target market for the insurer.

iii. Method:


  • The expropriation price is the price at which a unit would be cancelled and is determined as: ➢ The net asset value of the fund on a "bid basis"; ➢ Divided by the number of units existing at the time of calculation (before any units are cancelled).

  • The net asset value of the fund on a "bid basis" is calculated as: ➢ The market value of the assets held by the fund on a bid basis. ➢ Less the expenses that would be incurred in the sale. ➢ Plus the value of any current assets (e.g. cash on deposit). ➢ Less the value of any current liabilities (e.g. investments purchased but not yet settled). ➢ Plus any accrued income (e.g. interest income on deposits) net of any outgo (e.g. fund charges). ➢ Less any allowance for accrued tax, if applicable.

iv. Examples include:


  • The unit price includes accruals and the actual cashflows may be different to the accrual. ➢ For example, when an asset is sold, the actual capital gains tax (CGT) may be different to the accrual for CGT due to a change in the CGT rules. If the tax accrual was understated (overstated), then policyholders who previously sold (bought) units, would have benefitted from the actual tax being different to the accrual relative to the current (previous) generation of policyholders.

#3 1. Life insurance contracts 1.4 Endowment Assurances - Structures ASSA/F102 Life Insurance Principles/Summary/1. Life insurance contracts/1.1 Endowment assurances - Structures 0.7422

1.4 Endowment Assurances - Structures — ASSA/F102 Life Insurance Principles/Summary/1. Life insurance contracts/1.1 Endowment assurances - Structures:

Without-profits:

  • Offers a guaranteed amount of money at the end of the term or upon earlier death in exchange for single or regular premiums

With-profits (Participating):

  • The initial sum assured is enhanced by the declaration of bonuses (reversionary, special or terminal). Policyholders expect better returns than without-profits version, though premiums are typically higher.

Unit-linked:

  • Premiums are invested in pooled funds, and the maturity benefit depends on the performance of underlying assets and the level of charges levied by the insurer. Highly versatile, allowing policyholders to choose between protection-heavy or savings-heavy designs therefore can be used to meet different needs.
#4 1. Life insurance contracts 4.1.2 Unit-linked contracts - Customer needs Customer needs 0.7407

4.1.2 Unit-linked contracts - Customer needs — Customer needs:

  • Affordability: Consumers obtain a higher expected level of benefit for a given premium or pay a lower expected premium for a given benefit compared to non-linked versions.
  • Flexibility is build into the design:
  • Flexibility of Investment choice: Consumers can choose from a range of investment funds that align with their risk appetite and objectives.
  • Flexibility of Premium structure & frequency: Customers can vary premiums or even miss premium payments for ad-hoc periods without lapsing or being made paid up immediately.
  • Flexibility in the type & levels of cover: Policyholders can also select and change the desired mix or savings and protection as their life circumstances evolve.
  • Inflation protection: Consumers can choose investments in real assets like equities and property which can provide real returns and protect against the erosion of benefits by inflation.
  • Savings: They can be used as vehicles for retirement savings or as a means to repay the capital on interest only-loans.
  • Wealth transfer: the can be used to transfer wealth to the next generation (similar to endowments).
  • Group benefits: employers utilize unit-linked group contracts to provide retirement and death-in-service benefits to employees.
#5 13. Alterations 3. Methods of calculation example 0.7403

3. Methods of calculation — example:

For a whole life assurance at duration $t$, the equation of value is:


$$(PUSA)_t \cdot A_{x+t} + e \cdot \ddot{a}_{x+t} + f \cdot A_{x+t} = (SV)_t$$


Components


  • $(PUSA)_t$: The new, reduced paid-up sum assured.
  • $(SV)_t$: The surrender value (or prospective reserve) at the time of alteration.
  • $A_{x+t}$: The present value of 1 payable on death at the attained age.
  • $e$: Level annual renewal administration expenses (note that renewal commission is removed since no further premiums are paid).
  • $\ddot{a}_{x+t}$: The present value of a life annuity of 1 per annum.
  • $f$: The cost of processing the final claim.

If a specific administrative alteration expense ($C$) is charged, it is typically subtracted from the value before alteration.

F102_NOVEMBER_2025_Paper1_Q4

2025 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 4


An insurer sells regular premium conventional with-profits 10-year endowment assurances. Bonuses are added using the 'additions to benefits' method. The reserves are calculated using a gross premium valuation method.

i. Describe 3 distinct types of data checks, with examples for each, that could be done on the

policy data prior to the valuation.


ii. Describe how the reserves for the portfolio would be calculated using cashflow projections.


Immediately following the valuation, the insurer experiences a financial market crash characterised by a sudden fall in equity prices and a reduction in interest rates.

iii. Explain the impact this could have on the insurer's solvency (assets less liabilities).


iv. Suggest possible actions the insurer could take to reduce the impact of the crash on its solvency.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 4


i. Policy data checks:


  • Data reconciliation checks whereby the current data is checked against the previous data as follows: ➢ Data at previous investigation + business come onto the books - business gone off the books = data at current investigation. ➢ This can be done for appropriate groups of contracts, such as by year of entry. ➢ For example, this check can be done for:

  • the number of contracts,

  • basic sum assured,

  • premiums, or

  • amount of attaching bonuses.

  • Consistency checks whereby metrics per appropriate group are sensible and consistent with previous, for example: ➢ Averages of asset shares, sums assured, reversionary bonuses and premiums ➢ Ratios of asset shares and sums assured to premiums ➢ Ratios of reversionary bonuses to sums assured.

  • Consistency of data between different sources, for example: ➢ The movements data (business coming on and going off during the period) can be checked against appropriate accounting data (specifically premiums and benefit payments). ➢ Investment data from fund managers (e.g. investment income and assets) can be checked against accounting data. ➢ Cashflows (premiums less claims and expenses) received by fund managers can be checked against accounting data.

  • Unusual values and spot checks, for example: ➢ Bonuses accrued should not exceed plausible levels based on historical declared rates ➢ Terms only 10 years ➢ No zeroes or missing values ➢ Ages at entry and start dates within expected ranges ➢ A paid-up policy should have a reduced sum assured and zero premium ➢ Only in-force policies

ii. Reserves valued using a cashflow projection:


  • Project the expected cashflows in each future year, including: ➢ Premiums ➢ Claims ➢ Expenses including ongoing commission (if any)

  • Future new business is excluded.

  • This is done per policy, or using appropriate grouped model points.

  • The starting benefit amount is the basic sum assured plus all vesting reversionary bonuses to date.

  • Allowance is made for expected future reversionary bonuses consistent with the expected investment returns on the assets backing the portfolio, ➢ as well as other considerations, such as company bonus philosophy and policyholder reasonable expectations.

  • Allow for all guarantees if any, such as minimum surrender or maturity values.

  • The expected future net outgo (claims + expenses - premiums) at each future time period is discounted to the present.

iii. Impact on solvency:


  • The market value of equities will fall whereas the market value of bonds will rise.

  • The overall impact will depend on the mix of assets held, which will depend on the maturity of the book and the split between terminal and reversionary bonuses.

  • The reserves will increase due to the lower interest rates, all else being equal.

  • The net effect may be a deterioration of the insurer's solvency position.

iv. Possible mitigating actions include:


  • The insurer could apply temporary market value adjustments to surrender values.

  • Terminal bonuses could be reduced, or removed entirely, if the impact of the crash is particularly severe.

  • Depending on the outlook for recovery, future bonus rate assumptions could be reduced or deferred, reducing reserves.

  • Policyholders' reasonable expectations must be considered when changing bonus structures.

  • It might be possible, although likely costly, to adjust the investment portfolio temporarily to limit further potential losses (including the use of derivatives).

  • If particularly severe, management may consider reducing non-essential expenses.

  • If warranted, basis changes may be considered to weaken the basis and reduce reserves.

  • If solvency is at risk, capital raising exercises may be considered, including use of financial reinsurance.

  • The insurer could close to new business temporarily, thereby removing new business strain and avoiding a further deterioration in solvency in the short term. However, this will reduce profitability in the longer term.

(i) and (ii) were primarily bookwork, while weaker candidates tended to provide too few points

or presented their answers in a poorly structured manner.

For part (ii), many students focused excessively on describing valuation bases and margins rather than identifying the key cashflows. A common omission was the failure to account for bonuses within the model. Several students also incorrectly treated reserves as PV of inflows minus PV of outflows, rather than the correct formulation of PV of outgo minus PV of inflow.

Part (iii) was generally poorly answered, with many responses being overly prescriptive.

Statements suggesting that a particular outcome "will" occur were not credited--candidates were expected to discuss likelihoods rather than certainties. Many students also overlooked bonds in their explanations, and some made the fundamental error of failing to note that a decrease in interest rates increases present values.

Part (iv) was also weakly answered. Many candidates did not produce enough distinct points or repeated the same ideas. Additionally, several suggestions were made without consideration of their implications--for example, changes to investment strategy may carry significant cost.

9. Cost of capital approach — The Three-Step Calculation Process:

1. Project Required Capital: The insurer projects the future capital required to be held $(C_t​)$ for each period during the "run-off" of the business. (this is the SCR)

2. Apply Cost of Capital Rate: These projected capital amounts are multiplied by a cost of capital rate (e.g., 6% per annum).

3. Discount to Present Value: The resulting annual costs are discounted back to the valuation date using risk-free (market-consistent) interest rates to produce the total risk margin. $$\text{Risk margin} = \displaystyle{\sum_t \dfrac{k_tC_t}{(1 + r_t)^t}}$$

#3 16. Reinsurance 3.2 Retention limits Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve 0.7425

3.2 Retention limits — Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve:

In this approach, insurers aim to minimize the total cost of two components:

  • the cost of obtaining reinsurance and
  • the cost of financing a mortality fluctuations reserve.

The process follows these steps:

1. Set a risk criterion: such as a maximum 1% probability that net losses will exceed a specific amount e.g. 25m

2. Model total costs: for different retention limits, the insurer stochastically models the expected net loss by varying the mortality rates. As the retention limit increases, the cost of reinsurance decreases, but the size of the required fluctuations reserve (and its associated financing cost) increases.

3. Calculate the financing cost: The cost of the reserve ($M$) is calculated as $M \times (j - i)$, where $j$ is the required rate of return on the company's capital and $i$ is the actual investment return earned on the reserve's assets.

4. Optimize: The insurer identifies the specific retention limit where the combined cost of the reserve and reinsurance is lowest while still satisfying the ruin probability target.

  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#5 14. Guarantees and options 2. Valuing an investment guarantee How are investment guarantees valued using stochastic simulation? 0.7388

2. Valuing an investment guarantee — How are investment guarantees valued using stochastic simulation?:

  • Identify the underlying assets
  • Project asset values: use a stochastic model to simulate future asset prices or returns based on a chosen probability distribution (e.g. mean and variance) for the underlying assets
  • Model Policyholder behaviour: Incorporate assumptions about when policyholders are likely to exercise the option (when it is in the money).
  • Identify shortfalls: In each simulation, compare the projected fund value against the guaranteed amount. If the fund is lower, the difference is the cost of the guarantee for that specific scenario. For paths where the fund value is above the guarantee, the cost is recorded as zero.
  • Discounting: Discount the cost of each individual path back to the valuation date e.g. using the risk-free rate under market consistent frameworks
  • Expected cost: Take the average of the simulated costs across all runs, which provides the expected present value for the guarantee,

Question

QUESTION 5


A large life insurance company sells accumulating with-profits and unit-linked products.

i. Compare and contrast the product features of an accumulating with-profits and a unit-linked

product.


The company is about to undertake the supervisory valuation for its unit-linked contracts.

ii. Outline how you would set the main assumptions for calculating the liabilities on a best estimate

basis, and for each assumption explain the direction of a suitable margin for prudence.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 5


i. Product features of an accumulating with-profits and a unit-linked product:


  • Both an accumulating with-profits and unit-linked product have an explicit link between the premiums/contributions to date and the benefit payable to the policyholder.

  • In the case of a unit-linked policy, the policyholders' contributions are invested into the chosen underlying fund and the policyholders fund value moves in line with the performance of the underlying fund. ➢ Fixed and fund-related charges may be deducted from the policyholder's fund and returns for calculating unit price may be net of asset management costs.

  • For accumulating with-profits, the policyholder's premiums/contributions are accumulated over-time and bonuses are added to the fund value based on the bonuses declared by the insurer. ➢ Fixed and fund-related charges may be deducted from the policyholder's fund, and bonuses declared may be net of some costs (e.g. asset management).

  • Bonuses declared may depend on the insurer's discretion or can be based on a pre-determined formula.

  • While accumulating with-profit bonuses are generally smoothed over time to provide stable growth, reflecting past investment performance of the with-profit fund, they may also be influenced by historical bonuses declared and future expected investment return.

  • Special once-off bonuses can be applicable on the accumulating with-profits policies, particularly where there are materially higher returns which are not expected to repeat.

  • For both products, surrender values are often stipulated as a function of the fund balance less surrender penalties.

  • However, in the accumulating with-profits instance, market value adjustors might be applied in some circumstances in order to prevent anti selection.

ii. Setting assumptions:


  • The company may start from prior experience investigations used for pricing or reserving.

  • The company should consider the requirements of the regulator and any professional guidance.

  • The assumptions should not be arbitrarily different from the previous valuation assumptions, and assumption changes should be suitably supported and documented and their impact disclosed.

  • Unit fund growth: ➢ Determine an expected growth rate by asset class as a risk-free rate, probably based on government bonds of suitable term, plus a suitable risk premium that varies by asset class.

  • The risk premiums could be based on past investment returns or a CAPM model for risky assets. ➢ The overall risk premium and expected growth rate is based on an expected split of unit funds by asset class based on the investment mandate of the fund. ➢ Prudence would require a lower unit growth rate.

  • Demographic assumptions: ➢ Use recent own demographic experience based on investigations and adjusted for known or expected future changes. ➢ For surrenders (full or partial), a prudent assumption will likely be higher than best estimate given that it will reduce the future fund charges in excess of expenses and cost of benefits (assuming this excess is positive). ➢ The mortality assumption is not such a key assumption given that the additional death benefit is small and the mortality rates are likely to be low. May use standard mortality tables adjusted for experience. ➢ A higher than best estimate assumption will be prudent.

  • Expenses: ➢ Use recent expense investigation i.e. the expenses allocated to this product. ➢ Need to allow for expected in force volumes to capture the spread of overhead. ➢ A higher than best estimate expense assumption is prudent.

➢ Prudent to assume higher expense inflation and lower consumer prices inflation (for the charges).


  • Discount rate/valuation interest rate: ➢ Likely to consider yields on the assets backing the non-unit reserve. Likely to use a risk-free rate based on government bonds or cash. ➢ A lower rate is more prudent in the event of positive reserves. Examiner's Comments Candidates performed quite well on the question. Part (i) was largely bookwork and candidates were able to compare the two products appropriately. Part (ii) was generally well answered and candidates who did better were able to discuss a variety of assumptions and describe the margins required in order for it to be a prudent valuation.

#3 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7476

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#4 6. Unit pricing and actuarial funding 12.2 Actuarial funding The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor 0.7362

12.2 Actuarial funding — The mechanism - Actuarial funding factor:

Instead of being "fully funded", where assets held exactly match the bid value of allocated units, the company holds the actuarial present value of the unit fund. This approach is possible because the unit fund is a contingent liability, it is only required when events like death or survival to maturity occur.

  • Funding factor: The normal fund value is multiplied by an actuarial funding factor, typically an endowment assurance function ($A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}}$), to determine the required reserve. So the present value of a unit-linked endowment assurance at policy duration $t$ allowing for the contingency of death would be

$$ (UF)_t(A_{x+t:\overline{n-t|}})$$

  • Where:
  • $(UF)_t$ is the fully funded value of the unit fund at policy duration $t$
  • $x$ is the entry age
  • $n$ is the policy term
  • Discount rate: The interest rate used in this calculation is usually set to less than annual fund management charge the company wishes to pre-fund. To allow for some of the FMC to cover renewal expenses.
#5 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.2 Addition to benefits - accumulating with profits Unitised with-profits 0.7343

9.1.2 Addition to benefits - accumulating with profits — Unitised with-profits:

If the contract is structured as unitised with-profits, the regular bonuses are delivered in one of two ways:

  • Constant unit price: the price of a unit remains fixed and the insurer allocates additional units to each contract (usually annually) at the bonus declarations. There could be a minimum bonus declaration of zero or some positive percentage.
  • Variable unit price: The insurer changes the price of the units (usually on a daily basis). The increase is made up of a guaranteed part (possibly zero) and a bonus part.

F102_NOVEMBER_2025_Paper1_Q6

2025 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 6


An insurer in a developing country has been selling without-profits immediate annuities for a number of years. Annuitants can choose between level annuity payments and payments which increase annually at a fixed rate.

The insurer is considering adding a with-profits immediate annuity to its current offering. The payments may be increased by annual bonuses declared using an "additions to benefits" approach. The intention is for annuity increases to be at least equal to local Consumer Price Inflation (CPI).

i. Explain possible reasons for the company considering offering the new product.


ii. Discuss the types of investments that the company might use for matching the liabilities of the

new product.


The insurer instead decides to offer a without-profits immediate annuity that is guaranteed to increase at CPI for life.

iii. Explain the 2 key risks to the insurer of offering this product.


The insurer also sells unit-linked endowment assurances with guaranteed annuity options (GAOs) that are purchased at policy inception and can be exercised at maturity. The insurer wishes to extend its GAO offering to include the option to effect the new CPI-linked without-profits immediate annuity at maturity.

iv. Explain how the insurer could use market option-pricing techniques to estimate the expected

cost of this GAO.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 6


i. Reasons for the new product:


  • Competitive reasons: other insurers offer this product, or if they don't this may provide a competitive advantage - the insurer hopes to increase its overall sales.

  • Enhance its brand - especially if no/few other insurers offer this product, customers may view the insurer as being innovative and a leader in the industry.

  • Meeting customer needs better - increasing uncertainty about future inflation is increasing customer needs for products that provide some protection against higher inflation.

  • Regulatory changes might now be creating a market (or bigger market) for this product - e.g. inclusion as a default product for pension schemes.

  • Insufficient suitable assets in the market (i.e. fixed-interest bonds of adequate term) for matching without-profits liabilities - while the new product also has fixed guarantees they should be lower.

  • Capital efficiency - fewer guarantees should require lower capital requirements, thus freeing up capital for other purposes. ➢ The product may lead to higher return on capital for shareholders - i.e. higher profitability.

ii. Suitable investments:


  • The guaranteed benefits (comprising initial income plus declared increases) are fixed in monetary terms and hence: ➢ This may be best matched by government fixed interest bonds of suitable term. ➢ The insurer may invest in high-quality corporate bonds to enhance its returns, however, these carry default loss risk.

  • Discretionary benefits (comprising future increases) are real in nature (and not index-linked) and hence best matched by: ➢ Index linked bonds will provide the minimum real return being targeted if they are held to maturity. ➢ Equity and property can be expected to provide positive real returns over longer time periods, although they will be associated with volatility over shorter periods.

  • Expenses are mostly staff and IT-related and real in nature. ➢ This will be best matched by a combination of equity, property and index linked bonds.

  • Cash would be held as working capital to meet short-term obligations.

  • The insurer is likely to prefer direct investment, however this may be impractical for some types of assets such as property and offshore investment, in which case an indirect form of investment may be used.

iii. Key risks:


  • Mortality risk - risk of mortality being lighter than expected: ➢ As this is a new product, the annuitant profile may differ from existing products. ➢ The scope for mortality improvements in a developing country may be difficult to quantify.

  • Investment risk - risk of returns being lower than required: ➢ The insurer may not be able to match the CPI-linked increase for life. ➢ As this is a developing country, there may not be sufficient stock of indexlinked bonds of varying terms available in the local market. ➢ Default on ILBs will leave the insurer with insufficient assets to meet liabilities. ➢ Investment risk is exacerbated if mortality is lighter than expected as this may require re-investment at unknown future terms.

iv. Market option pricing techniques:


  • Market prices of options replicating the guarantee are required.

➢ Call option of suitable term (reflecting endowment term) on an index-linked bond (of duration reflecting expected lifespan at GAO exercise date) with strike being equal to the ILB price corresponding to the guaranteed real interest rate.


  • If market prices are not available estimates may be available from market participants.

F102_NOVEMBER_2025_Paper1_Q7

2025 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 7


i. List 8 factors to be considered by an insurer in setting its reinsurance retention limit.


Gondor Life is a direct writer that has insured the group income protection (IP) cover for a mediumsized mining company for the last three years. The mining company has made group IP cover compulsory for all its employees, and the benefit levels are determined by a fixed formula related to salary.

Gondor has approached Rivendell Re to quote a rate on the mining company's group IP scheme.

Rivendell Re will also set a free cover limit (FCL).

ii. Explain why Rivendell Re might quote better terms for this group scheme compared to a book

of individual life IP policies.


The pricing actuary at Rivendell Re has decided to use a claim inception and disability annuity approach to price this business.

iii. Explain the likely reasons for this choice.


**

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 7


i. Factors to consider include:


  • Average benefit level for the product and the expected distribution of the benefit.

  • Company's insurance risk appetite.

  • Level of the company's free assets and the importance attached to the stability of its free asset ratio.

  • Terms on which reinsurance can be obtained and the dependence of such terms on the retention limit.

  • Level of familiarity of the company with underwriting the type of business involved.

  • Company's expertise in pricing such a product vis-à-vis the reinsurer's expertise.

  • Any regulatory requirements with regards to minimum / maximum level of session.

  • Effect on the company's regulatory capital requirements of increasing or reducing the retention limit.

  • Existence of a profit-sharing arrangement in the reinsurance treaty.

  • Company's retention on its other products.

  • Nature of any future increases in sum assured.

ii. Reasons:


  • Group schemes are typically repriced annually based on the most recent claims experience. This short feedback loop allows the reinsurer to adjust premiums quickly in response to emerging trends, reducing the long-term risk of pricing inadequacy. In contrast, individual IP policies often involve long-term guarantees, increasing pricing risk.

  • Gondor Life can request quotes from multiple reinsurers each year. This competitive dynamic incentivises Rivendell Re to offer more attractive terms to retain the business, especially if the experience is favourable.

  • The application of an FCL reduces the number of medically underwritten lives referred to the reinsurer. This lowers administrative costs and simplifies risk acceptance processes, which can be reflected in more competitive pricing.

  • The group scheme likely comprises a sufficiently large number of members with similar risk characteristics--such as occupation (mining industry) and geographic location. This homogeneity allows for more accurate pricing through risk pooling.

  • Compulsory membership ensures that both good risks and bad risks are gained, which reduces or eliminates anti-selection risk. This allows for better cross subsidising of risk and therefore will impact the actual claims costs.

  • Benefits are determined by a fixed formula linked to salary, which prevents antiselection through over- or under-insurance. This design ensures that benefit levels are proportionate to earnings, aligning incentives and reducing moral hazard.

  • With three years of claims experience available, Rivendell Re can perform a more informed actuarial analysis. This enhances pricing accuracy and may justify more favourable terms if the experience has been stable or better than expected.

iii. Reasons:


  • Group schemes often lack detailed member-level data. In this case, Gondor Life is unlikely to provide: ➢ Full policy histories or transitions between health states. ➢ Information on lives entering or exiting claim during the deferred period. ➢ Recovery data or transitions back to premium-paying status. ➢ The available data is likely limited to basic demographic data (e.g., sex, date of birth, salary, NRA) and current claim information.

  • Given the data constraints, a multi-state model would be impractical due to insufficient granularity of data.

  • It focuses on estimating the expected cost of claims incepting in a given year, which aligns with the annual repricing cycle typical of group schemes.

  • It simplifies the modelling process by separating the estimation of claim incidence rates from the expected duration and cost of claims via a disabled life annuity factor.

  • For group schemes, members may enter and exit the scheme regularly as they change employers meaning that there may be even less information available about different states a member may be in over time.

  • It is efficient to implement, especially when data is sparse or aggregated.

  • It is flexible, allowing for adjustments based on emerging experience or changes in benefit design.

may be more favourable than for individual IP policies. Instead, weaker answers drifted into generic comments about competitiveness or reinsurer behaviour, without contrasting group versus individual business.

Part (iii) was the weakest-scoring part of the question. A large proportion of candidates failed to identify the key rationale: namely, that the alternative to the chosen pricing approach would typically be a multi-state model, and that such a model is inappropriate or impractical given the limited, aggregate nature of group scheme data. Many answers simply described features of inception/disability annuity pricing without explaining why this method was chosen over the multi-state alternative.

#2 16. Reinsurance 3.2 Retention limits Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve 0.7521

3.2 Retention limits — Stochastic simulation – reinsurance with fluctuations reserve:

In this approach, insurers aim to minimize the total cost of two components:

  • the cost of obtaining reinsurance and
  • the cost of financing a mortality fluctuations reserve.

The process follows these steps:

1. Set a risk criterion: such as a maximum 1% probability that net losses will exceed a specific amount e.g. 25m

2. Model total costs: for different retention limits, the insurer stochastically models the expected net loss by varying the mortality rates. As the retention limit increases, the cost of reinsurance decreases, but the size of the required fluctuations reserve (and its associated financing cost) increases.

3. Calculate the financing cost: The cost of the reserve ($M$) is calculated as $M \times (j - i)$, where $j$ is the required rate of return on the company's capital and $i$ is the actual investment return earned on the reserve's assets.

4. Optimize: The insurer identifies the specific retention limit where the combined cost of the reserve and reinsurance is lowest while still satisfying the ruin probability target.

#3 16. Reinsurance 3. Considerations before reinsuring What are the considerations before reinsuring? 0.7513

3. Considerations before reinsuring — What are the considerations before reinsuring?:

Before deciding whether and how to reinsure, an insurer evaluates several strategic and financial factors:

  • Type of reinsurance: The type of reinsurance (whether it is OTR, Risk premiums or excess of loss or Fin Re), will depend will depend on:
  • The reason the insurance company is using reinsurance
  • The reinsurance cost
  • The type of insurance business for which the reinsurance is to be arranged
  • Cost of Reinsurance: Because reinsurers include their own profit margins and expenses, which reduce the insurer's absolute profit level. the insurer must balance security versus return. It must determine if the reduction in volatility justifies the reduced expected return.
  • Retention Limits must be set by considering the company's risk appetite, its level of free assets, and the distribution of sum assured across its portfolio. A company with higher free assets can generally afford a higher retention limit.
  • Counterparty (Credit) Risk: The insurer retains liability according to the contract, to pay benefits even if the reinsurer cannot meet claim payments (becomes insolvent)
  • Alternatives, such as holding a mortality fluctuation reserve may be more cost-effective than purchasing reinsurance.
  • Legal Risks: Finally the company should consider legal risk by ensuring treaties are legally watertight.
#4 7. Modelling 13.5 Model uses Pricing 0.7258

13.5 Model uses — Pricing:

The model is used to determine a premium, or charging structure for a new or existing product that will meet a life insurance company's profit requirement.

1. Model point selection: select model points that represent the expected new business mix

2. Cashflow projection: for each time point, the model projects

  • withdrawal death and maturity benefits
  • premiums, investment income, claims, expenses, tax)
  • reserving and solvency requirements ((increases or releases of reserves)
  • Allow for interaction between variables (e.g. investment return and inflation, investment returns and bonus rates)

3. Assumptions: for expected future experience:

  • mortality withdrawal and expenses

4. Consistency: All assumptions should be consistent with each other and allow for interactions between variables (e.g. investment return and expense inflation assumption and surrender rates could be linked to the economic scenario)

5. Time period: Month/annual

6. The net cashflow will be the net non-unit cashflow less the increase in the non-unit reserve

7. Discounting: the resulting net cashflows are discounted back to the inception date using a risk discount rate (RDR).

8. Profit criteria: the model produces a Profit signature, which is then summarized into a single profit criterion.

  • NPV: sum of discounted profit often as a percentage of discounted premiums (market share) or initial commission (effort)
  • IRR: the discount rate at which the NPV is zero. This may not always exist or may be more than one solution if the net cashflows change signs more than once.
  • DPP: Discounted Payback Period, is suitable for long term contracts where the initial capital layout is large.

9. Capital requirements: by scaling up the model points into a full model office. The insurer can assess whether it has sufficient capital (either on a regulatory or economic capital basis) to finance the expected volumes of sales (New Business Strain). If not, it may reconfigure the design of the product so as to reduce the capital requirement.

10. Marketability: if the modelled premium is too high to be competitive, the model can be used to test changes in product features, distribution channels or profit targets to improve marketability and/or reduce risk or to make a decision on whether to proceed with the product or not..

11. Sensitivity analysis: varying parameter values (like mortality, interest rates or lapses) to see how profit is affected. This helps the actuary to assess the need for additional prudential margins in the assumptions to guard against adverse future experience.

#5 3. Asset shares and profit distribution 9.1.3 Revalorisation (conflict 2026-04-07-05-57-05) Distributed Profit (Pt​) 0.7255

9.1.3 Revalorisation (conflict 2026-04-07-05-57-05) — Distributed Profit (Pt​):

In many jurisdictions, if $i_t​<g$, the revalorisation rate $r_t$​ is simply 0, but the insurer must still credit the guarantee $g$. This creates the "shortfall risk", where the insurer's equity must fund the gap.

F102_NOVEMBER_2025_Paper1_Q8

2025 · NOVEMBER
Question

QUESTION 8


A recently established life insurance company is building its portfolio of conventional without-profits term assurance policies designed to appeal to younger, tech-savvy customers. The basis of its offering is that after initial acceptance, policyholders may adjust their sums assured and premiums, without underwriting at specified life events such as marriage, purchasing a car or a home or the birth of a child.

Interaction with the company is through a mobile phone application (app) where, in addition to doing policy administration, the policyholders are encouraged to disclose personal information that may trigger benefit increase events. The company uses this information to offer benefit increases which are easily accepted and verified with minimal paperwork. Premiums are adjusted as required and policyholders are notified of their new premiums or benefits via the app.

i. Outline briefly the main experience items that the company should monitor regularly, and

suggest reasons for why these items should be monitored.


Three years after launching the product the company decides to conduct an analysis of its expense experience.

ii. Describe how the company could go about conducting such an experience analysis.


Total

Examiner's Solution

QUESTION 8


i. Experience to monitor:

New business


  • Monitor number of policies as well as the premiums and/or benefits.

  • Since this is a recently established company, it will be important to achieve the sales targets. Lapses

  • Monitor the lapses in terms of premiums and/or benefits.

  • Higher than expected lapses will affect the insurer's revenues and profits.

  • This may also indicate that there are other problems that need investigation e.g. the sales process or uncompetitive premiums. Engagement

  • Monitor the data (if any) provided by each policyholder for benefit increase triggers. ➢ Or social media profile sharing from which such information might be gathered. ➢ Or how often the policyholder interacts with the app.

  • This is needed to measure the success of the mobile phone app as a general means for interacting.

  • The success of the take-up offer in particular depends on policyholders disclosing the necessary information. Take-up rates on offers made

  • The percentage of offers taken up. ➢ Split by type and also the percentage of the total additional benefit take up.

Mortality experience


  • Compare actual vs expected for the entire portfolio and for benefit increases separately.

  • As this is still likely to be a small portfolio, it may be difficult to understand the effect of random variation.

  • Benefit increases should ideally be split by type and also the percentage of the total additional benefit take up. ➢ May be difficult to split into smaller categories until more policies are available to ensure credibility of each category.

  • May provide early indications of anti-selection.

  • May provide early indication of changes required to offer assumptions and pricing. Expenses

  • Monitor against pricing assumptions and expense loadings.

  • As well as against business plans.

  • This is important for maintaining control over expenses based on the size of the book. ➢ Especially if the book is not growing according to the business plan.

ii. Conducting an expense analysis:


  • Collect and summarise expenses for the last three years: salaries and related costs, property costs, computer costs, investment costs, marketing costs and commission.

  • Start by classifying the company's non-commission expenses by department/function into: ➢ new business (or initial) expenses; ➢ existing business (or renewal) expenses; ➢ termination expenses; and ➢ investment expenses.

  • Each of the first three can be further split according to whether the expense is proportional to: ➢ the number of policies written or in-force; ➢ the premiums written or in force; or ➢ the sum assured written or in force.

  • This creates a series of 'cells' for dividing expenses into.

  • Since there are only term assurance policies expenses do not have to be split between products.

  • Administration costs, overheads and systems running costs could be split by costs associated with new business and costs associated with in-force business. ➢ Possibly proportional to the sum assured (or premium) for new business and the in-force business.

➢ It is unlikely to be a significant expense in this case as term assurance policies do not build-up large reserves and it is still early in the policy / company lifetime.


  • Commission is generally known and can be excluded from the expense analysis and loaded explicitly.

  • System development costs can be amortised over the expected lifetime of the system.

  • The per policy costs can then be determined as: ➢ Initial expenses allocated divided by the amount of new business; ➢ Renewal expenses allocated divided by the amount of existing business; and ➢ Termination expenses divided by the number of terminations. Examiner's Comments In part (i) there were many points that could be made on monitoring that all insurance companies would want to do. Candidates received limited credit for generic points. The better solutions addressed the specific issues in the question i.e. a new company with limited experience, potentially random (good or bad) claims experience and a need to understand if their business/product is going to be successful. Part (ii) is a standard question, asked often, with small changes in application. While there were some excellent solutions, the solutions were generally disappointing. There was also some evidence of time pressure for this last question, indicating poor exam planning and/or discipline.

#1 4. External environment 10. The external environment Condensed exam-style answer 0.7492

10. The external environment — Condensed exam-style answer:

The insurer should consider the expected volume and mix of new business, since low volumes may not justify fixed development and administration costs, while rapid growth may create new business strain and solvency pressure. The mix of business by age, benefit level, policy duration, distribution channel and underwriting class will affect the risk profile, expenses, reserves and capital needs.


The insurer should assess customer demand and affordability in the target market. Policyholders must understand the product and its limitations, otherwise there is a risk of poor take-up, complaints, policyholder dissatisfaction and regulatory intervention.


The distribution channel should be considered, including the training and incentives of distributors. Commission structures may encourage mis-selling, policy churning or poor-quality business if they reward sales volume rather than persistency or customer outcomes.


The insurer should consider competition in the market, including competition on price, benefits, underwriting, claims service and distribution access. Competitive pressure may reduce margins or lead to higher lapses if better products become available.


Economic conditions are relevant because inflation, interest rates, investment returns, unemployment and disposable income affect affordability, persistency, claims costs, expenses, reserves and profitability.


Legal, regulatory and tax developments should also be considered. Changes in solvency requirements, disclosure rules, commission regulation, tax treatment or consumer protection laws could affect product design, demand, profitability and capital requirements.


The insurer should consider expense risk and operational capability. Actual expenses, claims handling costs, system costs and compliance costs may exceed those assumed in pricing, especially where premiums or charges are guaranteed.


Finally, the insurer should consider claims experience, policyholder behaviour, reinsurance availability, capital requirements and reputational risk, as all of these may affect the profitability and sustainability of the business.

#3 19. Further risk management 2. Policy retention How can an insurer monitor and improve persistency rates? 0.7237

2. Policy retention — How can an insurer monitor and improve persistency rates?:

  • Monitor persistency rates by
  • distribution channel and
  • by the salesperson/broker concerned
  • updating pricing and valuation assumptions if lapse experience changes
  • Align sales incentives with persistency through:
  • Lower initial commissions and higher renewal commission
  • Clawing back initial commission on lapse
  • Financial underwriting to ensure affordability
  • Identify systematic reasons:
  • Customer relationship
  • Reliable Payment methods
  • Policy design addresses customer needs
  • Professional training of sales staff reduces the incentive to over-sell
  • Product design and flexibility
  • Premium holidays: allow policyholders to skip premiums for a time without the policy lapsing during financial hardship
  • Linked-claim periods: See Income Protection (IP) contracts - Features
  • Capping premium increases: For reviewable products, capping annual can reduce lapses and prevent selective withdrawal
  • Fair alteration terms: to prevent lapse and re-entry
  • Surrender penalties: to reduce investment selection against the company
  • training sales staff
  • building brand and reputation

#5 4. External environment 10.1 Consumer propensity To buy or not to buy? 0.7099

10.1 Consumer propensity — To buy or not to buy?:

  • Lack of awareness: Many consumers are simply unaware that they need a life insurance product until its too late, or they operate under the belief that negative events won't happen to them.
  • Information imbalance: Insurers possess full information regarding charges and competitiveness, while consumers have very little.
  • Usefulness of benefits: in the long run a life insurer will run a risk to profit if it does not sell product with useful benefits to consumers
  • Need for education: consumers need to be educated and informed about the benefits of life insurance and the company's products
